t2d.title: Type 2 diabetes and prediabetes
summary: There is no single right diet for type 2 diabetes. Mediterranean-style, low-carbohydrate, plant-based, and DASH patterns all have evidence. The one you can keep is the one that works.

Carbohydrate is the main lever for blood sugar. Watch how much you eat and where it comes from: fill half the plate with non-starchy vegetables, choose whole grains and beans over refined grains, and cut added sugar.
Skip sugar-sweetened drinks. This is the firmest food rule in the module.
If you carry extra weight, losing 5 to 7 percent of your body weight improves blood sugar and heart risk. More than 10 percent can put type 2 diabetes into remission.
Aim for at least 14 g of fiber per 1,000 calories, keep sodium under 2,300 mg a day, and keep alcohol moderate at most.
If you take insulin, a sulfonylurea, or a GLP-1 medication, your clinician sets the plan. The app supports that plan; it never sets those targets.

sections.heading: What this condition is
paragraphs: Type 2 diabetes is a condition in which the body no longer keeps blood glucose (blood sugar) in the normal range. Prediabetes means glucose is above normal but not yet in the diabetes range. Both respond to how you eat, how much you move, and body weight. For prediabetes, the Diabetes Prevention Program, a large randomized trial published in NEJM in 2002 with 10 and 15 year follow-ups, showed that lifestyle change lowers the chance of progressing to diabetes.

sections.heading: What the evidence says
paragraphs: The evidence rating for this module is STRONG. It rests on a major society guideline, the American Diabetes Association Standards of Care in Diabetes 2026 (Section 5 covers nutrition), the ADA nutrition therapy consensus report (Evert et al., 2019), the Diabetes Prevention Program randomized trial and its long-term follow-ups, and the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics evidence-based practice guideline for diabetes.

The ADA does not name one ideal split of carbohydrate, fat, and protein. It endorses several eating patterns with evidence behind them: Mediterranean-style, low-carbohydrate, plant-based, and DASH. The 2026 Standards added patient-facing resources for Mediterranean-style and low-carb patterns, especially for prevention. Monitoring carbohydrate intake is the primary strategy for glycemic control, and the Diabetes Plate method remains the ADA's default teaching tool.

Weight matters when someone has overweight or obesity. A 5 to 7 percent loss improves glycemia and cardiometabolic risk, and a loss over 10 percent can produce remission. The ADA frames calorie restriction as individualized, not universal.

sections.heading: What to eat more of
paragraphs: Non-starchy vegetables: leafy greens, broccoli, cauliflower, peppers, green beans, tomatoes, cucumbers, zucchini. These fill half the plate in the Diabetes Plate method.

Whole foods over highly processed ones. Whole grains (oats, brown rice, barley, whole-wheat bread), legumes (beans, lentils, chickpeas), and vegetables raise fiber, and higher fiber from these foods improves glycemia. The general target is at least 14 g of fiber per 1,000 calories; going higher is better.

Any of the ADA-endorsed patterns works as a frame. A Mediterranean-style plate (olive oil, fish, vegetables, legumes, nuts) or a DASH plate (vegetables, fruit, whole grains, low-fat dairy, poultry, fish, legumes, nuts) also satisfies the blood pressure and cholesterol modules, so families managing several conditions can use one plan.

sections.heading: What to limit or avoid
paragraphs: Avoid sugar-sweetened beverages (regular soda, sweet tea, energy drinks, juice drinks, sweetened coffee drinks). This is a must-strength rule in the app. It is not an allergen-style hard block, so you can still log one, but the plan never includes them.
Minimize added sugars and refined grains (white bread, white rice, pastries, most crackers, sugary cereal). This is a soft rule: the app steers away from them and lets you decide at the margins.
Sodium under 2,300 mg a day, the same as the general population. Alcohol moderate at most. Both are soft rules.

Non-nutritive sweeteners (aspartame, sucralose, stevia and the like) are optional. The ADA position is that they are an acceptable short-term replacement for sugar, with the goal of reducing overall sweet intake over time.

sections.heading: Numbers that matter
paragraphs: Weight loss, if you have overweight or obesity: 5 to 7 percent of body weight improves glycemia; over 10 percent can produce remission. For a 200 lb person, 5 to 7 percent is 10 to 14 lb.
Fiber: at least 14 g per 1,000 calories. On a 2,000 calorie day that is 28 g.
Sodium: under 2,300 mg a day.

Numbers that require a clinician: any carbohydrate target tied to insulin dosing, any plan for someone on a GLP-1 medication, and any calorie target for someone who is not overweight. The app does not generate these.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and myths
paragraphs: Treating low-carb as the answer. Very low carbohydrate diets have good short-term glycemic data but weaker long-term adherence data. Low-carb is one valid option, not the answer.
Treating intermittent fasting or meal timing as guideline-level advice. It is emerging, not established. Some evidence, individual decision, with clinician input.
Assuming everyone with type 2 diabetes should count calories. The evidence supports weight loss as a goal for many but not all. Your priority goals decide whether calories are shown at all.

A newer ADA nutrition consensus report: one was said to be expected in 2026, but as of September 30, 2026 none has been published, and the 2026 Standards of Care still point to the 2019 report. No rule in the app depends on it (VERIFY: check again for a new report).

sections.heading: When to talk to a clinician
paragraphs: Before starting a low-carbohydrate pattern if you take insulin, a sulfonylurea, or an SGLT2 inhibitor. Insulin and sulfonylureas raise hypoglycemia risk and doses may need adjusting; SGLT2 inhibitors carry a ketoacidosis caution with very low carbohydrate intake.
If you take insulin or a sulfonylurea and drink alcohol, because alcohol raises hypoglycemia risk.
If you take a GLP-1 medication, or if you are pregnant or planning pregnancy. Diabetes in pregnancy has its own rules and clinician-set targets.
If you have unexplained weight loss, very high or very low readings, or symptoms you cannot explain. This app is a wellness tool; it does not diagnose or treat.

sections.heading: How this app applies it
paragraphs: This module has no phases and no modes. It runs all the time once selected. At onboarding it asks two medication questions: whether you take insulin or a sulfonylurea (which turns on hypoglycemia awareness notes and requires a clinician-set plan) and whether you take an SGLT2 inhibitor (which turns on the low-carb ketoacidosis caution).
Compatible modules: hypertension, heart-healthy, and MASLD. DASH and Mediterranean patterns satisfy all of them at once, so the plan does not change much when they are combined.

Soft conflicts: the low-histamine trial (MCAS) excludes many foods this pattern relies on, so that trial is time-limited. Low-carb or ketogenic eating is allowed but asks for acknowledgment and the medication screen. Gastroparesis wins on food texture; fiber then comes from soluble, cooked, or blended sources.
Hard conflict: pregnancy. Carbohydrate targets in pregnancy and gestational diabetes are clinician-set, and the app will not generate them.

hypertension.title: Hypertension (high blood pressure)
summary: Follow the DASH eating pattern: vegetables, fruits, whole grains, low-fat dairy, poultry, fish, legumes, and nuts, with less red meat, sweets, and sugary drinks. It is the strongest-evidence diet for blood pressure.
Keep sodium under 2,300 mg a day and work toward under 1,500 mg.
Get 3,500 to 5,000 mg of potassium a day from food, unless you have kidney disease or take a medication that holds on to potassium. If you do, ask your clinician first.
A potassium-based salt substitute can help, with the same kidney and medication exceptions.
Cut back on alcohol or stop. If you are overweight, losing at least 5 percent of your body weight helps.
This app supports eating in a way that supports healthy blood pressure. It does not treat hypertension, and it never sets a sodium number when another condition pulls the other way.

sections.heading: What this condition is
paragraphs: Hypertension is blood pressure that stays above the range a clinician considers healthy for you. The 2025 AHA/ACC guideline covers how it is detected and managed; diet is one of the first tools it names, alongside medication when needed. Sodium raises blood pressure in most people, potassium from food lowers it, and the overall eating pattern matters more than any single food.

sections.heading: What the evidence says
paragraphs: The evidence rating for this module is STRONG. The 2025 AHA/ACC Multisociety Guideline for High Blood Pressure in Adults gives the DASH eating pattern, the sodium limit, and the potassium target Class 1, Level A recommendations, the highest grade a guideline gives. Behind those recommendations sit two foundational randomized controlled trials, DASH (NEJM 1997) and DASH-Sodium (NEJM 2001), and a large cluster-randomized trial of potassium-enriched salt, the Salt Substitute and Stroke Study (SSaSS, NEJM 2021).

DASH showed that a diet rich in fruits, vegetables, and low-fat dairy with less saturated fat lowered blood pressure. DASH-Sodium showed that lowering sodium on top of that pattern lowered it further. SSaSS showed that swapping regular salt for a potassium-enriched salt substitute reduced stroke, major cardiovascular events, and death in people with a history of stroke or with high blood pressure.

sections.heading: What to eat more of
paragraphs: Vegetables and fruits at most meals. Whole grains (oats, brown rice, whole-wheat bread, barley). Low-fat dairy (skim or 1 percent milk, plain low-fat yogurt). Poultry and fish instead of red meat. Legumes (beans, lentils, chickpeas) and unsalted nuts.

Potassium-rich foods: potatoes and sweet potatoes, beans, lentils, spinach and other greens, tomatoes, bananas, oranges, plain yogurt, and milk. The guideline prefers potassium from food over supplements.

Cook at home more. Most sodium in the American diet comes from restaurant and packaged foods, not the salt shaker, so a plan built on whole ingredients gets you most of the way to the sodium target on its own.

sections.heading: What to limit or avoid
paragraphs: Sodium: this is the firm rule. Under 2,300 mg a day, with 1,500 mg as the ideal. The app treats the 2,300 mg ceiling as a must-strength limit and the 1,500 mg figure as the goal it steers toward. The one exception is severe symptomatic orthostatic hypotension (fainting or near-fainting on standing), where the sodium limit is contraindicated; that is a clinician conversation.
Red meat, sweets, and sugar-sweetened beverages: limited under DASH. Soft rule.
Saturated fat: limited as part of the DASH pattern. The hypertension guideline gives no separate number; the heart-healthy module carries the percent-of-calories limit.
Alcohol: reduce or eliminate. Soft rule.
Salt substitutes are optional. Potassium-based substitutes can be useful, with the same exceptions as the potassium target: chronic kidney disease or medications that reduce potassium excretion.

sections.heading: Numbers that matter
paragraphs: Sodium: under 2,300 mg a day; ideal under 1,500 mg a day.
Potassium: 3,500 to 5,000 mg a day, preferably from food.
Weight: at least 5 percent loss if overweight.

Numbers that require a clinician: your potassium intake if you have chronic kidney disease or take an ACE inhibitor, an ARB, spironolactone, or a potassium-sparing diuretic (serum potassium must be monitored and the app suppresses the target); your sodium intake if you have severe orthostatic hypotension; and, per Phase 1, any sodium number at all if a high-sodium condition such as POTS is also present. Blood pressure targets themselves come from your clinician, not this app.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and myths
paragraphs: Believing the sodium debate applies to you. Population-level sodium targets are argued about in the academic literature; some cohort data suggest a J-shaped curve with the lowest risk around 3 to 5 g a day. For people who already have hypertension, the guideline position is clear, and the app follows it. The debate belongs here, in education, not in the rules engine.

Reaching for a salt substitute without checking medications. Potassium-enriched salt helped in SSaSS, but people with kidney disease or on potassium-retaining drugs were the exception, and they are the exception in the app too.
Expecting the app to lower your blood pressure. It does not claim to. It supports eating in a way that supports healthy blood pressure; measuring and treating blood pressure is your clinician's job.

Assuming the sodium rule is universal. Phase 1 flagged a hard conflict with POTS, which calls for high sodium. POTS is not a selectable module in this version, but the rule stands: the app never quietly picks a side. If both were present it would show the conflict, refuse to generate a sodium target, and build the rest of the plan from the shared rules.

sections.heading: When to talk to a clinician
paragraphs: Before raising potassium intake or using a potassium salt substitute if you have chronic kidney disease or take an ACE inhibitor, an ARB, spironolactone, or a potassium-sparing diuretic.
If you feel faint or dizzy on standing. Severe symptomatic orthostatic hypotension changes the sodium advice.
If you have kidney disease or heart failure. Those modules change what this one does.
For your blood pressure targets and any medication decision. The app does not track blood pressure devices in this version.

sections.heading: How this app applies it
paragraphs: No phases, no modes. One medication question at onboarding: do you take an ACE inhibitor, ARB, spironolactone, or a potassium-sparing diuretic? A yes suppresses the potassium target and the salt-substitute note, and the app says why.

Hard conflicts: chronic kidney disease (non-dialysis) and dialysis. The kidney module wins on potassium; the hypertension potassium target is suppressed with a visible notice. The sodium ceiling is the same in both, so it stays.

Compatible modules: type 2 diabetes, heart-healthy, and MASLD (DASH and Mediterranean satisfy all of them) and heart failure (same sodium ceiling, same DASH pattern; heart failure does not push the 1,500 mg ideal).

The sodium and potassium numbers are summed from the food database by grams, never estimated from text. Rotisserie chicken, canned goods, bread, and sauces are where the sodium hides, and the app counts them.

hyperlipidemia.title: Heart-healthy / LDL-lowering (high cholesterol)
summary: The single biggest thing you can do for LDL cholesterol is swap saturated fat (butter, fatty meat, full-fat dairy, coconut oil) for unsaturated fat (olive oil, canola oil, nuts, seeds, avocado, fish).
Keep saturated fat under 10 percent of calories; under 6 percent is the AHA target if you need to lower LDL. Cut out industrial trans fat completely.
Add soluble fiber: oats, barley, beans, lentils, psyllium. 5 to 10 g a day lowers LDL modestly.
Eat a Mediterranean or DASH pattern overall. In the PREDIMED trial a Mediterranean diet with olive oil or nuts reduced major cardiovascular events.
Limit added sugar, refined carbohydrate, and alcohol, especially if your triglycerides are high.
Eggs in moderation are fine for most people. US guidance no longer sets a number for dietary cholesterol.

sections.heading: What this condition is
paragraphs: High cholesterol (hyperlipidemia) means the blood carries more LDL cholesterol, triglycerides, or both than is healthy. LDL is the particle that drives atherosclerosis, the buildup in artery walls behind heart attacks and strokes. Diet changes LDL mainly through the type of fat you eat, not through the cholesterol in food, which is why this module is called heart-healthy or LDL-lowering rather than a low-cholesterol diet. The app has two doors into this module, a diagnosis of high cholesterol and a preference for heart-healthy eating, and both use the same rules.

sections.heading: What the evidence says
paragraphs: The evidence rating for this module is STRONG. It rests on the 2018 AHA/ACC Multisociety Guideline on the Management of Blood Cholesterol, the AHA 2021 Dietary Guidance to Improve Cardiovascular Health, the AHA 2019 science advisory on dietary cholesterol, a Cochrane systematic review of randomized trials on reducing saturated fat (Hooper et al., 2020), and the PREDIMED randomized trial (NEJM 2018 corrected re-analysis).

Replacing saturated fat with unsaturated fat is the single highest-evidence lever for LDL. The Cochrane review pooled long-term randomized trials and found that reducing saturated fat lowered combined cardiovascular events. PREDIMED showed that a Mediterranean pattern with extra-virgin olive oil or nuts lowered major cardiovascular events in people at high risk, about 30 percent in the corrected analysis. Soluble fiber and plant sterols each lower LDL by a modest, measurable amount.

sections.heading: What to eat more of
paragraphs: Unsaturated fats in place of saturated ones: extra-virgin olive oil, canola oil, nuts, seeds, avocado, and fish. The point is the swap, not adding fat on top.

Soluble fiber: oatmeal, barley, beans, lentils, chickpeas, and psyllium. 5 to 10 g of soluble fiber a day lowers LDL modestly. A bowl of oatmeal, a serving of beans, and an apple get you a good part of the way.
Vegetables, fruit, whole grains, legumes, nuts, fish, olive oil, and low-fat dairy: the Mediterranean or DASH pattern overall. Fish at least twice a week fits both.

Plant sterols and stanols (2 g a day, found mainly in fortified spreads and some fortified foods) lower LDL about 8 to 10 percent. This is a legitimate option with evidence, but food-based sources are limited and it borders on supplement territory, so the app presents it as an option, not a push.

sections.heading: What to limit or avoid
paragraphs: Industrial trans fat: eliminate. This is a must-strength rule with a target of zero. Look for partially hydrogenated oils on ingredient lists.

Saturated fat: under 10 percent of calories for everyone, and under 6 percent if you need to lower LDL. Must-strength limit. The main sources are fatty cuts of meat, processed meat, butter, cream, full-fat cheese and ice cream, coconut oil, and palm oil.

Cholesterol-rich foods: no numeric limit, but the AHA advisory still recommends a pattern low in them because they tend to travel with saturated fat. Eggs in moderation are acceptable for most people. Soft rule.
Added sugar, refined carbohydrate, and sugar-sweetened beverages: limit, mainly for triglycerides. Soft rule.
Alcohol: limit, especially if triglycerides are high. Soft rule.

sections.heading: Numbers that matter
paragraphs: Saturated fat: under 10 percent of calories (general population); under 6 percent (AHA target for lowering LDL). On a 2,000 calorie day, 10 percent is about 22 g and 6 percent is about 13 g.
Trans fat: 0 g industrial trans fat.
Soluble fiber: 5 to 10 g a day.
Plant sterols or stanols: 2 g a day lowers LDL about 8 to 10 percent (optional).
Dietary cholesterol: no numeric limit in current US guidance.
Numbers that require a clinician: your LDL, triglyceride, and other lab values, what they should be, and whether medication is warranted. The app handles food only.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and myths
paragraphs: Calling coconut oil heart-healthy. It is mostly saturated fat. The app does not treat it as heart-healthy, whatever the label says.

Believing the saturated fat question is settled the other way. The debate is loud online, but the clinical guideline position has not changed: saturated fat raises LDL, and LDL causes atherosclerosis. The app follows the AHA/ACC guideline.

Following a low-cholesterol diet in the old sense. Avoiding eggs and shrimp while eating butter and bacon misses the point. Dietary cholesterol no longer has a specific numeric limit; saturated fat does.
Treating sterol products as required. They work, but they are an option with the evidence attached, not something the app pushes.

sections.heading: When to talk to a clinician
paragraphs: To get and interpret your lipid panel, and to decide whether diet alone is enough or medication is also needed. The app does not make that call.
If your triglycerides are high, since the alcohol and sugar advice tightens.

If you also have kidney stones, gastroparesis, or are in a low-histamine trial, because several heart-healthy foods (nuts, spinach, tomatoes, citrus, fish) are limited under those modules and you may want help balancing them.

sections.heading: How this app applies it
paragraphs: No phases, no modes, no medication questions. Saturated fat and trans fat are summed from the food database by grams. Soluble fiber is a target the planner tries to reach.
Compatible modules: type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and MASLD. The Mediterranean pattern satisfies all of them.

Soft conflicts: the low-histamine trial (MCAS) excludes nuts, fish, tomatoes, citrus, olive oil, and legumes, which are the backbone of this pattern; the app time-limits that trial and asks you to acknowledge the overlap. Kidney stones share high-oxalate foods (nuts, spinach, beets) with this list; the fix is pairing them with calcium in the same meal, not removing them. Gastroparesis texture rules win over nuts and whole grains, with fiber then coming from soluble, cooked, or blended sources. Low-carb or ketogenic eating is allowed, but the saturated fat limit still applies: a low-carb diet built on processed meat and butter is not heart-healthy.

celiac.title: Celiac disease
summary: A strict, lifelong gluten-free diet is the only treatment for celiac disease. No wheat, barley, rye, or their relatives (spelt, kamut, farro, durum, semolina, triticale, malt, brewer's yeast from beer).
Watch for hidden gluten: soy sauce, malt vinegar, seasoning blends, processed meats, some medications and supplements, communion wafers.
Cross-contact counts as much as ingredients. Shared toasters, fryers, cutting boards, and bulk bins can make a gluten-free food unsafe.
Certified gluten-free oats are safe for most people with celiac disease; regular oats are not. The app allows certified oats by default and lets you turn them off.
Build meals on naturally gluten-free whole foods (rice, quinoa, buckwheat, beans, potatoes, corn) rather than packaged substitutes, which are often low in fiber and not fortified.
Follow up with a dietitian who knows celiac disease. Newly diagnosed people are often low in iron, folate, B12, vitamin D, calcium, and zinc.

sections.heading: What this condition is
paragraphs: Celiac disease is a permanent immune reaction to gluten, the protein in wheat, barley, and rye. Eating gluten damages the small intestine and can affect the whole body, which is why nutrient shortfalls are common at diagnosis. Unlike a preference or a sensitivity, there is no safe amount to work up to. The diet is the treatment, and it is for life.

sections.heading: What the evidence says
paragraphs: The evidence rating for this module is STRONG for the diet as treatment, because it is the only treatment. The governing sources are the American College of Gastroenterology clinical guideline on diagnosis and management of celiac disease (Rubio-Tapia et al., 2023), the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics celiac evidence-based practice guideline, the FDA gluten-free labeling rule (21 CFR 101.91), and patient materials from the Celiac Disease Foundation and Beyond Celiac for practical food lists.

The 2023 ACG guideline says gluten-free labeled oats are safe for most people with celiac disease, with a small subset reacting to oat avenin. It also recommends follow-up with a dietitian experienced in celiac disease. The FDA rule sets the legal meaning of a gluten-free label in the United States: under 20 parts per million of gluten.

sections.heading: What to eat more of
paragraphs: Naturally gluten-free whole foods: rice, quinoa, buckwheat, millet, corn, potatoes, sweet potatoes, beans, lentils, vegetables, fruit, eggs, plain meat, poultry, fish, plain dairy, nuts, and seeds. These carry the fiber and nutrients that packaged gluten-free substitutes often lack.
Certified gluten-free oats, if you tolerate them. They add fiber and a breakfast option. Regular oats are cross-contaminated with wheat during growing and processing, so the label matters.

Foods rich in the nutrients that run low at diagnosis: iron (meat, beans, lentils, fortified gluten-free grains), folate (leafy greens, beans), B12 (animal foods, fortified products), vitamin D and calcium (dairy or fortified alternatives), and zinc (meat, seeds, legumes). A dietitian can check whether you need testing or supplements.

sections.heading: What to limit or avoid
paragraphs: Hard rules, no override: wheat, barley, rye, and their derivatives (spelt, kamut, farro, durum, semolina, triticale, malt, brewer's yeast from beer). Regular oats. Hidden gluten sources: soy sauce, malt vinegar, seasoning blends, processed meats, some medications and supplements, communion wafers, and play-dough if it gets in the mouth.

Hard rule on process, not just ingredients: cross-contact. Shared fryers, toasters, cutting boards, and bulk bins can carry gluten into an otherwise safe food. Restaurant menus that say gluten-free without cross-contact protocols are not celiac-safe. The app separates celiac-safe from gluten-free ingredients.
Soft rule: packaged gluten-free substitutes (breads, crackers, cookies). They are allowed, but they are often low in fiber and not fortified, so the app steers toward whole foods.
Optional: certified gluten-free oats. On by default; a toggle turns them off if you are in the small group that reacts to oat avenin.

sections.heading: Numbers that matter
paragraphs: 20 parts per million: the maximum gluten content for a food labeled gluten-free under FDA rule 21 CFR 101.91.
Zero: the amount of wheat, barley, or rye the plan includes. There is no daily allowance.

Numbers that require a clinician: your iron, folate, B12, vitamin D, calcium, and zinc status, and whether you need supplements. Celiac blood tests and biopsy results are also clinician territory, and they are only reliable while you are still eating gluten.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and myths
paragraphs: Going gluten-free before testing. Phase 1 flags this as a patient-safety point: gluten-free eating before testing makes celiac testing unreliable. If celiac disease has not been ruled out, talk to a clinician before removing gluten.
Trusting a gluten-free menu label. Gluten-free ingredients with a shared fryer or toaster are not safe for celiac disease.
Worrying about gluten in cosmetics. It is not a concern unless it is swallowed. Lip products are the only practical issue.
Cutting all oats forever. Certified gluten-free oats are safe for most people with celiac disease; only a small subset react to oat avenin.
Living on packaged substitutes. They are gluten-free but often low in fiber and fortification, which makes the nutrient shortfalls worse.

sections.heading: When to talk to a clinician
paragraphs: Before starting a gluten-free diet if you have not been tested for celiac disease.
After diagnosis, for a referral to a dietitian experienced in celiac disease, which the ACG guideline recommends.
For nutrient testing (iron, folate, B12, vitamin D, calcium, zinc), especially in the first year.
If symptoms continue on a strict diet, or if you are pregnant, because celiac rules stay on in pregnancy and nutrient needs rise.

sections.heading: How this app applies it
paragraphs: No phases, no modes. The gluten rules are hard: no setting, preference, or acknowledgment can override them. The ingredient screener uses a maintained hidden-gluten dictionary with exact matching. Anything it does not recognize is reported as not recognized, never assumed safe.
Certified gluten-free oats are allowed by default with a toggle to exclude them. Regular oats are always excluded.

Compatible modules: low FODMAP (the FODMAP wheat restriction is about fructans, not gluten; certified gluten-free oats are low FODMAP in limited portions), pregnancy (celiac rules stay on), and iron-deficiency anemia (celiac disease is a common hidden cause; if iron deficiency is selected without celiac, the app mentions screening).
Caregiver mode lets an adult manage a child's celiac and allergen rules under the same hard-exclusion logic.

lactose-intolerance.title: Lactose intolerance
summary: Lactose intolerance is about dose, not all-or-nothing. Most people handle about 12 g of lactose at a time, roughly one cup of milk, especially with food, and more when it is spread across the day.
Well tolerated: hard aged cheeses (near zero lactose), yogurt with live cultures, butter, lactose-free milk, and lactase enzyme tablets taken with dairy.
Highest lactose: milk, ice cream, soft cheeses, cream, milk-based sauces, whey products, and some protein powders. Limit these by portion rather than cutting them out.
Keep calcium and vitamin D up. The app counts fortified alternatives and non-dairy calcium sources.
It is not a milk allergy. A cow's milk protein allergy is a hard exclusion of all dairy and lives under Food allergies.
Self-diagnosis is often wrong. A hydrogen breath test confirms lactose intolerance; many people who think they have it have IBS or something else.

sections.heading: What this condition is
paragraphs: Lactose is the sugar in milk. People with lactose intolerance make less of the enzyme (lactase) that breaks it down, so undigested lactose reaches the large intestine and causes gas, bloating, cramps, or diarrhea. How much lactose you can handle depends on how much enzyme you still make, whether you eat it with other food, and how it is spread through the day. It is a digestive intolerance, not an immune reaction.

sections.heading: What the evidence says
paragraphs: The evidence rating for this module is STRONG, because the mechanism and the management are well established. The governing sources are the 2010 NIH Consensus Development Conference Statement on Lactose Intolerance and Health, NIDDK patient materials on lactose intolerance, and Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics practice materials.

The NIH consensus panel concluded that lactose intolerance is dose-dependent, that most people with lactose malabsorption tolerate about 12 g of lactose in a single dose, especially with a meal, and that total dairy avoidance is not necessary for most of them. It also stressed that calcium and vitamin D adequacy must be maintained when dairy is reduced.

sections.heading: What to eat more of
paragraphs: Low-lactose dairy: hard aged cheeses such as cheddar, parmesan, Swiss, and aged gouda are near zero lactose. Yogurt with live cultures is better tolerated because the cultures digest some of the lactose. Butter carries very little. Lactose-free milk is regular milk with the lactose already broken down.
Lactase enzyme tablets taken with a dairy meal, if you want to eat something higher in lactose.

Calcium and vitamin D sources that do not depend on milk: fortified plant milks and juices, canned salmon or sardines with bones, tofu set with calcium, leafy greens such as kale and bok choy, and fortified cereals. The app counts these toward calcium so a lower-dairy plan stays complete.

sections.heading: What to limit or avoid
paragraphs: Soft rule: high-lactose foods. Milk, ice cream, soft and fresh cheeses (ricotta, cottage cheese, cream cheese), cream, milk-based sauces, whey-based products, and some protein powders. The app limits these by dose, not by elimination. About 12 g in one sitting is the typical threshold; a cup of milk is roughly that.
Hidden lactose, worth knowing but rarely a problem at the amounts involved: bread, processed meats, salad dressings, instant potatoes, and some medications, where lactose is used as a filler.

There are no hard rules in this module. Total dairy avoidance is a preference choice, not a medical necessity for most people with lactose intolerance. If you want to avoid all dairy, set it under Preference avoidances so the app treats it as your choice, not a medical rule.

sections.heading: Numbers that matter
paragraphs: About 12 g of lactose per sitting is what most people with lactose malabsorption tolerate, especially with a meal. One cup (8 oz) of milk has about that much.
Near zero: the lactose in hard aged cheeses.
More across the day than in one dose: spreading lactose out raises the total you can handle.

Numbers that require a clinician: your individual tolerance, which only trial and error or testing can set, and your calcium and vitamin D needs if you are older, pregnant, or have bone concerns. The app does not have a lactose nutrient field; it works from food tags (high, low, hidden) and portion notes.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and myths
paragraphs: Cutting out all dairy. For most people with lactose intolerance this is a preference, not a medical need, and it makes calcium and vitamin D harder to get.
Diagnosing yourself. Self-diagnosed lactose intolerance is often actually IBS or another issue. A hydrogen breath test confirms it.
Confusing it with milk allergy. Cow's milk protein allergy is an immune reaction and a hard exclusion of all dairy. Lactose intolerance is dose-dependent. They are different settings in the app.
Assuming yogurt and hard cheese are off limits. They are the dairy foods most people with lactose intolerance tolerate best.

sections.heading: When to talk to a clinician
paragraphs: To confirm the diagnosis with a hydrogen breath test, especially if symptoms are ongoing or do not track with dairy.
If cutting dairy does not help, since IBS or another condition may be the real cause.
If you have reacted to dairy with hives, swelling, wheezing, or vomiting, which points to milk allergy rather than intolerance.
If you have reduced dairy and are unsure whether you are getting enough calcium and vitamin D.

sections.heading: How this app applies it
paragraphs: No phases, no modes, no medication questions. The rules run through food tags: lactose-high foods are limited by portion, lactose-low foods are preferred, lactose-hidden foods carry an information note. No food is hard-blocked.
If you also select IBS (low FODMAP), this module is switched off and the FODMAP rules take over, because lactose is the D in FODMAP and the FODMAP rules already cover it.
Milk allergy is handled separately under Food allergies as a hard exclusion of all dairy. Selecting lactose intolerance never triggers that, and the two settings do not interfere with each other.
The planner counts calcium and vitamin D from fortified alternatives and non-dairy sources, so a lower-dairy plan does not silently run short.

ibs-low-fodmap.title: IBS and the low FODMAP protocol
summary: Low FODMAP is a three-step process, not a permanent diet: cut high-FODMAP foods for 2 to 6 weeks, then spend 6 to 8 weeks adding each group back one at a time, then eat everything you tolerate.
About 50 to 75 percent of people with IBS get meaningful relief. Not everyone does.
Portion size decides FODMAP load. Many foods are fine in small amounts and a problem in large ones, so the app uses serving-size thresholds, not a simple allowed or avoid list.
Do this with a dietitian if you can. Staying in the elimination phase long term harms your gut bacteria and your nutrition.

Simpler first-line advice (regular meals, less alcohol, caffeine, fat, and gas-producing food, soluble fiber, peppermint oil) has weaker evidence but is easier, and some guidelines suggest trying it first.
The FODMAP food data in this app comes from published studies and USDA data. It is not Monash-verified.

sections.heading: What this condition is
paragraphs: Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) is a disorder of how the gut and brain communicate, producing abdominal pain with bloating, diarrhea, constipation, or both, without visible damage on testing. FODMAPs are short-chain carbohydrates that are poorly absorbed in the small intestine and fermented by gut bacteria: oligosaccharides (fructans and galacto-oligosaccharides in wheat, rye, onion, garlic, and legumes), disaccharides (lactose), monosaccharides (excess fructose in honey, apples, mango, and high-fructose corn syrup), and polyols (sorbitol and mannitol in stone fruits and sugar-free gum). In people with IBS, the gas and water they draw into the gut trigger symptoms.

sections.heading: What the evidence says
paragraphs: The evidence rating for this module is MODERATE to STRONG for short-term symptom relief and MODERATE for the full three-phase protocol. The American College of Gastroenterology IBS guideline (Lacy et al., 2021) gives a conditional recommendation for a limited trial of a low FODMAP diet. The key randomized controlled trial is Halmos et al. (Gastroenterology 2014), a crossover trial in which a low FODMAP diet reduced IBS symptoms compared with a typical Australian diet. The AGA clinical practice update on diet in IBS (Chey et al., 2022) and the British Dietetic Association guideline (McKenzie et al., 2016) set out the three-phase structure and the need for dietitian support. Monash University runs the primary lab-tested food composition database.

The evidence for the elimination phase is stronger than for the reintroduction and personalization phases. Both the ACG guideline and the AGA update say the diet should be delivered with dietitian support, and that long-term elimination without reintroduction harms the microbiome and nutrition.

sections.heading: What to eat more of
paragraphs: During elimination, low-FODMAP staples in the portions the database allows: rice, oats, quinoa, potatoes, carrots, zucchini, spinach, tomatoes, cucumber, green beans, firm bananas, oranges, strawberries, kiwi, lactose-free milk, hard cheeses, eggs, plain meat, poultry, fish, firm tofu, and small servings of nuts and seeds.
Soluble fiber sources such as oats and psyllium, which are part of the first-line IBS advice and fit the elimination phase.

After reintroduction, everything you tolerated. The long-term goal is the widest diet your symptoms allow, because variety and fiber feed a healthy gut. The personalization phase is where you get those foods back.

sections.heading: What to limit or avoid
paragraphs: During elimination (2 to 6 weeks), the app steers away from high-FODMAP foods: wheat and rye products, onion, garlic, most legumes, milk and soft cheeses, honey, apples, mango, high-fructose corn syrup, stone fruits, and sugar-free gum and candy sweetened with sorbitol or mannitol. These are soft rules by design: FODMAP status depends on portion, so the database carries serving-size thresholds rather than blanket bans.

During reintroduction (6 to 8 weeks), you add one FODMAP group back at a time, in rising portions, and track symptoms. The must-strength rules in this phase are about process: test each group, then decide.
During personalization, only the groups that clearly bothered you stay limited, and only at the portions that bothered you.
There are no hard, allergen-style rules in this module. Low FODMAP is a diagnostic tool, not a lifelong restriction.

sections.heading: Numbers that matter
paragraphs: Elimination phase: 2 to 6 weeks. The app prompts you to move on once you pass the maximum.
Reintroduction phase: 6 to 8 weeks, testing FODMAP subgroups one at a time.
50 to 75 percent: the share of people with IBS who get meaningful relief.
Serving-size thresholds: each tagged food carries the portion at which it changes from low to high FODMAP. The number is the portion, not the food.
Numbers that require a clinician: none in this module are clinician-set, but the diagnosis of IBS itself should come from a clinician, and a dietitian should ideally guide the phases.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and myths
paragraphs: Treating low FODMAP as a permanent lifestyle. The app will not let you stay in elimination without reintroduction prompts. Long-term elimination harms the microbiome and nutrition.
Treating foods as simply allowed or forbidden. FODMAP load depends on portion. A small serving of a high-FODMAP food is often fine.
Assuming everyone gets relief. About a quarter to a half of people do not.
Assuming this data is Monash-verified. Monash's food data is proprietary and this app does not license it. The FODMAP tags here come from published studies and USDA data.

Skipping the simpler advice. First-line IBS advice (regular meals; less alcohol, caffeine, fat, and gas-producing food; soluble fiber; peppermint oil) has weaker evidence but is easier, and some guidelines recommend it first.
Confusing this with gluten-free. The wheat restriction is about fructans, not gluten.

sections.heading: When to talk to a clinician
paragraphs: To get an IBS diagnosis before starting, and to get a referral to a dietitian trained in the low FODMAP protocol.
Before cutting wheat if you have never been tested for celiac disease. Celiac testing becomes unreliable once gluten is out of the diet.
If you have not improved after the elimination phase, or if you cannot get through reintroduction on your own.
If you are also running another elimination diet, are pregnant, or have inflammatory bowel disease. Each changes how this module runs.

sections.heading: How this app applies it
paragraphs: This module has three phases and the app enforces all of them: elimination (2 to 6 weeks), reintroduction (6 to 8 weeks), and personalization. When a phase passes its maximum length the app prompts you to move on and requires an acknowledgment to stay. You cannot select low FODMAP as a permanent lifestyle.

Soft conflicts: the gut-health module's fiber and fermented-food advice runs against elimination, because many prebiotic foods are high FODMAP; the app states this, time-limits elimination, and restores those foods in reintroduction. Running a low-histamine trial (MCAS) at the same time raises restriction load; both are time-limited and count toward the restriction-load check-in. In inflammatory bowel disease, low FODMAP can help coexisting IBS symptoms in remission (limited evidence) and is presented that way, not as an IBD treatment.
Subsumed module: lactose intolerance. If both are selected, the FODMAP rules cover lactose and the lactose module is switched off.
Compatible: celiac disease. The FODMAP wheat restriction and the celiac gluten restriction are about different things, and certified gluten-free oats are low FODMAP in limited portions.
Hard conflict: pregnancy mode disables every elimination protocol except allergen and celiac rules, including this one.

mcas.title: MCAS and the low-histamine trial
summary: Doctors who treat MCAS often suggest trying a low-histamine diet for a few weeks to see if it helps. There are no large clinical trials proving it works, and food lists vary. The goal is to find your personal triggers, not to stay restricted forever.
The trial lasts 4 to 6 weeks, then you add foods back to find your own triggers. This is the same structure as low FODMAP.
Freshness and cooking method have the clearest food-chemistry basis: fresh over leftovers, frozen fish over aged, boiling and steaming over long braising and fermenting.

Commonly reported triggers: alcohol, aged and fermented foods, cured meats, shellfish, tomatoes, spinach, citrus, chocolate, nuts, spicy foods, and food additives. These are patient-reported patterns, not trial-confirmed.
Histamine intolerance and MCAS are different conditions. Someone with MCAS may not react to dietary histamine at all.
Tracking symptoms against meals is the most useful thing you can do. The app does not recommend DAO supplements or any so-called mast cell stabilizing foods.

sections.heading: What this condition is
paragraphs: Mast cell activation syndrome (MCAS) is a condition in which mast cells, immune cells that release histamine and other chemical mediators, release them abnormally, causing symptoms across several body systems. Two competing sets of diagnostic criteria exist (Valent et al., 2019 and 2020 variants), so the diagnosis itself is contested territory. Histamine intolerance is a different problem: reduced activity of the DAO enzyme that breaks down histamine from food. The two get conflated, and the diet advice for one is often applied to the other without evidence.

sections.heading: What the evidence says
paragraphs: The evidence rating for this module is LIMITED. It rests on expert consensus and one 2025 professional-society practice update, with little controlled trial evidence. The governing sources are the AGA Clinical Practice Update on GI manifestations and autonomic or immune dysfunction in hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (Aziz et al., 2025), which covers MCAS and POTS in that context and issues Best Practice Advice statements rather than graded recommendations; two reviews of the histamine intolerance literature (Comas-Baste et al., 2020; Evidence for Dietary Management of Histamine Intolerance, 2025); the Swiss Interest Group Histamine Intolerance (SIGHI) food compatibility list, which is widely used but not peer-reviewed; the Valent diagnostic criteria; and the 2017 German guideline on adverse reactions to ingested histamine (Reese et al.).

The strongest professional-society language available is the 2025 AGA update, which says that low-histamine, low-FODMAP, gluten-free, and dairy-free elimination diets can be considered for GI symptoms when MCAS is suspected, delivered with nutrition counseling to avoid the harms of restrictive eating. That is permissive language, not a recommendation.

Only one systematic review has examined restrictive low-histamine diets in mastocytosis, and it found no clinical trial evidence of a histamine-release mechanism in foods; the support is in vitro and animal data. Food histamine content varies enormously by freshness, storage, fermentation, and cooking method, and published food lists disagree with each other.

sections.heading: What to eat more of
paragraphs: Fresh food, cooked and eaten the same day. Histamine builds up as food ages, so freshness is the single most defensible principle in this diet.
Frozen fish and freshly cooked meat and poultry, rather than aged, cured, smoked, or canned versions.
Simple cooking: boiling, steaming, quick sauteing. Long braises, slow-cooker meals, and fermented preparations raise histamine.
Plain grains (rice, oats, quinoa), most fresh vegetables other than the reported triggers, fresh fruit other than citrus, and eggs and fresh dairy if tolerated. The app builds trial meals from these.

sections.heading: What to limit or avoid
paragraphs: During the 4 to 6 week trial, the app steers away from foods tagged high-histamine, fermented, or aged, and from alcohol: aged cheeses, cured and processed meats, fermented foods (sauerkraut, kimchi, kombucha, soy sauce, vinegar), shellfish, canned and smoked fish, leftovers more than a day old, and the commonly reported triggers listed above (tomatoes, spinach, citrus, chocolate, nuts, spicy foods, food additives).

All of these are soft rules, and the app labels them may-strength on purpose. They are patient-reported and clinician-observed patterns, not trial-confirmed, and the published lists disagree. Nothing in this module is a hard, allergen-style block.
After the trial, foods come back one at a time. The must-strength rule in this module is reintroduction: the trial ends, and you test what you removed.

Not part of this module at all: DAO enzyme supplements, and foods promoted as mast cell stabilizers (quercetin, luteolin, high-dose vitamin C). The evidence is preclinical and Phase 1 classed those claims as supplement marketing.

sections.heading: Numbers that matter
paragraphs: 4 to 6 weeks: the length of the low-histamine trial. The app prompts reintroduction when you reach the maximum and requires acknowledgment to continue.
There are no nutrient targets in this module and no clinician-set numbers. The numbers that matter are your own symptom scores logged against meals.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and myths
paragraphs: Staying on the diet forever. Many low-histamine avoid foods are healthy, high-nutrient foods: spinach, tomatoes, citrus, nuts, fish, fermented foods. Long-term restriction conflicts with heart-health, gut-health, and diabetes patterns. The time limit is the safeguard.

Assuming MCAS means you react to histamine in food. Someone with MCAS may not react to dietary histamine at all, because their symptoms are driven by other mediators (tryptase, prostaglandins, leukotrienes).
Trusting one food list as definitive. The SIGHI list is the most widely used, but it is not peer-reviewed, and other lists disagree with it.
Buying DAO supplements or mast cell stabilizing foods on the strength of this diet. The evidence is preclinical. The app does not recommend them.
Treating the low-histamine diet as proven treatment. There are no large clinical trials. It is a time-limited diagnostic trial.

sections.heading: When to talk to a clinician
paragraphs: Before starting, to confirm that a low-histamine trial makes sense for your diagnosis and to arrange nutrition counseling. The 2025 AGA update ties the diet to counseling because restrictive eating has harms.
If symptoms include throat swelling, trouble breathing, or fainting. Those need medical care, not a diet.
If you are on another elimination diet, or are pregnant. Pregnancy mode disables this trial.
If the trial ends and you are not sure what you learned. A dietitian can read the symptom log with you.

sections.heading: How this app applies it
paragraphs: This module has three phases: the low-histamine trial (4 to 6 weeks), reintroduction, and personalization. The app shows the evidence rating prominently and uses the plain language above. Symptom tracking tied to meals is turned on for this module because it is the highest-value feature for this population.

Soft conflicts, all resolved by the time limit: heart-healthy and the Mediterranean pattern (nuts, fish, tomatoes, citrus, olive oil, and legumes overlap the avoid list, and the app asks you to acknowledge that), gut health (fermented and high-fiber foods are excluded, then restored in reintroduction), and type 2 diabetes. Running this alongside low FODMAP raises restriction load; both count toward the restriction-load check-in, a plain nutrition-adequacy notice that suggests working with a dietitian.
Hard conflict: pregnancy mode disables this trial along with every other elimination protocol except allergen and celiac rules.
Phase 1 treats MCAS, POTS, and hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome as a cluster. POTS is not a selectable module in this version.

anti-inflammatory-mediterranean.title: Mediterranean diet (anti-inflammatory)
summary: The evidence-based version of an anti-inflammatory diet is the Mediterranean pattern: extra-virgin olive oil as the main fat; vegetables, fruit, whole grains, beans, and nuts every day; fish at least twice a week.
Moderate poultry, eggs, and dairy. Not much red or processed meat, sweets, refined grains, or ultra-processed food.
It earns its reputation from heart outcomes. In the PREDIMED trial it reduced major cardiovascular events by about 30 percent. Its effect on inflammation markers is modest and inconsistent.
Nightshade avoidance, lectin avoidance, dairy elimination, and alkaline foods are not part of an evidence-based anti-inflammatory diet. The app does not encode them.
Turmeric, ginger, and other spices are fine as foods. They are not medicine, and the app makes no health claims about them.
Fish oil supplements are not recommended for the general population. Eat the fish.

sections.heading: What this pattern is
paragraphs: Anti-inflammatory diet is a marketing term that covers many different things online. The version with evidence behind it is the Mediterranean eating pattern, a way of eating drawn from the traditional diets of countries around the Mediterranean and tested in randomized trials. The app uses that pattern and only that pattern under this label. The idea of scoring foods for inflammatory potential comes from the Dietary Inflammatory Index literature (Shivappa et al.), which is observational and supplies the concept, not the rules.

sections.heading: What the evidence says
paragraphs: The evidence rating for this module is STRONG for cardiovascular outcomes and metabolic markers, MODERATE for inflammatory biomarkers, and LIMITED for specific inflammatory diseases. The governing sources are the PREDIMED randomized trial (Estruch et al., NEJM 2018 corrected re-analysis), in which a Mediterranean diet supplemented with extra-virgin olive oil or nuts reduced major cardiovascular events by about 30 percent in people at high risk; the Cochrane systematic review of Mediterranean-style diets for primary and secondary prevention of cardiovascular disease (Rees et al., 2019); the AHA 2021 Dietary Guidance to Improve Cardiovascular Health; and the Dietary Inflammatory Index literature for the concept.

Omega-3 fats from fish (EPA and DHA) have the best data within the pattern. Fish oil supplements for the general population have mixed results and are not recommended. Whether the diet lowers CRP and IL-6 meaningfully in healthy people is modest and inconsistent; the cardiovascular outcome data is what justifies the pattern.

sections.heading: What to eat more of
paragraphs: Extra-virgin olive oil as the main fat, for cooking and dressing.

Vegetables and fruit every day, in variety. Whole grains (whole-wheat bread, brown rice, bulgur, farro, oats). Legumes (chickpeas, lentils, white beans) several times a week. A handful of nuts most days.
Fish and seafood at least twice a week, especially oily fish such as salmon, sardines, mackerel, and trout, which carry the EPA and DHA.
Herbs and spices freely, including turmeric and ginger, for flavor. They have mechanistic and small-trial data, not outcome data, so the app treats them as food, not treatment.

sections.heading: What to limit or avoid
paragraphs: Soft rules, all of them. This module has no hard exclusions.
Limit red and processed meat, sweets and added sugar, refined grains, and ultra-processed food. Keep them occasional rather than daily.
Poultry, eggs, and dairy in moderation. They are part of the pattern, not banned from it.

Things this module deliberately does not restrict: nightshades (tomatoes, peppers, eggplant, potatoes), lectin-containing foods (beans, grains), dairy as a category, or foods judged by an acid or alkaline score. None of those restrictions is evidence-based, and tomatoes and beans are staples of the pattern.

sections.heading: Numbers that matter
paragraphs: Fish and seafood: at least 2 servings a week.
About 30 percent: the reduction in major cardiovascular events with the Mediterranean diet plus olive oil or nuts in PREDIMED, in people at high cardiovascular risk.

No numbers in this module require a clinician. If you also have high cholesterol, high blood pressure, or diabetes, those modules add their own limits (saturated fat, sodium, fiber), and this pattern satisfies them.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and myths
paragraphs: Buying the online version. Anti-inflammatory diets as marketed (no nightshades, no lectins, no dairy, alkaline foods) are not evidence-based, and the app explicitly does not encode them.
Expecting a big drop in inflammation markers. In healthy people the effect on CRP and IL-6 is modest and inconsistent. The reason to eat this way is the heart outcome data.
Expecting it to treat a specific inflammatory disease. The evidence there is limited, and the app does not claim it.
Taking fish oil instead of eating fish. Fish has the best data; supplements for the general population have mixed results.
Treating turmeric or ginger as medicine. Fine as food; no health claims.

sections.heading: When to talk to a clinician
paragraphs: If you have a diagnosed inflammatory or autoimmune condition and want to know what diet can and cannot do for it. The evidence for specific diseases is limited, and your specialist can put it in context.
If you are considering any supplement, including fish oil or turmeric extracts. The app does not recommend them.
If you have kidney stones, gastroparesis, or are in a low-histamine trial, because several staples of this pattern are limited under those modules.

sections.heading: How this app applies it
paragraphs: No phases, no modes, no medication questions. The pattern runs through prefer tags (olive oil, vegetables, fruit, whole grains, legumes, nuts, fish) and soft avoid tags (red and processed meat, added sugar, refined grains, ultra-processed food). Fish is a weekly target of 2 servings.

Soft conflicts: the low-histamine trial (MCAS) excludes tomatoes, citrus, nuts, fish, and fermented foods, which are central here; the app time-limits that trial and asks you to acknowledge the overlap. Kidney stones share high-oxalate foods (spinach, nuts, beets) with this pattern; the fix is pairing them with calcium in the same meal rather than removing them. Gastroparesis texture rules win over nuts and whole grains.
This pattern also satisfies the type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and heart-healthy modules, so it is the natural default when a family is managing several of them.

low-added-sugar.title: Low added sugar
summary: The target is added sugar, not the sugar naturally in fruit or in plain milk and yogurt.
AHA limits: under 25 g a day (6 teaspoons) for women, under 36 g a day (9 teaspoons) for men. WHO: under 10 percent of calories, ideally under 5 percent.
Sugary drinks are the biggest single source of added sugar and the first thing to cut.
Read the Added Sugars line on the Nutrition Facts label. Sugar hides under 60-plus names in ingredient lists (dextrose, maltose, cane juice, agave, rice syrup, fruit juice concentrate).
Non-nutritive sweeteners are an acceptable short-term bridge. WHO advises against using them for weight control long term.

sections.heading: What this pattern is
paragraphs: Added sugars are sugars and syrups put into foods and drinks during processing or preparation, plus the sugars in honey, syrups, and fruit juice concentrates. They are different from the sugars that occur naturally in whole fruit and plain dairy, which come packaged with fiber, protein, or other nutrients. A low added sugar pattern cuts the first group and leaves the second alone. Since 2016 the FDA Nutrition Facts label has carried a separate Added Sugars line, which makes this the easiest pattern in the app to check at the store.

sections.heading: What the evidence says
paragraphs: The evidence rating for this module is STRONG. The governing sources are the American Heart Association scientific statement on dietary sugars (Johnson et al., Circulation 2009; a children's statement followed in 2016), which sets the 25 g and 36 g daily limits; the WHO guideline on sugars intake for adults and children (2015), which recommends free sugars under 10 percent of calories and suggests a further cut to under 5 percent; and the FDA Nutrition Facts label rule (2016) that created the Added Sugars line.

For non-nutritive sweeteners, the WHO 2023 guideline advises against using them for weight control or to reduce the risk of diet-related disease, based on long-term observational data. Short-term use as a bridge away from sugar is acceptable. The app presents both positions.

sections.heading: What to eat more of
paragraphs: Whole fruit, which is not the concern. An apple, a banana, or a bowl of berries counts as fruit, not added sugar.
Plain dairy (milk, unsweetened yogurt) and unsweetened plant milks. The sugar on their label is natural lactose or none at all; check that the Added Sugars line reads 0 g.
Water, sparkling water, unsweetened tea and coffee, and milk as the default drinks.

Foods with 0 g on the Added Sugars line: plain oats, plain nuts, eggs, meat, fish, vegetables, beans, plain grains. Sweetness from fruit, cinnamon, vanilla, or a small amount of a sugar you add yourself so you can see it.

sections.heading: What to limit or avoid
paragraphs: Sugar-sweetened beverages: soda, sweet tea, energy drinks, sports drinks, juice drinks, sweetened coffee and flavored milk. Soft rule in the app, but the first and biggest cut. They are the largest source of added sugar in the diet.
Sweets, desserts, sweetened cereal, flavored yogurt, granola bars, and sauces and dressings with sugar high on the ingredient list. Soft rule: the plan keeps them small and occasional.

Hidden sugar under other names. The app's ingredient parser carries a dictionary of 60-plus label names for sugar, including dextrose, maltose, evaporated cane juice, agave, brown rice syrup, and fruit juice concentrate, and counts them.
Non-nutritive sweeteners: optional. Fine as a short-term replacement while you cut back; not a long-term weight-control tool.
There are no hard rules in this module.

sections.heading: Numbers that matter
paragraphs: Added sugar: under 25 g a day for women, under 36 g a day for men (AHA). That is 6 and 9 teaspoons. One 12 oz can of regular soda carries about a day's worth on its own.
Free sugars: under 10 percent of calories, ideally under 5 percent (WHO). On a 2,000 calorie day, 10 percent is 50 g and 5 percent is 25 g.
0 g: the Added Sugars line on plain, whole foods.
No numbers in this module require a clinician. If you have diabetes, the diabetes module adds its own rules, and the two agree.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and myths
paragraphs: Cutting fruit. Fruit sugar in whole fruit is not the concern, and the app does not flag it. Total sugar on a label includes natural sugar; the Added Sugars line is what to read.
Treating diet soda as a weight-loss tool. WHO 2023 advises against non-sugar sweeteners for weight control, based on long-term observational data. They are a bridge, not a destination.
Trusting the front of the package. Words like natural, organic, or made with honey do not change the Added Sugars number. Honey, agave, and maple syrup are added sugars.
Missing the sauces. Ketchup, barbecue sauce, teriyaki, flavored yogurt, and granola can carry as much sugar per serving as dessert.

sections.heading: When to talk to a clinician
paragraphs: If you have diabetes or prediabetes and take medication, since cutting sugar can change your readings.
If you are pregnant, breastfeeding, or managing a child's diet, where the numbers differ and the app applies other modules.
If cutting added sugar leaves you eating very little, or if you have a history of disordered eating. This module is meant to change what you drink and snack on, not to shrink your diet.

sections.heading: How this app applies it
paragraphs: No phases, no modes, no medication questions, and no conflicts with other modules. Added sugar is summed from the food database by grams against the AHA limit for your sex (25 g women, 36 g men) and shown against the WHO percent-of-calories limit as well.
The label reader keys on the Added Sugars line, and the ingredient parser matches the 60-plus sugar names dictionary. Fruit and plain dairy sugars are never counted as added sugar.
Sugar-sweetened beverages are a soft avoid tag; non-nutritive sweeteners carry an information note with both the ADA short-term position and the WHO long-term position, and you decide.

soy-free.title: Soy-free
summary: If you have a diagnosed soy allergy, set it under Food allergies, not here. That makes it a hard exclusion covering soybeans, edamame, tofu, tempeh, miso, natto, soy milk, soy protein, textured vegetable protein, soy flour, and most soy sauce.
Soy hides in vegetable broth, baked goods, processed meats, protein bars, Asian sauces, vegetarian meat substitutes, some peanut butters, and natural flavors.
Highly refined soybean oil and soy lecithin are tolerated by most people with soy allergy. The app excludes them by default for allergy and lets you relax that with your allergist's input.
If you avoid soy for other reasons (hormone or GMO concerns), that is a preference. The evidence does not show harm from soy foods in normal amounts.
Soy-free plus vegetarian or vegan narrows your protein options. The app surfaces alternatives: other legumes, seitan if gluten is fine, eggs and dairy if permitted, quinoa, hemp.

sections.heading: What this pattern is
paragraphs: Soy-free means two very different things depending on why you chose it. For a confirmed soy allergy, avoidance is the treatment, and soy is one of the nine major allergens that US law requires on food labels. For everyone else, avoiding soy is a personal preference, and the app files it that way. This module explains both and points allergy to the right place.

sections.heading: What the evidence says
paragraphs: The evidence rating for this module is STRONG for confirmed soy allergy, where avoidance is the treatment, and preference otherwise. The governing sources are the AAAAI and ACAAI food allergy practice parameter (Sampson et al., 2014) and the 2023 anaphylaxis practice parameter, the NIAID-sponsored food allergy guidelines (2010), and the FDA Food Allergen Labeling and Consumer Protection Act (FALCPA, 2004).

FALCPA requires packaged foods containing soy to say so, typically as Contains: Soy. Highly refined soybean oil is exempt from allergen labeling and is tolerated by most people with soy allergy. Soy lecithin is usually tolerated. For preference avoidance, Phase 1 notes that the evidence does not support harm from soy foods in normal amounts.

sections.heading: What to eat more of
paragraphs: Other protein sources, which matter most if you are also vegetarian or vegan: lentils, chickpeas, black beans, kidney beans, peas, and peanuts (if no peanut allergy); quinoa; hemp seeds; seitan if gluten is not a problem; eggs and dairy if your pattern permits them; and meat, poultry, and fish if you eat them.
Cooking sauces without soy: coconut aminos, fish sauce (if no fish allergy), salt and citrus, or homemade sauces where you control the ingredients.
Whole, plain foods that do not need a label check: fresh vegetables and fruit, plain grains, plain meat and fish, eggs, nuts and seeds.

sections.heading: What to limit or avoid
paragraphs: For allergy (hard rule, no override, set under Food allergies): soybeans, edamame, tofu, tempeh, miso, natto, soy milk, soy protein isolate, textured vegetable protein, soy flour, and most soy sauce, which also contains wheat.

For allergy, hidden soy: vegetable broth, baked goods, processed meats, protein bars, Asian sauces, vegetarian meat substitutes, some peanut butters, and natural flavors in some products. The label check catches most of these; the Contains: Soy line is the thing to read.

For allergy, configurable: highly refined soybean oil and soy lecithin. Most people with soy allergy tolerate them, and FALCPA exempts refined oil from labeling. The app excludes both by default and lets you turn them back on with your allergist's input.
For preference (soft rule, override any time): whatever soy foods you choose to skip. The app plans around them and never treats the choice as a medical rule.

sections.heading: Numbers that matter
paragraphs: Nine: the number of major allergens US law requires on labels (milk, egg, fish, crustacean shellfish, tree nuts, peanuts, wheat, soybeans, sesame). Soy has been on the list since FALCPA in 2004.
Zero: the amount of soy the plan includes for a confirmed allergy.
There are no nutrient targets in this module. The number that requires a clinician is your allergist's decision on refined soybean oil and soy lecithin.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and myths
paragraphs: Setting an allergy here instead of under Food allergies. This module is soft. The allergen module is the one nothing can override.

Avoiding soy because of hormone or GMO fears and calling it medical. The evidence does not support harm from soy foods in normal amounts. The app offers a neutral explainer and files this under preference.
Assuming soy sauce is only a soy problem. Most soy sauce also contains wheat, which matters for celiac disease and wheat allergy.

Cutting refined soybean oil and lecithin without asking. Most people with soy allergy tolerate them. That is an allergist conversation, and the default exclusion is there so nothing slips through before you have had it.

sections.heading: When to talk to a clinician
paragraphs: To confirm a soy allergy with an allergist before treating it as one. Self-diagnosed food allergy leads to needless restriction.
To decide whether you can relax the refined soybean oil and soy lecithin exclusions.
If you are vegetarian or vegan and soy-free, and want help keeping protein adequate.

sections.heading: How this app applies it
paragraphs: No phases, no modes. This module carries an information rule pointing confirmed allergy to Food allergies, a soft avoid rule for preference soy avoidance that you can override at any time, a hidden-soy information note, and a configurable rule for refined soybean oil and soy lecithin that defaults to exclude when the soy allergen is selected.
Soft conflict with vegetarian and vegan preferences: soy avoidance narrows the plant-protein base, so the planner surfaces the alternatives listed above rather than leaving a gap.

gut-health.title: Gut health support
summary: Eat 25 to 38 g of fiber a day from a wide variety of plant foods, and add it gradually with plenty of fluid.
Eat many different plants across the week. The 30-plants idea is a reasonable rule of thumb from observational data, not a proven target.
Include some live-culture fermented foods: yogurt, kefir, sauerkraut, kimchi. A small but well-designed trial found they increased microbiome diversity.
Cut back on ultra-processed food, added sugar, and excess alcohol.
Probiotic supplements are not recommended for general gut health, and microbiome test kits are not clinically validated. The app does not recommend either.
If you are in a low FODMAP or low-histamine elimination phase, this module pauses and comes back during reintroduction.

sections.heading: What this pattern is
paragraphs: Gut health support is an eating pattern aimed at feeding the community of microbes in the large intestine and at the outcomes that travel with a high-fiber, plant-diverse diet. It is not a treatment for any digestive disease. The strongest evidence is for fiber and for variety; the evidence for fermented foods is smaller and newer; and most gut-health product claims have no evidence at all.

sections.heading: What the evidence says
paragraphs: The evidence rating for this module is MODERATE for fiber and dietary diversity, LIMITED for fermented foods and specific probiotic foods, and INSUFFICIENT for most gut-health product claims. The governing sources are a series of systematic reviews and meta-analyses commissioned by WHO (Reynolds et al., Lancet 2019), a randomized trial of fermented foods (Wastyk et al., Cell 2021), the American Gut Project observational study (McDonald et al., mSystems 2018), the AGA clinical practice guideline on probiotics (Su et al., 2020), ISAPP consensus statements on prebiotics, probiotics, and fermented foods, and the Institute of Medicine dietary reference intake for fiber.

Reynolds et al. found that eating 25 to 29 g of fiber a day was associated with a 15 to 30 percent lower risk of all-cause and cardiovascular death, and lower rates of type 2 diabetes and colorectal cancer. Wastyk et al. randomized 36 people for 10 weeks and found that a high fermented-food diet increased microbiome diversity and lowered inflammatory markers; small, but well designed. The American Gut Project found that people eating 30 or more plant types a week had more diverse microbiomes, which is observational. The AGA 2020 guideline does not recommend probiotics for most GI conditions outside specific narrow uses.

sections.heading: What to eat more of
paragraphs: Fiber from whole plant foods: vegetables, fruit, whole grains (oats, barley, brown rice, whole wheat), legumes (beans, lentils, chickpeas), nuts, and seeds. Work up to 25 to 38 g a day over a few weeks, and drink more water as you do, or you will get gas and bloating.

Variety. Count different plants across the week: every vegetable, fruit, grain, legume, nut, seed, herb, and spice is a separate plant. Thirty is a reasonable heuristic, not a target you fail by missing.

Live-culture fermented foods most days if you tolerate them: plain yogurt, kefir, sauerkraut, kimchi, and similar foods labeled as containing live cultures. Shelf-stable, pasteurized versions do not carry live cultures.

sections.heading: What to limit or avoid
paragraphs: Soft rules: ultra-processed food, added sugar, and excess alcohol. The app steers away from them; nothing is blocked.
Not recommended, and not in the plan: probiotic supplements for general gut health. The AGA guideline does not support them outside specific narrow uses, and this app never recommends them.
Not recommended: microbiome test kits and personalized microbiome diets. They are not clinically validated.
There are no hard rules in this module.

sections.heading: Numbers that matter
paragraphs: Fiber: 25 to 38 g a day depending on sex and age (Institute of Medicine; 25 g for women, 38 g for men, from the 14 g per 1,000 calorie reference).
25 to 29 g a day: the fiber intake associated with 15 to 30 percent lower all-cause and cardiovascular mortality in Reynolds et al.
30 plant types a week: the American Gut Project heuristic. Observational, not a proven target.
36 people, 10 weeks: the size of the fermented-food trial. Enough to be encouraging, not enough to be definitive.
No numbers in this module require a clinician.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and myths
paragraphs: Buying probiotics for general gut health. The AGA does not recommend them for most GI conditions. The app does not either.
Paying for a microbiome test and a diet built on it. Not clinically validated.
Treating 30 plants a week as a pass-or-fail target. It is a rule of thumb from observational data.
Adding a lot of fiber at once. Gas, bloating, and constipation follow. Increase gradually with fluid.
Believing gut-health product claims. Most have insufficient evidence, and the app makes none of them.

sections.heading: When to talk to a clinician
paragraphs: If you have ongoing digestive symptoms (pain, bloating, diarrhea, constipation, blood, weight loss). This module is for general support, not for diagnosing or treating a condition.
If you have IBS, inflammatory bowel disease, gastroparesis, or diverticular disease, since those modules change what this one does.
Before taking a probiotic supplement for a specific condition. There are narrow uses with evidence, and a clinician can tell you whether yours is one.

sections.heading: How this app applies it
paragraphs: No phases, no modes, no medication questions. Fiber is a daily target of 25 to 38 g summed from the food database. Plant diversity and live-culture fermented foods run through prefer tags; ultra-processed food, added sugar, and alcohol run through soft avoid tags.

Soft conflicts resolved by time limit: the low FODMAP elimination phase (many prebiotic foods are high FODMAP) and the low-histamine trial (fermented and many high-fiber foods are excluded). The app pauses this module's fiber and fermented-food push during those phases and restores it in reintroduction.

Other soft conflicts: gastroparesis wins on texture, with fiber then coming from soluble, cooked, or blended sources. Kidney stones share high-oxalate plants (spinach, nuts, beets); pair them with calcium rather than removing them. During an IBD flare, low-fiber eating temporarily overrides the fiber target; in remission adequate fiber is part of the IBD pattern. During cancer treatment, diarrhea calls for less fiber and constipation for more, so the target follows symptoms.
