food-allergies.title: Food allergies
summary: Food allergens are the one thing in this app that nothing can override. No preference, mode, or acknowledgment removes an allergen exclusion.
The nine FDA major allergens are milk, egg, fish, crustacean shellfish, tree nuts, peanuts, wheat, soybeans, and sesame. You can add your own custom allergens, and they get the same hard treatment.
Avoidance is the treatment for a confirmed food allergy. Diagnosis, testing, and emergency planning belong to your allergist.

Whether you also avoid foods labeled may contain or made in a shared facility is your call. Many people with allergies do; the evidence on actual risk is mixed. The app excludes them by default and lets you change that.
If the app does not recognize an ingredient, it says so. It never assumes an unknown ingredient is safe.
Milk allergy is not lactose intolerance. Milk allergy excludes all dairy; lactose intolerance is about dose.

sections.heading: What this restriction is
paragraphs: A food allergy is an immune reaction to a food protein. Reactions can be mild or life-threatening (anaphylaxis), and the only reliable way to prevent them is to avoid the food. US law (the Food Allergen Labeling and Consumer Protection Act of 2004, with sesame added by the FASTER Act in 2021) requires packaged foods to declare nine major allergens. This module is the app's safety-critical component: Phase 1 says a confirmed allergen slipping through is the single worst failure the app can have.

sections.heading: What the evidence says
paragraphs: The evidence rating for this module is STRONG: avoidance is the treatment for confirmed food allergy. The governing sources are the AAAAI and ACAAI food allergy practice parameter (Sampson et al., 2014), the AAAAI and ACAAI anaphylaxis practice parameter (2023), the NIAID-sponsored guidelines for the diagnosis and management of food allergy in the United States (2010), FALCPA (2004), and the FASTER Act (2021).

FALCPA requires the presence of a major allergen to be declared on the label. Highly refined soybean oil is exempt from allergen labeling and is tolerated by most people with soy allergy; soy lecithin is usually tolerated. Precautionary labels (may contain, made in a facility that also processes) are not required and not standardized, and the evidence on the actual risk they represent is mixed.

sections.heading: What to eat more of
paragraphs: Whole, single-ingredient foods where nothing needs decoding: fresh vegetables and fruit, plain grains, plain meat, poultry, and fish (if not allergic), eggs (if not allergic), beans and lentils.

Replacements that keep the plan complete. Milk allergy: fortified plant milks and non-dairy calcium sources. Egg allergy: other proteins and egg-free binders in baking. Wheat allergy: rice, quinoa, corn, buckwheat, potatoes. Fish or shellfish allergy: other proteins, with omega-3 from flax, chia, and walnuts if nuts are permitted. Nut allergy: seeds, if tolerated. Soy allergy: other legumes, seitan if wheat is fine, eggs and dairy if permitted, quinoa, hemp.
Recipes the app has screened against your allergens. Every recipe passes through the same exact-match screener, and any recipe with an unrecognized ingredient fails rather than passes.

sections.heading: What to limit or avoid
paragraphs: Hard rules, no override: each selected major allergen (milk, egg, fish, crustacean shellfish, tree nuts, peanuts, wheat, soybeans, sesame) and each custom allergen you add. Milk allergy excludes all dairy. Soy allergy excludes soybeans, edamame, tofu, tempeh, miso, natto, soy milk, soy protein isolate, textured vegetable protein, soy flour, and most soy sauce.

Hard by default, configurable with allergist input: highly refined soybean oil and soy lecithin for soy allergy. Most people with soy allergy tolerate them; the app excludes them until you and your allergist decide otherwise.
Configurable, default exclude: foods labeled may contain or made in a shared facility. Many people with allergies avoid these; the evidence on actual risk is mixed. You choose.
Never counted as safe: any ingredient the parser does not recognize. It is reported as not recognized, and the food or recipe fails the allergen check.

sections.heading: Numbers that matter
paragraphs: Nine: the major allergens US law requires on labels. Sesame became the ninth on January 1, 2023 under the FASTER Act.
Zero: the amount of a selected allergen in your plan. There is no threshold, no small-portion allowance, and no acknowledgment path.

Numbers that require a clinician: none of the food rules are numeric. What your allergist decides is which foods are allergens for you, whether refined soybean oil and lecithin can be allowed, whether baked forms of milk or egg are tolerated (the app does not model that), and your emergency plan.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and myths
paragraphs: Confusing lactose intolerance with milk allergy. Lactose intolerance is dose-dependent and lives in its own module. Cow's milk protein allergy is a hard exclusion of all dairy and lives here.
Setting a preference where an allergy belongs. Preference avoidances and the soy-free pattern are soft. Only this module is absolute.
Assuming a food is safe because the app did not flag it, when the app said it did not recognize an ingredient. Not recognized means not checked.
Treating may contain labels as either meaningless or definitive. The evidence on actual risk is mixed, which is why the setting is yours.
Diagnosing an allergy from symptoms alone. Self-diagnosed food allergy leads to needless restriction. Confirm with an allergist.

sections.heading: When to talk to a clinician
paragraphs: To confirm any suspected food allergy before you set it here, and to review the list periodically, since some allergies change over time.
For an emergency plan and any prescribed medication. The app does not cover reactions; it only screens food.
Before relaxing the refined soybean oil and soy lecithin exclusions, or the may-contain setting.
If you are managing a child's allergies. Caregiver mode is available, and the child's allergist should set the list.

sections.heading: How this app applies it
paragraphs: No phases, no modes. Each selected allergen is a hard avoid rule. The ingredient parser and recipe screener use maintained dictionaries with exact matching and never rely on a language model. A hard fail is reported for any allergen match and for any unrecognized ingredient when an allergen is selected. Nothing in settings, preferences, modes, or acknowledgments can override an allergen exclusion.
Caregiver mode lets an adult account holder manage a child's diagnosed food allergies under the same rules, with an age gate on the account holder and pediatrician-reviewed content.

Interactions: soy allergy plus vegetarian or vegan preferences narrows protein options, so the planner surfaces alternatives (other legumes, seitan if no gluten issue, eggs and dairy if permitted, quinoa, hemp). Lactose intolerance and milk allergy are separate settings that do not interfere with each other. Allergen rules stay on in pregnancy mode and through every elimination protocol.

medical-avoidances.title: Medical avoidances
summary: Medical avoidances are the foods the app steers you away from because of a condition you selected. They come from the condition modules; you do not enter them.
Each one shows the condition rule it came from, that rule's evidence rating, and its citation.
You can add notes, but you cannot remove one without acknowledging the condition rule behind it.
Medical and preference avoidances are kept separate. Allergens are stricter still and cannot be removed at all.

sections.heading: What this list is
paragraphs: This is not a condition. It is the app's running list of everything your selected conditions ask you to limit or avoid. Phase 1 defines it simply: derived automatically from selected conditions; the user can annotate but not remove them without acknowledging the condition rule.

sections.heading: What the evidence says
paragraphs: This module is information only, so each avoidance carries the rating of the module it came from: a sodium limit carries the hypertension module's STRONG rating and its 2025 AHA/ACC citation; a low-histamine avoid tag carries the MCAS module's LIMITED rating and its consensus sources. The one source this module cites on its own is the FDA General Wellness policy (revised January 6, 2026), which shapes the wording: the app describes what a guideline recommends for people with a condition; it does not claim to treat the condition.

sections.heading: How firm each item is
paragraphs: Hard items, such as gluten for celiac disease, behave like allergens inside the plan.
Must and should items, such as sugar-sweetened beverages for diabetes or sodium over 2,300 mg for hypertension, are followed by the plan; removing one requires acknowledging the rule.
Time-limited items from low FODMAP and the low-histamine trial appear only while the phase is active, with the phase clock visible.
Suppressed items are shown with the reason when two modules conflict, such as the hypertension potassium target when kidney disease is selected. Nothing is dropped silently.

sections.heading: Numbers that matter
paragraphs: Every numeric limit here (sodium in mg, saturated fat as a percent of calories, added sugar in g, fiber in g) is summed from the food database by grams, never estimated from text. If a module needs a clinician-set number and you have not entered one, the list says that parameter was not applied and names it.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
paragraphs: Deleting an item because it is inconvenient. The acknowledgment step makes the decision deliberate and recorded. Adding a personal dislike here; that belongs under Preference avoidances, where it stays soft.

sections.heading: When to talk to a clinician
paragraphs: Before removing a medical avoidance permanently, ask the clinician managing the condition. When an item shows as suppressed or not applied, the app is telling you a number needs to come from your clinician.

sections.heading: How this app applies it
paragraphs: The list is generated, not typed. Selecting or deselecting a condition changes it. Annotations persist; removals require acknowledging the specific rule and are logged. The list stays separate from preference avoidances in settings and in the planner, so a soft choice is never mistaken for a medical rule.

preference-avoidances.title: Preference avoidances
summary: Preference avoidances are foods you choose not to eat. The app plans around them, and you can override them any time, including for a special occasion.
Halal, kosher, vegetarian, and vegan are ready-made options. Vegetarian and vegan also bring nutrition rules from the vegetarian-vegan module.
Preferences are soft. Medical rules and allergens are not, and a preference can never loosen either.
If a food you avoid is really a medical issue (a diagnosed allergy, celiac disease), set it in the right module so the app treats it as firm.

sections.heading: What this list is
paragraphs: Phase 1 defines preference avoidances as free-form, soft exclusions the user can override at any time, with religious and ethical patterns (halal, kosher, vegetarian, vegan) as pre-built options. This is the place for anything you avoid by choice. The app respects it in every plan and grocery list but never treats it as a medical fact.

sections.heading: What the evidence says
paragraphs: This module is information only and has no evidence rating of its own, because it encodes your choices, not clinical findings. The FDA General Wellness policy (revised January 6, 2026) frames how the app talks about food choices as lifestyle support. The Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics position paper on vegetarian dietary patterns for adults (Raj et al., 2025), which replaced the 2016 paper, is the source behind the vegetarian and vegan options.

sections.heading: How the pre-built options work
paragraphs: Halal and kosher: Phase 1 gives no food rules for these, so each is a soft, user-defined exclusion set. The app does not certify anything as halal or kosher.

Vegetarian and vegan: these switch on the vegetarian-vegan module, which adds nutrition guidance (for example, that vegans need vitamin B12 from fortified foods or a supplement). Custom: any food or category you name.

sections.heading: What is soft and what is not
paragraphs: Soft: everything here. Override an item for one meal or remove it outright, no acknowledgment needed. Not soft: allergens (never overridable) and medical avoidances (removable only with acknowledgment). A preference can restrict on top of those but cannot loosen them.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
paragraphs: Filing a real allergy or celiac disease here, where the app treats it as optional. Avoiding all dairy here because of lactose intolerance and assuming the app is enforcing a medical rule; total dairy avoidance is a preference for most people with lactose intolerance, which is why it belongs here.

sections.heading: When to talk to a clinician
paragraphs: If a preference is standing in for a symptom you have not had checked, or if your combined preferences and medical rules leave few foods (vegan and soy-free, for example, where protein and B12 need attention).

sections.heading: How this app applies it
paragraphs: Preferences are stored per person and applied to recipes and grocery lists as soft filters. Overrides are one tap. When three or more restrictive patterns are active at once, the app shows a plain nutrition-adequacy notice and suggests a dietitian; it does not block anything.

weight-management-glp1.title: Weight management and GLP-1 medications
summary: Weight loss comes from a sustained calorie deficit of about 500 to 750 kcal a day. The eating pattern you can actually keep is the right one.
Losing 5 to 10 percent of your body weight is the goal that improves health; you do not need to reach an ideal weight.
On a GLP-1 medication: eat smaller meals, put protein first, drink enough fluid, get fiber for constipation, and skip very large or fatty meals.
Protect muscle and bone during fast loss with higher protein, about 80 to 120 g a day, plus resistance exercise.
Most people regain weight after stopping a GLP-1, so the plan for keeping weight off matters more than the plan for losing it.
If you also have kidney disease, are pregnant, or are in cancer treatment, your clinician's numbers override this module.

sections.heading: What this condition is
paragraphs: Overweight and obesity mean carrying more body fat than is healthy for you, usually judged by body mass index and waist size together with blood pressure, blood sugar, and cholesterol. GLP-1 medications (semaglutide, tirzepatide, and related drugs) reduce appetite and slow stomach emptying, so people eat less and lose weight quickly. That speed is what makes nutrition matter: eating too little, losing muscle, and falling short on vitamins and minerals are the practical risks.

sections.heading: What the evidence says
paragraphs: The evidence rating is strong that a sustained calorie deficit produces weight loss, moderate that no single diet composition beats the others, and limited (consensus-based) for nutrition advice specific to GLP-1 medications.

The strong part rests on the 2013 AHA/ACC/TOS obesity guideline, a major society guideline built on randomized trials. The moderate part comes from DIETFITS, a 12-month randomized trial in JAMA (2018) in which a healthy low-fat diet and a healthy low-carbohydrate diet produced the same weight loss.

The GLP-1 advice comes from two 2025 to 2026 expert documents: a joint advisory from four societies (ACLM, ASN, OMA, and TOS) in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition, and a modified Delphi consensus led by Sievenpiper in Obesity Pillars with 52 statements. Both are drawn mostly from indirect evidence and bariatric surgery nutrition guidelines. The advisory drew published letters criticizing it for calling itself evidence-based when much of it is extrapolated, and its authors acknowledge the gap. Treat the GLP-1 advice as sensible expert practice, not proven fact.

sections.heading: What to eat more of
paragraphs: Protein at every meal, and eat it first when your appetite is small: eggs, Greek yogurt, cottage cheese, fish, poultry, tofu, beans, and lentils. Fiber from vegetables, fruit, beans, and whole grains, which also helps the constipation that GLP-1 medications commonly cause. Water and other unsweetened fluids through the day.

Any of the well-studied patterns works when calories are controlled: Mediterranean, DASH, low-carbohydrate, or plant-based. Choose the one that fits how you already like to eat, because the pattern you stick with is the one that works.

sections.heading: What to limit or avoid
paragraphs: Soft rules (recommended, not enforced): very large meals and high-fat meals, because they trigger nausea and reflux on a GLP-1; sugary drinks and snack foods that spend your small appetite on foods with little protein or fiber.

Hard rules the app enforces on itself rather than on your food: it does not offer meal replacements or very-low-calorie diets, which are legitimate only under medical supervision. It does not compute a personal calorie number for you.
Optional: there are no banned foods in this module. Alcohol is not addressed by the sources here; other modules you select may limit it.

sections.heading: Numbers that matter
paragraphs: Calorie deficit: 500 to 750 kcal per day below what you burn. The app shows this as a habit and does not calculate your energy needs, so it never sets a daily calorie target.
Weight-loss goal: 5 to 10 percent of starting body weight. For a 200 lb (91 kg) person that is 10 to 20 lb (4.5 to 9 kg).

Protein on a GLP-1: about 80 to 120 g a day. The joint advisory offers this fixed target because per-kilogram targets based on actual body weight can overstate needs in people with obesity; higher targets, such as 1.2 to 1.6 g per kg a day, have also been proposed during active loss. With kidney disease, your clinician sets the protein number instead.
Micronutrients flagged during GLP-1 therapy: iron, vitamin B12, vitamin D, calcium, and folate. The app does not set supplement doses.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and myths
paragraphs: Myth: one diet is best for weight loss. DIETFITS found no difference between healthy low-fat and healthy low-carbohydrate eating at 12 months. Myth: calories do not matter. This is the one area where the experts say they do, so the app talks about a deficit here and almost nowhere else.

Mistake: eating so little on a GLP-1 that protein, fluid, and vitamins fall short. Both GLP-1 documents say to screen for undereating. Mistake: treating the medication as the whole plan; weight regain after stopping is the norm, so build the habits you will keep.
Mistake: using meal replacements or crash diets on your own. They are supervised medical tools, not app features.

sections.heading: When to talk to a clinician
paragraphs: Before starting any weight-loss plan if you have a history of disordered eating; both GLP-1 documents call for screening first. If nausea or vomiting keeps you from eating or drinking, if you feel weak or dizzy, or if you are losing weight faster than your prescriber expected. If you have kidney disease, are pregnant or breastfeeding, or are in cancer treatment. And before stopping a GLP-1, so you have a maintenance plan.

sections.heading: How this app applies it
paragraphs: The app shows the calorie deficit and the 5 to 10 percent goal as habits; it does not calculate your calorie needs. GLP-1 meal habits (smaller meals, protein first, fluids, fiber) appear as reminders. Protein counts toward a daily target of 80 to 120 g.

The guidelines call for screening for disordered eating before weight-focused advice. This app's version is a plain nutrition-adequacy notice when you stack restrictions; it is not a clinical screen, so tell your clinician if you have any eating-disorder history.

Conflicts: with kidney disease (not on dialysis) the protein guidance is a hard conflict and needs a clinician-set protein number. Pregnancy turns this module off entirely. Active cancer treatment flips the goal to preventing weight loss, and the clinician decides. PCOS is compatible; the app does not push calorie restriction on PCOS users who are not overweight.

ckd-non-dialysis.title: Chronic kidney disease, stages 1 to 4
summary: Keep sodium under 2,300 mg a day (the guidelines say under 2 g). This is the rule with the strongest evidence.
Protein around 0.8 g per kg of body weight a day for stages 3 to 5, and never above 1.3 g per kg.
Potassium and phosphorus limits depend on your blood tests. The app never sets them; you enter the numbers your nephrologist or renal dietitian gave you.
Avoid phosphate additives in processed foods and colas before worrying about the natural phosphorus in beans, nuts, and whole grains.
Plant-forward and Mediterranean-style eating is encouraged and is linked with slower progression.
Do not use potassium-based salt substitutes; that hypertension tip does not apply in kidney disease.

sections.heading: What this condition is
paragraphs: Chronic kidney disease means the kidneys have been damaged or have lost filtering ability for at least three months, staged 1 (mild) to 5 (kidney failure). Stages 1 to 4 are managed without dialysis. Diet matters because the kidneys clear sodium, potassium, phosphorus, and the waste from protein; when they work less well, those can build up. Diabetes and high blood pressure are the usual causes, so this condition rarely travels alone.

sections.heading: What the evidence says
paragraphs: The evidence rating is strong for sodium restriction, moderate for protein restriction, and potassium and phosphorus are individualized by lab values and must not be set by an app.

The rules come from three society guidelines: KDIGO 2024 (Kidney International), the KDOQI Nutrition in CKD 2020 update (American Journal of Kidney Diseases), and the KDIGO 2022 guideline on diabetes in CKD. These are systematic-review based guidelines. The protein recommendation is graded lower because trials of protein restriction are smaller and less consistent than the sodium evidence. The link between plant-forward eating and slower progression is observational, so it is encouraged but not proven.

sections.heading: What to eat more of
paragraphs: Vegetables, fruit, whole grains, beans and lentils, and olive oil, in a Mediterranean or plant-forward pattern. Plant foods carry potassium and phosphorus, but the body absorbs less of both from plants than from meat or from additives, and current guidelines encourage plant-forward eating in kidney disease.
Fresh or plain frozen foods cooked at home, which lets you control the salt. Herbs, spices, garlic, lemon, and vinegar for flavor in place of salt.

sections.heading: What to limit or avoid
paragraphs: Hard rules: sodium under 2,300 mg a day, and protein never above 1.3 g per kg of body weight a day. No potassium-based salt substitutes (such as those made with potassium chloride) unless your kidney team approves them.

Soft rules: protein around 0.8 g per kg a day. Avoid phosphate additives: look for 'phos' in ingredient lists (phosphoric acid, sodium phosphate, calcium phosphate, and similar) in colas, processed meats, packaged baked goods, and some cheeses.

Clinician-only rules: any numeric potassium or phosphorus limit, and the supervised low-protein diet of 0.55 to 0.60 g per kg that KDOQI allows for metabolically stable patients. The app does not choose either.

sections.heading: Numbers that matter
paragraphs: Sodium: under 2,300 mg a day; KDIGO and KDOQI both say under 2 g. Protein: 0.8 g per kg a day for CKD stages 3 to 5 not on dialysis (KDIGO 2024), also 0.8 g per kg if you have diabetes. For a 70 kg (154 lb) person that is about 56 g of protein a day. Ceiling: below 1.3 g per kg, which is about 91 g for the same person.

Potassium and phosphorus: the app never sets these numbers. There is no blanket potassium restriction in kidney disease; it applies only when your blood potassium is high, and how much depends on your labs and medications. Phosphorus limits, when needed, also come from labs. Enter the targets your nephrologist or renal dietitian gave you. Without them, the app runs in sodium-and-protein-only mode and says so on screen.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and myths
paragraphs: Myth: everyone with kidney disease must avoid bananas, potatoes, tomatoes, and beans. That is only true when blood potassium is high, and plant potassium is less absorbed than potassium from additives. Cutting plant foods without a reason costs fiber and heart benefits.

Myth: a salt substitute is a safe way to cut sodium. Most are potassium chloride, which is exactly what a damaged kidney may not clear. Mistake: eating high-protein to be healthy; above 1.3 g per kg is a hard ceiling here, and popular high-protein and GLP-1 protein advice conflicts with it.

Mistake: trusting an AI chatbot's nutrient estimates. Published studies show language models get sodium, potassium, and phosphorus wrong. Every number in this app comes from USDA FoodData Central and arithmetic, never from a model's guess.

sections.heading: When to talk to a clinician
paragraphs: Ask your nephrologist or renal dietitian for your potassium, phosphorus, and protein targets and enter them in the app. Talk to them before starting any high-protein, low-carbohydrate, or ketogenic plan, and if you also have heart failure, take a diuretic, ACE inhibitor, ARB, or spironolactone, or have been told your potassium is high. If you start dialysis, switch to the dialysis module; the rules change completely.

sections.heading: How this app applies it
paragraphs: On its own the app applies two things: sodium under 2,300 mg and protein around 0.8 g per kg with a 1.3 g per kg ceiling. Potassium and phosphorus are Tier 2: you enter clinician numbers or the app shows a notice that they were not applied. Phosphate-additive and potassium-additive ingredients are flagged as soft avoids.

Conflicts: the hypertension potassium target (3,500 to 5,000 mg) and any heart-failure DASH potassium encouragement are suppressed; kidney disease wins and the app says why. High-protein older-adult, GLP-1, cancer-treatment, and osteoporosis protein rules all need a clinician-set protein number when combined with this module. Low-carbohydrate and ketogenic patterns need a clinician decision. Dialysis replaces this module entirely, and kidney stones plus CKD sends fluid and protein to the clinician.

masld.title: MASLD (fatty liver disease)
summary: Weight loss is the treatment: losing 5 percent of body weight reduces liver fat, and 7 to 10 percent improves inflammation and scarring.
Eat Mediterranean-style: vegetables, fruit, whole grains, beans, nuts, fish, and olive oil.
Cut sugar-sweetened drinks and added fructose, especially high-fructose corn syrup.
Avoid or minimize alcohol. If you have fibrosis, stop completely.
Unsweetened coffee, 2 to 3 cups a day, is linked to lower fibrosis risk. It is worth mentioning, not a prescription.
This module fits alongside the diabetes, cholesterol, and blood-pressure modules with no conflicts.

sections.heading: What this condition is
paragraphs: MASLD stands for metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, the new name for non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD). Fat builds up in the liver in people with excess weight, type 2 diabetes, high triglycerides, or high blood pressure. In some people the fat leads to inflammation (MASH) and then scarring (fibrosis), which can progress to cirrhosis. It usually causes no symptoms, so it is found on blood tests or imaging.

sections.heading: What the evidence says
paragraphs: The evidence rating is strong for weight loss as treatment, moderate for the Mediterranean pattern, and moderate for limiting fructose and alcohol.

The governing source is the 2023 AASLD Practice Guidance on NAFLD (Hepatology), the American liver society's expert guidance built on trials and cohort studies, with the ADA Standards of Care 2026 covering liver screening in type 2 diabetes. The weight-loss thresholds come from trials that measured liver fat, inflammation, and fibrosis at different amounts of loss. The coffee finding is observational.

sections.heading: What to eat more of
paragraphs: Vegetables, fruit, whole grains, beans and lentils, nuts, fish, and olive oil as the main fat. This Mediterranean pattern is the recommended default because it improves liver fat even before much weight comes off and fits the diabetes and heart conditions that usually come with MASLD.
Water, unsweetened tea, and plain coffee in place of sugary drinks. If you already drink coffee, 2 to 3 cups a day without sugar or cream-heavy additions is associated with lower fibrosis risk.

sections.heading: What to limit or avoid
paragraphs: Soft rules: minimize sugar-sweetened beverages (soda, sweet tea, energy drinks, juice drinks) and foods with added fructose, especially high-fructose corn syrup. Avoid or minimize alcohol.
Hard rule for one group: if you have been told you have fibrosis, abstain from alcohol entirely.
Optional: nothing else is banned. Red meat, eggs, and dairy are not singled out by the liver guidance; the Mediterranean pattern simply keeps them modest.

sections.heading: Numbers that matter
paragraphs: Weight loss: 5 percent of body weight reduces liver fat; 7 to 10 percent improves inflammation and fibrosis. For a 220 lb (100 kg) person, 5 percent is 11 lb (5 kg) and 10 percent is 22 lb (10 kg).

Coffee: 2 to 3 cups a day, unsweetened, is the amount associated with lower fibrosis risk. Alcohol: none if fibrosis is present; otherwise as little as possible. The app sets no calorie target for weight loss; see the weight-management module for how loss is handled.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and myths
paragraphs: Myth: a supplement or detox cleans the liver. The guidance names weight loss and the eating pattern as the treatment; the app does not claim any food or plan treats liver disease. Myth: you need to give up all fat. Olive oil, nuts, and fish are part of the recommended pattern.
Mistake: switching soda for fruit juice. Juice delivers fructose just as effectively. Mistake: treating coffee as medicine; it is an association, and adding sugar and syrups undoes the point.
Mistake: assuming a little alcohol is fine because the disease is 'non-alcoholic'. Alcohol adds to liver injury, and with fibrosis the advice is zero.

sections.heading: When to talk to a clinician
paragraphs: Ask whether you have fibrosis, because that changes the alcohol rule from 'minimize' to 'none'. Talk to your clinician if you have type 2 diabetes and have not been screened for liver disease, if you plan a weight-loss medication or surgery, or if you want to lose more than 10 percent of your weight. Yellowing skin, swelling, or confusion need urgent care.

sections.heading: How this app applies it
paragraphs: The app shows the 5 and 7 to 10 percent weight-loss targets as goals, prefers Mediterranean-pattern foods (vegetables, fruit, whole grains, legumes, nuts, fish, olive oil) in meal plans, and flags sugar-sweetened beverages and added sugar as soft avoids. Alcohol is a soft avoid; you can note fibrosis to make it firm. Coffee appears as an information note only.
There are no conflicts. This module is fully compatible with the type 2 diabetes, high cholesterol, and hypertension modules, which is the usual combination.

gerd.title: GERD and acid reflux
summary: If you carry extra weight, losing some is the single strongest lifestyle lever for reflux.
Stop eating 2 to 3 hours before lying down, and raise the head of your bed for nighttime symptoms.
Eat smaller meals with less fat in each one.
Classic trigger foods (coffee, chocolate, citrus, tomato, spicy, fatty, fizzy drinks, mint, alcohol) are not banned. Avoid only the ones that bother you.
Diet supports treatment; it does not replace medication your clinician prescribed.

sections.heading: What this condition is
paragraphs: Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) is stomach acid flowing back up into the esophagus often enough to cause heartburn, regurgitation, or damage to the lining. The valve at the top of the stomach relaxes or is pushed open by pressure from a full stomach, extra abdominal weight, or lying flat after eating. Diet and habits change that pressure and timing; they are one part of treatment alongside medication when it is needed.

sections.heading: What the evidence says
paragraphs: The evidence rating is moderate for weight loss and meal timing, and limited for eliminating specific trigger foods.

The governing source is the 2022 ACG Clinical Guideline on GERD (American Journal of Gastroenterology), a society guideline built on a systematic review with graded recommendations. Weight loss and not eating before lying down have the best support. The guideline specifically declines to recommend blanket elimination of the classic trigger foods, because the studies behind those lists are weak; it recommends avoiding the foods that trigger you personally.

sections.heading: What to eat more of
paragraphs: The guideline does not name foods that treat reflux. What helps is the shape of eating: smaller portions, meals lower in fat, and an earlier evening meal. If you need to lose weight, the weight-management and Mediterranean modules provide the pattern.
Practical swaps that lower fat per meal: grilled or baked instead of fried, lean cuts and poultry, vegetables and whole grains filling more of the plate, and sauces used lightly.

sections.heading: What to limit or avoid
paragraphs: Soft rules: no eating within 2 to 3 hours of lying down; smaller meals; less fat per meal; weight loss if you are overweight.

Optional toggles, off by default: coffee, chocolate, citrus, tomato, spicy food, fatty and fried food, carbonated drinks, mint, and alcohol. Turn on only the ones you have noticed trigger your symptoms. The app shows the evidence note with each toggle.
There are no hard food rules in this module.

sections.heading: Numbers that matter
paragraphs: Time between your last food and lying down: 2 to 3 hours. Head-of-bed elevation for nighttime symptoms (raise the bed frame or use a wedge; the guideline gives no single height).
The app sets no calorie, fat-gram, or portion-size number for reflux. 'Smaller meals' and 'less fat per meal' are habits; if a weight-loss target applies, it comes from the weight-management module.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and myths
paragraphs: Myth: everyone with reflux must give up coffee, tomatoes, citrus, and chocolate. The evidence for blanket elimination is limited, and cutting foods you tolerate just narrows your diet. Test one at a time if you suspect it.

Mistake: eating a big late dinner and then lying on the couch. Meal size and timing matter more than most individual foods. Mistake: expecting diet to replace a prescribed acid-suppressing medication; the app does not claim the plan treats reflux.
Mistake: skipping the weight lever because it feels indirect. It is the lifestyle change with the strongest evidence.

sections.heading: When to talk to a clinician
paragraphs: See a clinician if you have trouble or pain swallowing, unexplained weight loss, vomiting, black or bloody stools, anemia, or symptoms that persist despite treatment; those need evaluation, not diet changes. Also talk to them before stopping a reflux medication and if symptoms wake you at night despite the timing and elevation changes.

sections.heading: How this app applies it
paragraphs: The app applies the timing rule (no eating 2 to 3 hours before lying down), the smaller-meal and lower-fat-per-meal habits, and the weight-loss habit if you have flagged that your clinician said loss would help. The nine classic trigger foods are optional toggles that are off until you turn them on; nothing is excluded by default.

There are no conflicts with other modules. If you also use the weight-management module, its goals apply; if you use the Mediterranean or DASH modules, their food preferences apply and reflux adds only timing and portion habits.

ibd.title: Inflammatory bowel disease
summary: In remission, eat a Mediterranean-style diet with enough fiber; do not restrict more than you need to. Malnutrition is the bigger danger in IBD.
In remission, go easy on ultra-processed food, emulsifier additives, and added sugar.
During a flare or with a stricture, switch to flare mode: soft cooked vegetables, low fiber, and no nuts, seeds, raw vegetables, or skins, only for as long as needed.
You switch between remission and flare mode. The app never decides you are flaring, and flare mode expires and asks you to check in.
Lactose intolerance is common during active disease, but that is not a reason to give up dairy for good.
Ask your care team to check iron, B12, vitamin D, zinc, and folate.

sections.heading: What this condition is
paragraphs: Inflammatory bowel disease covers Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis, two conditions in which the immune system inflames the digestive tract. Symptoms come and go: periods of remission and periods of active inflammation called flares. Medication controls the disease. Diet's job is to keep you well nourished, help symptoms during flares, and support long-term health, because weight loss, anemia, and vitamin deficiencies are common and harmful in IBD.

sections.heading: What the evidence says
paragraphs: The evidence rating is moderate for a Mediterranean pattern in remission, strong for exclusive enteral nutrition in children with Crohn's (a medical therapy outside this app), limited for named diets such as the Specific Carbohydrate Diet and the Crohn's Disease Exclusion Diet, and insufficient for most diets promoted online.

The sources are the 2024 AGA Clinical Practice Update on diet in IBD (Gastroenterology), an expert review from the American gastroenterology society; the 2020 dietary guidance from the International Organization for the Study of IBD; and DINE-CD, a 2021 randomized trial in Gastroenterology that compared the Specific Carbohydrate Diet with a Mediterranean diet in adults with Crohn's disease and found the SCD was not superior.

sections.heading: What to eat more of
paragraphs: In remission: vegetables, fruit, whole grains, beans and lentils, fish, and olive oil, with enough fiber. Variety protects you against the deficiencies IBD causes, and the Mediterranean pattern matched a far more restrictive diet in the DINE-CD trial.

In a flare: soft, well-cooked, small-particle foods such as peeled cooked vegetables, smooth soups, white rice, eggs, yogurt if tolerated, tender fish and poultry, and ripe bananas. The goal is to keep eating enough while the gut heals.

sections.heading: What to limit or avoid
paragraphs: Soft rules in remission: limit ultra-processed foods, products with emulsifier additives (look for carboxymethylcellulose, polysorbate 80, and carrageenan on labels), and added sugar.

Soft rules in flare mode or with a stricture, temporary only: avoid nuts, seeds, raw vegetables, skins and hulls, and high-fiber, large-particle foods. Prefer low-residue eating until symptoms settle.

Not rules: dairy is not banned. Lactose intolerance is common while the disease is active and often improves; the guidance says it is not a reason for permanent dairy avoidance. There are no hard food rules in this module.

sections.heading: Numbers that matter
paragraphs: The IBD guidance does not give gram targets for fiber, protein, or calories, and the app does not invent them. 'Adequate fiber' in remission and 'low fiber' in a flare are food-texture rules, not numbers.

Flare mode: the app's check-in prompt fires after 14 days. That is an app default for the reminder, not a clinical number; the guidance says only that flare eating should be temporary. Labs to ask for: iron, vitamin B12 (especially after ileal resection), vitamin D, zinc, and folate.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and myths
paragraphs: Myth: a special diet treats IBD. The Specific Carbohydrate Diet was not better than a Mediterranean diet in DINE-CD; the Crohn's Disease Exclusion Diet has limited evidence; 'autoimmune protocol' and most online IBD diets have insufficient evidence. The app does not encode any of them as treatments.

Myth: low FODMAP is an IBD diet. It can ease irritable-bowel symptoms that coexist with IBD in remission (limited evidence), and the app presents it that way, never as a treatment for the inflammation.
Mistake: staying on flare-mode eating for months. Long-term restriction is how malnutrition happens. Mistake: cutting dairy permanently after one bad week during a flare.

sections.heading: When to talk to a clinician
paragraphs: Contact your gastroenterologist if you think you are flaring; the app cannot tell you that. Also if you are losing weight, have blood in your stool, fever, severe pain, or vomiting, or if a flare-mode diet is not helping within days. Ask for the nutrient labs above, and ask before any elimination diet, especially if you have had surgery on the small intestine or have a stricture.

sections.heading: How this app applies it
paragraphs: Two modes. Remission is the default: Mediterranean-pattern foods are preferred and ultra-processed food, emulsifier additives, and added sugar are soft avoids. Flare mode: nuts, seeds, raw vegetables, skins, and high-fiber large-particle foods become soft avoids and soft cooked foods are preferred. You switch the mode; the app never diagnoses a flare. Flare mode expires after 14 days and asks whether you still need it.

Conflicts: flare mode temporarily overrides the gut-health module's fiber target, and remission restores it. With the IBS low-FODMAP module, the app notes that low FODMAP may help coexisting IBS symptoms in remission and is not an IBD treatment. Nutrient risks are shown as a reminder to get labs, not as supplement doses.

pcos.title: PCOS
summary: There is no special PCOS diet. Healthy eating principles apply, shaped to what you like and can keep.
If you carry extra weight, losing 5 to 10 percent improves metabolic, reproductive, and mood outcomes.
If you are not overweight, this app will not push calorie restriction on you.
Lower glycemic index and Mediterranean-style eating have some support for insulin resistance, but nothing decisive.
Gluten-free, dairy-free, and the 'PCOS diets' sold online have no guideline support.

sections.heading: What this condition is
paragraphs: Polycystic ovary syndrome is a hormonal condition affecting women of reproductive age. It involves irregular periods, higher androgen (male-type hormone) levels, and often insulin resistance, which raises long-term risk of type 2 diabetes and heart disease. Weight gain is common but not universal. Because insulin resistance is central, eating patterns that improve blood sugar handling are the natural target, but the evidence for any particular diet is thinner than the marketing suggests.

sections.heading: What the evidence says
paragraphs: The evidence rating is moderate for weight loss (when overweight) and general healthy eating, and limited for any specific diet composition.

The governing source is the 2023 International Evidence-based Guideline for PCOS (Teede and colleagues), published jointly in four endocrinology and fertility journals. It is a systematic-review-based guideline from an international consortium. Its nutrition conclusion is plain: no diet composition is superior, and healthy eating tailored to preference is the recommendation. The guideline also warns explicitly about weight stigma and the risk of disordered eating in this population.

sections.heading: What to eat more of
paragraphs: Vegetables, fruit, whole grains, beans and lentils, nuts, fish, and olive oil. Lower glycemic index choices (intact grains, legumes, most fruit and vegetables over refined starches and sweets) and a Mediterranean-style pattern have supportive but not decisive evidence for insulin resistance, so they are reasonable defaults rather than requirements.
The best pattern is the one you enjoy and can sustain. The guideline's message is that adherence matters more than composition.

sections.heading: What to limit or avoid
paragraphs: There are no hard food rules for PCOS. Soft suggestion: fewer refined starches and sweets, in line with the lower glycemic index pattern.
Optional and only if overweight: a modest calorie deficit aimed at 5 to 10 percent weight loss. This is off unless you have flagged that your clinician said weight loss would help.
Not rules at all: gluten-free and dairy-free eating. The guideline gives them no support for PCOS, and the app does not encode them.

sections.heading: Numbers that matter
paragraphs: Weight loss, only if overweight: 5 to 10 percent of body weight. For a 180 lb (82 kg) person that is 9 to 18 lb (4 to 8 kg). The app sets no calorie target; it shows the goal as a habit and refers to the weight-management module.
There are no PCOS-specific carbohydrate, protein, or fat numbers in the guideline, and the app does not add any.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and myths
paragraphs: Myth: you must go gluten-free or dairy-free. Neither has guideline support for PCOS. Myth: a branded PCOS diet or supplement stack fixes hormones. The guideline found no superior diet composition.

Mistake: dieting when you are not overweight because PCOS is 'a weight condition'. The guideline warns about weight stigma and disordered eating, and the app will not push calorie restriction on you. Mistake: chasing very low carbohydrate on your own; low-carb is not a PCOS recommendation, and if you take diabetes medications it needs a clinician.

sections.heading: When to talk to a clinician
paragraphs: Talk to your clinician about whether weight loss would help you before turning on weight-focused features, and before any restrictive diet if you have ever struggled with eating. See them if periods stop, if you are trying to conceive, or for screening of blood sugar and cholesterol. If you have a history of disordered eating, say so; the guideline calls for screening, and a dietitian can plan with you safely.

sections.heading: How this app applies it
paragraphs: The app prefers Mediterranean and lower glycemic index foods in meal plans and shows the 5 to 10 percent weight-loss goal only when the 'clinician said weight loss would help' flag is on. Without that flag, no calorie restriction is suggested.

The guideline's call for disordered-eating screening is met in this personal app by a plain nutrition-adequacy notice when restrictions stack up, not a clinical screen. Conflicts: none. PCOS is compatible with the weight-management module, and the weight rule applies only if overweight.

gout.title: Gout
summary: Diet helps with gout but does not control it. Urate-lowering medication is the treatment.
Limit alcohol, especially beer and spirits.
Cut back on purine-rich foods: organ meats and some seafood such as anchovies, sardines, and shellfish.
Avoid high-fructose corn syrup and sugar-sweetened drinks.
A DASH or Mediterranean pattern with low-fat dairy is linked with lower urate, and losing weight helps if you carry extra.
Cherries and vitamin C have limited evidence; the app does not promote them.

sections.heading: What this condition is
paragraphs: Gout is arthritis caused by uric acid (urate) crystals forming in joints, most often the big toe, producing sudden, very painful attacks. Urate comes from the breakdown of purines, which the body makes and which also come from food. Blood urate rises when the kidneys clear less or the body makes more. Food affects urate modestly; medication that lowers urate is what prevents attacks and joint damage.

sections.heading: What the evidence says
paragraphs: The evidence rating is moderate for diet as an adjunct; medication is the primary treatment.

The governing source is the 2020 American College of Rheumatology Guideline for the Management of Gout (Arthritis Care and Research), a society guideline with systematic review and graded recommendations. Its dietary recommendations are conditional, meaning the evidence is lower quality or the benefit small, and it states that diet alone is unlikely to control gout. The dairy finding is an association with lower urate, not a trial result.

sections.heading: What to eat more of
paragraphs: A DASH or Mediterranean pattern: vegetables, fruit, whole grains, beans and lentils, and low-fat dairy such as skim milk and low-fat yogurt, which is associated with lower urate. Water and unsweetened drinks in place of sugary ones.

Plant foods, including beans and lentils, are part of the recommended pattern even though some contain purines; the guideline's purine concern is organ meats and certain seafood, not vegetables and legumes.

sections.heading: What to limit or avoid
paragraphs: Soft rules (recommended, not enforced): limit alcohol, with beer and spirits singled out; limit organ meats (liver, kidney, sweetbreads) and purine-rich seafood such as anchovies, sardines, and shellfish; limit high-fructose corn syrup and sugar-sweetened beverages; lose weight if you are overweight.
There are no hard food rules in this module. Nothing must be cut to zero, and moderate portions of ordinary meat and fish are not banned by the guideline.

sections.heading: Numbers that matter
paragraphs: The ACR guideline does not set gram or milligram limits for purines, alcohol, or fructose, and the app does not invent them. The rules are about categories and frequency: less alcohol, fewer high-purine foods, fewer sugary drinks.

Weight loss if overweight is a habit here with no number attached; if you also use the weight-management module, its 5 to 10 percent goal applies. Your urate target is a medical number your clinician sets and monitors; the app never sets it.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and myths
paragraphs: Myth: you can manage gout with diet instead of medication. The ACR states diet alone is unlikely to control gout; urate-lowering therapy is the treatment. The app says this plainly and never claims the plan controls gout.

Myth: cherries, cherry juice, or vitamin C tablets treat gout. The evidence is limited, and the app does not promote them. Myth: all purines are equal. Organ meats and certain seafood are the concern; beans and vegetables are part of the recommended pattern.
Mistake: swapping beer for sugary soda. Sugar-sweetened drinks and high-fructose corn syrup raise urate too.

sections.heading: When to talk to a clinician
paragraphs: See your clinician if you have recurrent attacks, tophi (lumps of urate under the skin), kidney stones, or kidney disease, all of which are reasons to start or adjust urate-lowering medication. Do not stop medication because your diet has improved. Ask before large weight-loss efforts or fasting, which can trigger attacks, and if you also have kidney disease, because the two modules interact through protein and fluid.

sections.heading: How this app applies it
paragraphs: The app tags alcohol, high- and moderate-purine foods, sugar-sweetened beverages, and added sugar as soft avoids, prefers DASH and Mediterranean foods with low-fat dairy, and shows weight loss as a habit if the overweight flag is on. A standing notice states that medication, not diet, is the treatment.
There are no module conflicts. If you use the vegetarian or vegan module, the purine avoids mostly disappear on their own; if you use the DASH or Mediterranean module, the patterns match.

heart-failure.title: Heart failure
summary: Avoid excessive sodium. Under 2,300 mg a day is the working number; the guideline gives no firm threshold.
Do not chase very low sodium. In the SODIUM-HF trial, going below 1,500 mg did not reduce hospitalizations or deaths, though people felt somewhat better.
Fluid limits of 1.5 to 2 L a day apply only in advanced heart failure or low blood sodium, on your cardiologist's instruction. The app never sets a fluid limit.
A DASH eating pattern is reasonable.
Heart-failure medications change how your body handles potassium, so tell the app which ones you take.

sections.heading: What this condition is
paragraphs: Heart failure means the heart cannot pump well enough to meet the body's needs, so fluid backs up in the lungs, legs, and abdomen and people feel short of breath and tired. Sodium makes the body hold water, which is why salt has been the center of heart-failure diet advice for decades. Medications (diuretics, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, and others) do most of the work; diet supports them and interacts with them.

sections.heading: What the evidence says
paragraphs: The evidence rating is moderate for avoiding excessive sodium, limited for any specific sodium number, and limited for fluid restriction.

The governing source is the 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA Guideline for the Management of Heart Failure (Circulation), which gives a Class 2a recommendation to avoid excessive sodium without naming a threshold. The number in this module is informed by SODIUM-HF, a 2022 randomized trial in the Lancet: restricting sodium to under 1,500 mg a day did not reduce clinical events compared with usual care, though quality-of-life measures improved. Fluid restriction rests on expert opinion and applies only to advanced disease or hyponatremia.

sections.heading: What to eat more of
paragraphs: A DASH pattern: vegetables, fruit, whole grains, low-fat dairy, poultry, fish, beans, and nuts. Fresh and plain frozen foods prepared at home, seasoned with herbs, spices, citrus, and vinegar instead of salt.
One caution: DASH is naturally high in potassium, and several heart-failure medications raise blood potassium. The app asks about your medications before it encourages potassium-rich foods.

sections.heading: What to limit or avoid
paragraphs: Soft rule: sodium under 2,300 mg a day. The biggest sources are restaurant food, processed meats, canned soups, frozen meals, breads, cheese, and sauces, not the salt shaker.

Clinician-only rule: a fluid limit of 1.5 to 2 L a day, which applies only in advanced heart failure or low blood sodium and only on your cardiologist's instruction. Without that instruction the app applies no fluid limit at all.
Not a rule: pushing sodium under 1,500 mg. The app does not do it for heart failure, and it does not carry the hypertension module's 1,500 mg ideal into this one.

sections.heading: Numbers that matter
paragraphs: Sodium: under 2,300 mg a day. Fluid: 1.5 to 2 L (about 50 to 68 fl oz) a day only when your clinician tells you to restrict. The app never sets a fluid limit; if you have been told to restrict, enter the number your cardiologist gave you and turn on the advanced heart failure flag.

Potassium: no target is set. Whether you should eat more or less depends on your medications and blood tests, so the app suppresses potassium encouragement once you report a diuretic, ACE inhibitor, ARB, spironolactone or another MRA, or a potassium-sparing diuretic, and reminds you that your potassium should be monitored.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and myths
paragraphs: Myth: the lower the sodium, the better. That was standard advice for decades and SODIUM-HF did not support it; under 1,500 mg did not prevent hospitalizations or deaths. Excessive sodium is still worth avoiding.

Myth: everyone with heart failure must limit fluids. Fluid restriction has limited evidence and is reserved for advanced disease or low blood sodium, on clinician instruction. Mistake: loading up on potassium-rich foods or potassium salt substitutes while taking spironolactone or an ACE inhibitor; that combination can push blood potassium dangerously high.
Mistake: judging sodium by taste. Bread, cheese, and deli meat carry far more than you can taste.

sections.heading: When to talk to a clinician
paragraphs: Call your cardiology team if you gain weight quickly (they will tell you the amount to watch), if swelling or breathlessness worsens, or if you become dizzy or faint. Ask them whether you need a fluid limit and what number, whether your potassium needs monitoring on your medications, and before starting any salt substitute. If you also have kidney disease, both teams need to agree on potassium and fluid.

sections.heading: How this app applies it
paragraphs: Sodium under 2,300 mg is applied as a Tier 1 limit. The fluid rule appears only when you set the 'told by your cardiologist to restrict fluids' flag, and then only with the number you enter; the app never generates one. DASH foods are preferred. The medication question about diuretics, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, and MRAs suppresses potassium encouragement and adds a monitoring reminder.

Conflicts: with chronic kidney disease, any potassium encouragement is suppressed because CKD potassium is set by labs. With hypertension the sodium ceiling and DASH pattern match, and heart failure does not push the 1,500 mg ideal. With dialysis, both modules carry clinician-set fluid limits and your clinicians reconcile them.

vegetarian-vegan.title: Vegetarian, vegan, and pescatarian
summary: Appropriately planned vegetarian and vegan diets can be nutritionally adequate for adults and are linked with lower heart and metabolic risk.
If you are vegan, vitamin B12 must come from fortified foods or a supplement. There is no plant food source, and this is the one supplement the app says is required.

Watch vitamin B12, iodine, iron (pair it with vitamin C, and skip tea and coffee at meals), choline, and vitamin D, and calcium if you are vegan. Zinc and omega-3 from flax, chia, and walnuts matter too.
Protein is easy with variety: beans, lentils, soy, whole grains, nuts, and seeds.
Pescatarians keep fish and seafood, which supplies EPA and DHA omega-3 directly.
If you avoid soy too, the app surfaces other proteins: other legumes, seitan if gluten is fine, quinoa, hemp, and eggs or dairy if you eat them.
Pregnant or breastfeeding: the Academy's 2025 position does not cover these stages, so get a plan from your doctor or dietitian.

sections.heading: What this pattern is
paragraphs: Vegetarian eating leaves out meat, poultry, and fish; vegan eating also leaves out dairy, eggs, and other animal products; pescatarian eating leaves out meat and poultry but keeps fish and seafood. People choose these patterns for health, ethics, religion, or the environment. Well-planned versions supply everything the body needs, with a short list of nutrients that take deliberate attention, and one, vitamin B12, that a fully plant-based diet cannot supply from food.

sections.heading: What the evidence says
paragraphs: The evidence rating is strong that well-planned vegetarian and vegan diets are nutritionally adequate and associated with lower cardiometabolic risk.

The governing source is the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics position paper Vegetarian Dietary Patterns for Adults (2025, in effect until 2032), which replaced the 2016 paper for adults who are not pregnant or breastfeeding. It states that appropriately planned vegetarian and vegan dietary patterns can be nutritionally adequate and can offer long-term health benefits, and it names vitamin B12, iodine, iron, choline, and vitamin D as the micronutrients of concern, with calcium also a concern for vegans. Two large cohort studies, EPIC-Oxford in the United Kingdom and Adventist Health Study 2 in North America, followed tens of thousands of people and found lower rates of heart disease and metabolic conditions among vegetarians. The retired 2016 paper is still cited for zinc, which the 2025 paper does not discuss.

sections.heading: What to eat more of
paragraphs: Protein from variety: beans, lentils, chickpeas, tofu, tempeh, edamame, whole grains, nuts, and seeds. Iron-rich plant foods (lentils, beans, tofu, spinach, fortified cereals) paired with vitamin C (peppers, citrus, tomatoes, strawberries) in the same meal to improve absorption.

Calcium from fortified plant milks, tofu set with calcium, and leafy greens; iodine from iodized salt or seaweed in modest amounts; omega-3 ALA from ground flax, chia, and walnuts, with algae-based EPA and DHA as an optional supplement. Choline from nuts, beans and lentils, soy foods, and whole grains every day. Vegans: B12-fortified foods (nutritional yeast, fortified plant milks and cereals) or a B12 supplement every day.
Pescatarians: fish and seafood two or more times a week cover EPA and DHA directly, and provide iodine and B12 as well.

sections.heading: What to limit or avoid
paragraphs: The exclusions are soft, preference-based rules the app applies to recipes and foods: vegetarian excludes red meat, poultry, fish, and processed meat; vegan also excludes dairy and eggs; pescatarian excludes red meat, poultry, and processed meat and keeps fish.
Hard rule for vegans: a B12 source is required. The app will not present a vegan plan as complete without one. Soft rule: tea and coffee away from iron-rich meals, because they block iron absorption.
Optional: algae-based EPA and DHA. The app does not recommend supplements beyond B12 for vegans.

sections.heading: Numbers that matter
paragraphs: The position papers do not set gram targets that differ from general dietary reference intakes, and the app does not add any. The rule that matters is a yes-or-no: vegans have a daily B12 source, from fortified food or a supplement.
Nutrients the app lists in your plan: vitamin B12, iodine, iron, choline, and vitamin D, calcium for vegans, and zinc and omega-3. They are reminders; the app does not prescribe doses.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and myths
paragraphs: Myth: plant diets cannot supply enough protein. With variety they do; the cohorts of long-term vegetarians are the evidence. Myth: spirulina, fermented foods, or unwashed produce give vegans B12. There is no reliable plant source; fortified food or a supplement is required.

Mistake: living on pasta, bread, and cheese and calling it vegetarian. Adequacy comes from legumes, whole grains, nuts, seeds, and vegetables. Mistake: drinking tea or coffee with your lentils, which cuts iron absorption. Mistake: going vegan and soy-free at once without planning; the protein base gets narrow and the app will point you to alternatives.

sections.heading: When to talk to a clinician
paragraphs: Ask for iron, B12, and vitamin D checks if you are vegan or have been vegetarian for years, especially with fatigue, and before pregnancy or while breastfeeding, when needs rise. See a clinician or dietitian if you have kidney disease (plant potassium and phosphorus are handled differently), a soy allergy, or a history of disordered eating, because a restrictive pattern can hide one. The Academy's 2025 position covers adults who are not pregnant or breastfeeding, so a vegetarian or vegan plan for pregnancy or breastfeeding should come from your clinician or a dietitian.

sections.heading: How this app applies it
paragraphs: Three variants: vegetarian, vegan, and pescatarian. Each is a soft exclusion set applied to recipes and foods (the vegan variant maps egg ingredients through the egg allergen tag to catch them). The vegan variant adds the required B12 rule as a supplement-or-fortified-food reminder; no daily food number is enforced. Iron and vitamin C pairing and the tea-and-coffee timing appear as habits, and legumes, soy, whole grains, nuts, and seeds are preferred. If you are pregnant or breastfeeding, the plan adds a reminder to get specific guidance, because the 2025 position does not cover those stages.

Conflicts: with the soy-free module or a soy allergy, the app surfaces alternative proteins because the base narrows. Iron-deficiency anemia raises the iron guidance automatically. The thyroid module is compatible; soy at normal intake with adequate iodine is fine, and only levothyroxine timing applies.

low-carb-ketogenic.title: Low-carbohydrate and ketogenic
summary: Low-carb means under 130 g of carbohydrate a day. Ketogenic means under 50 g, usually 20 to 50 g.
Both can improve blood sugar and weight in the short term. Long-term evidence is thinner.

Before starting, talk with your clinician if you take an SGLT2 inhibitor, insulin, or a sulfonylurea; are pregnant or breastfeeding; or have kidney disease, past pancreatitis, a rare metabolic disorder, or a history of disordered eating. Each changes whether this is safe for you. The app asks about the medicines and pregnancy, and flags kidney disease if it is on your list. It cannot check for the rest.
Build it on non-starchy vegetables, unsaturated fats, and fiber. Processed meat and butter do not make a heart-healthy low-carb diet.
Ketogenic diets for epilepsy are real medicine, prescribed and monitored by clinicians, and are outside this app.

sections.heading: What this pattern is
paragraphs: A low-carbohydrate diet cuts starches and sugars (bread, rice, pasta, potatoes, sweets, sugary drinks) and replaces the calories with protein, fat, and non-starchy vegetables. A ketogenic diet goes further, low enough in carbohydrate that the body switches to burning fat and producing ketones. Both lower blood sugar and insulin quickly, which is why people with type 2 diabetes and people trying to lose weight use them, and why they interact with diabetes medications.

sections.heading: What the evidence says
paragraphs: The evidence rating is moderate for short-term blood sugar control and weight loss, limited for long-term outcomes, and strong for ketogenic diets in drug-resistant epilepsy, which is medically supervised and outside this app.

The ADA Standards of Care 2026 accept low-carbohydrate eating as one acceptable pattern for diabetes. DIETFITS, a 12-month randomized trial in JAMA (2018), found no difference in weight loss between a healthy low-carbohydrate and a healthy low-fat diet. The epilepsy evidence is a 2020 Cochrane systematic review of randomized trials, which is why that use is clinician territory.

sections.heading: What to eat more of
paragraphs: Non-starchy vegetables in volume: leafy greens, broccoli, cauliflower, peppers, zucchini, mushrooms, tomatoes. Unsaturated fats: olive oil, avocado, nuts, seeds, and fatty fish such as salmon and sardines. Fiber from those vegetables, nuts, seeds, and (in the low-carb tier) modest portions of beans and berries.
Protein from fish, poultry, eggs, tofu, and dairy. The version of this pattern with the best heart profile looks like a Mediterranean diet with the starch removed.

sections.heading: What to limit or avoid
paragraphs: Soft rules: carbohydrate under 130 g a day (low-carb) or under 50 g a day (ketogenic), applied as a daily limit in meal plans. Processed meat is a soft avoid, and the saturated fat ceiling from the cholesterol module still applies if you use it.

Hard rules: the app will not start this pattern for someone who is pregnant or breastfeeding (pregnancy mode disables ketogenic and low-carb under 175 g). Kidney disease requires a clinician decision. If you take an SGLT2 inhibitor, insulin, or a sulfonylurea, the app shows a warning that the pattern needs your clinician's sign-off before you follow it.
Not offered at all: therapeutic ketogenic diets for epilepsy or other neurological conditions.

sections.heading: Numbers that matter
paragraphs: Low-carb: under 130 g of carbohydrate a day. Ketogenic: under 50 g a day, typically 20 to 50 g. For scale, one slice of bread or a medium apple is roughly 15 to 25 g, and a cup of cooked rice about 45 g.

No calorie, protein, or fat numbers are set by this module. If you take insulin or a sulfonylurea, the numbers that matter most are your medication doses, which must be adjusted by your prescriber before carbohydrate drops; the app never adjusts them.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and myths
paragraphs: Myth: low-carb beats low-fat for weight loss. DIETFITS found no difference at 12 months when both were built on whole foods. Myth: any low-carb diet is heart-healthy. One built on bacon, butter, and processed meat is not, and the saturated fat limit still applies.

Mistake: starting keto while on an SGLT2 inhibitor. That combination carries a risk of euglycemic ketoacidosis, a dangerous state with near-normal blood sugar. Mistake: cutting carbohydrate on insulin or a sulfonylurea without a dose change, which risks hypoglycemia.
Mistake: treating the epilepsy evidence as proof that keto treats other brain conditions; that use is strong only for drug-resistant epilepsy and only under medical supervision.

sections.heading: When to talk to a clinician
paragraphs: Before starting if you take an SGLT2 inhibitor, insulin, or a sulfonylurea; if you are pregnant, breastfeeding, or trying to conceive; if you have kidney disease, a history of pancreatitis, a rare metabolic disorder, or a history of disordered eating. During the diet if you feel faint, have severe nausea or abdominal pain, or notice symptoms of low blood sugar. Ask about cholesterol monitoring if your LDL rises.

sections.heading: How this app applies it
paragraphs: Two variants: low-carb (under 130 g a day, the default) and ketogenic (under 50 g a day). Two medication questions gate the module: SGLT2 inhibitor use and insulin or sulfonylurea use each require clinician sign-off and add a risk flag. Non-starchy vegetables, olive oil, nuts, seeds, and fish are preferred; processed meat is a soft avoid.

Conflicts: pregnancy wins and disables the pattern. Chronic kidney disease and dialysis send the decision to a clinician. Type 2 diabetes is a soft conflict handled by the medication screen. High cholesterol is a soft conflict: the saturated fat limit stays on. The restriction-load notice appears if you stack this with other elimination patterns.

higher-protein-older-adult.title: Higher protein for older adults
summary: After 65, you need more protein per kilogram than younger adults to hold on to muscle.
Healthy older adults: 1.0 to 1.2 g of protein per kg of body weight a day. With an acute or chronic illness: 1.2 to 1.5 g per kg.
Spread it out: 25 to 30 g of protein at each meal, not one big serving at dinner.
Pair protein with resistance exercise; the two work together.
If you have kidney disease, your clinician sets your protein number, not this module.

sections.heading: What this pattern is
paragraphs: With age, the body becomes less efficient at turning dietary protein into muscle, and muscle loss (sarcopenia) leads to weakness, falls, and loss of independence. Older adults also tend to eat less, so protein falls short just when it matters more. A higher-protein pattern is not a bodybuilding diet; it is enough protein, at each meal, to keep the muscle you have, combined with the strength training that tells the muscle to use it.

sections.heading: What the evidence says
paragraphs: The evidence rating is moderate.

The sources are the PROT-AGE Study Group position paper (Journal of the American Medical Directors Association, 2013), an international expert group's evidence review, and the 2022 ESPEN practical guideline on clinical nutrition and hydration in geriatrics (Clinical Nutrition), a European society guideline. Both are built on trials and observational studies of muscle, function, and protein intake in people over 65. The per-meal distribution and the exercise pairing come from PROT-AGE.

sections.heading: What to eat more of
paragraphs: A protein food at every meal: eggs, Greek yogurt, cottage cheese, milk, fish, poultry, lean meat, tofu, tempeh, beans, and lentils. Breakfast is where most people fall short; two eggs with a glass of milk or a cup of Greek yogurt with nuts gets you to the 25 to 30 g range.

If appetite is small, lean on protein-dense, easy foods: yogurt, cheese, eggs, canned fish, milk-based soups, and smoothies with milk or soy milk. Plant proteins count fully; variety and total amount matter.

sections.heading: What to limit or avoid
paragraphs: There are no food avoids in this module; it adds protein rather than removing anything. Soft rules: hit the per-kilogram target and distribute it as 25 to 30 g per meal.

Clinician-only rule: if you have chronic kidney disease not on dialysis, the higher target conflicts with kidney protein limits and the app will not apply it without a clinician-set number. On dialysis, the ranges overlap and the renal dietitian's number governs.

sections.heading: Numbers that matter
paragraphs: Healthy older adult (65-plus): 1.0 to 1.2 g of protein per kg of body weight a day. For a 70 kg (154 lb) person that is 70 to 84 g a day. With an acute or chronic illness: 1.2 to 1.5 g per kg, or 84 to 105 g a day for the same person.

Per meal: 25 to 30 g. For reference, a 3 oz (85 g) portion of cooked chicken or fish has about 20 to 25 g, one egg about 6 g, a cup of Greek yogurt about 17 to 20 g, and a cup of cooked lentils about 18 g. The app does not set a calorie target.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and myths
paragraphs: Myth: older people need less protein because they are less active. It is the reverse; they need more per kilogram to preserve muscle. Myth: protein harms healthy kidneys. The concern applies to people with existing kidney disease, which is why the app requires a clinician number in that case.

Mistake: eating almost all the day's protein at dinner. Muscle building responds to each meal, so 25 to 30 g three times a day beats 10, 10, and 60. Mistake: protein without strength training. Resistance exercise is half of the recommendation.
Mistake: choosing the 'illness' variant casually. The 1.2 to 1.5 g per kg range is for acute or chronic illness; use the healthy range otherwise.

sections.heading: When to talk to a clinician
paragraphs: Ask your clinician which range applies to you if you have a chronic illness, recent surgery, or a hospital stay. Talk to them before raising protein if you have kidney disease, liver disease, or are on dialysis. See them if you are losing weight without trying, feel weaker, or have fallen; unintended weight loss in older adults needs evaluation, and a dietitian can plan protein around a small appetite.

sections.heading: How this app applies it
paragraphs: Two variants you choose: 'healthy older adult' applies 1.0 to 1.2 g per kg, and 'older adult with an acute or chronic illness' applies 1.2 to 1.5 g per kg; the illness flag selects the second. Both apply the 25 to 30 g per meal spread. Protein-rich foods are preferred in meal plans; nothing is excluded.

Conflicts: chronic kidney disease not on dialysis is a hard conflict resolved only by a clinician-set protein number. Dialysis is compatible in range but the renal dietitian's number governs. If you also use the weight-management or GLP-1 module, the protein guidance there points the same direction.
