pregnancy-gdm-breastfeeding.title: Pregnancy, gestational diabetes, and breastfeeding
summary: Pregnancy: take 400 mcg of folic acid a day from before conception through the first trimester, plus a prenatal vitamin with iron, iodine, choline, DHA, vitamin D, and calcium.

Pregnancy: no alcohol, caffeine under 200 mg a day, 8 to 12 oz a week of low-mercury fish, and strict food safety (no unpasteurized dairy or juice, raw or undercooked meat, fish, or eggs, cold deli meats, refrigerated smoked seafood, or raw sprouts).

Pregnancy: the goal is healthy weight gain by your pre-pregnancy BMI, never weight loss. The app turns off weight loss, ketogenic and low-carb under 175 g, intermittent fasting, and elimination diets except allergen and celiac rules.
Gestational diabetes: nutrition therapy from a dietitian is the first treatment. Your clinician sets the carbohydrate target (at least 175 g a day); the app never generates it.
Breastfeeding: about 330 to 400 extra kcal a day, plenty of fluid, 290 mcg of iodine a day, continued DHA, minimal and timed alcohol, moderate caffeine.
Breastfeeding: do not cut foods from your own diet for infant colic or eczema unless a clinician confirms a cow's milk protein allergy.

sections.heading: What this covers
paragraphs: Three situations with different needs. Pregnancy raises the need for folate, iron, iodine, choline, DHA, and calories, while food-borne infections and mercury pose risks to the fetus. Gestational diabetes (GDM) is high blood sugar first found in pregnancy, treated first with medical nutrition therapy and glucose monitoring. Breastfeeding raises calorie, fluid, and iodine needs and reopens questions about alcohol and caffeine. This module has one variant for each.

sections.heading: What the evidence says
paragraphs: The evidence rating is strong for the core pregnancy nutrition rules, strong for GDM medical nutrition therapy, and moderate for breastfeeding-specific guidance.

The sources are society guidelines and government agencies: ACOG practice bulletins, including Bulletin 230 on obesity in pregnancy (2021) and Bulletin 190 on gestational diabetes (2018, reaffirmed 2026); the ADA Standards of Care 2026, Section 15 on diabetes in pregnancy; the Institute of Medicine 2009 weight-gain guidelines; the FDA and EPA 2021 fish advice; and the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics 2014 pregnancy position, which is no longer a current Academy position.

sections.heading: Pregnancy: what to eat more of and what to avoid
paragraphs: More of: folate-rich foods (leafy greens, beans, lentils, fortified grains) on top of the supplement; iron from lean meat, beans, and fortified cereal with vitamin C; iodine from iodized salt, dairy, and seafood; choline from eggs; calcium from dairy or fortified alternatives; and 8 to 12 oz a week of low-mercury fish such as salmon, sardines, trout, shrimp, cod, tilapia, and canned light tuna. Calories rise modestly: none extra in the first trimester, roughly 340 kcal a day in the second, and 450 in the third for a single baby.

Hard rules (enforced): no alcohol; no unpasteurized dairy or juice; no raw or undercooked meat, fish, or eggs; no deli meats or hot dogs unless heated steaming hot; no refrigerated smoked seafood; no raw sprouts; no shark, swordfish, king mackerel, tilefish, bigeye tuna, orange roughy, or marlin. Caffeine under 200 mg a day (about one 12 oz coffee). Weight-loss features are off.
Soft rules: the fish target and the calorie increases are guidance, not enforced limits.

sections.heading: Gestational diabetes: what changes
paragraphs: All pregnancy rules stay on. Added: medical nutrition therapy from a registered dietitian is the first-line treatment, and ACOG and ADA both call for it. Carbohydrate is not eliminated; the minimum is 175 g a day (the Dietary Reference Intake for pregnancy), spread over three meals and two to three snacks, favoring whole grains, beans, vegetables, fruit, and fiber, and avoiding concentrated sweets and sugary drinks (a soft avoid).

Two approaches are in use: older guidance capped carbohydrate at 33 to 40 percent of calories; newer evidence supports a higher complex-carbohydrate, lower-fat approach. Your dietitian chooses. Glucose readings drive the adjustments, and the app cannot see them unless you enter them. The app never generates a GDM carbohydrate target; without a clinician number it is education and referral only.

sections.heading: Breastfeeding: what changes
paragraphs: Roughly 330 to 400 extra kcal a day and enough fluid. Iodine 290 mcg a day (iodized salt, dairy, seafood, plus a prenatal vitamin); continue DHA. Alcohol minimal and timed away from feeds; caffeine moderate.

Do not start a maternal elimination diet for infant colic or eczema on your own; the evidence is weak. Removing cow's milk protein has some support only when a clinician has confirmed a cow's milk protein allergy in the infant. The app does not encode blanket maternal eliminations.

sections.heading: Numbers that matter
paragraphs: Pregnancy: folic acid 400 mcg a day supplemental (600 mcg dietary folate equivalents total); iodine 150 mcg a day supplemental per ACOG and the American Thyroid Association; caffeine under 200 mg a day; fish 8 to 12 oz a week; calories plus 340 kcal a day in the second trimester and plus 450 in the third. Weight gain: by your pre-pregnancy BMI category per the Institute of Medicine 2009 ranges, which your prenatal clinician gives you.
GDM: carbohydrate at least 175 g a day; the actual target is a clinician's number and the app never sets it. Breastfeeding: plus 330 to 400 kcal a day; iodine 290 mcg a day.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and myths
paragraphs: Myth: avoid all fish in pregnancy. Low-mercury fish is recommended at 8 to 12 oz a week; only the seven high-mercury species are off the list. Myth: gestational diabetes means cutting carbohydrate to the bone. Under 175 g a day is not safe in pregnancy, so the app disables it.

Mistake: dieting to control weight gain. Pregnancy is about gaining the right amount, not losing; weight-loss tools are disabled. Mistake: starting folic acid after the positive test; it matters most before conception and in the first weeks.

Mistake: cutting dairy, wheat, or eggs from your own diet while breastfeeding because the baby is fussy. Evidence is weak unless a cow's milk protein allergy is confirmed. This app does not 'manage' gestational diabetes; your clinician and dietitian do.

sections.heading: When to talk to a clinician
paragraphs: Before pregnancy, to start folic acid and review medications. At every prenatal visit for your weight-gain range. Immediately if you are diagnosed with gestational diabetes, for a dietitian referral and a carbohydrate target. If you have pre-existing diabetes, your carbohydrate plan is clinician-set. While breastfeeding, before any elimination diet, and if you are vegan (B12 and iodine need attention for both of you).

sections.heading: How this app applies it
paragraphs: Three variants: pregnant, gestational diabetes, and breastfeeding. Pregnancy mode enforces the food-safety and mercury avoids, the alcohol ban, and the caffeine limit, shows the folic acid and prenatal-vitamin rules, and disables weight loss, ketogenic eating, low-carb under 175 g, intermittent fasting, and every elimination protocol except allergen and celiac rules. The GDM variant is Tier 2: enter your clinician's carbohydrate target and the app builds around it; without one it shows education and a referral prompt. The breastfeeding variant shows the calorie, fluid, iodine, DHA, alcohol, and caffeine guidance and refuses blanket maternal eliminations.
Conflicts: pregnancy wins over the weight-management, low-carb, IBS low-FODMAP, and MCAS modules. Type 2 diabetes in pregnancy is clinician-set. Celiac and food-allergy rules stay on.

cancer-nutrition.title: Cancer nutrition
summary: After treatment, and for prevention, the best-supported pattern is plant-forward: vegetables, fruit, whole grains, and beans, with a healthy weight and regular activity.
Limit red and processed meat, sugar-sweetened drinks, and ultra-processed food. For cancer risk, no alcohol is best.
During treatment the goal flips: keep your weight and muscle, which often means eating more calorie-dense food. Your oncology dietitian sets the energy and protein targets; the app never does.
Side effects have practical workarounds: small frequent bland meals for nausea, soft non-acidic food for mouth sores, low-fiber low-fat food and fluids for diarrhea.
No food, diet, or supplement treats, shrinks, or prevents the return of cancer. The app will not claim otherwise.
The old restrictive 'neutropenic diet' is not supported by evidence; safe food handling is what matters.

sections.heading: What this covers
paragraphs: Two very different situations. Active treatment (chemotherapy, radiation, surgery recovery) often causes nausea, taste changes, mouth sores, diarrhea, or constipation, and the medical danger is losing weight and muscle, which worsens outcomes. Survivorship, after treatment ends, and prevention share the same goal as general healthy eating: lower the risk of recurrence and of other chronic disease. The module has a variant for each, and the active-treatment variant runs only with a clinician's numbers.

sections.heading: What the evidence says
paragraphs: The evidence rating is strong for the survivorship eating pattern, moderate for symptom-management strategies during treatment, and insufficient for so-called anti-cancer diets.

The survivorship pattern rests on the 2022 American Cancer Society guideline for cancer survivors (CA: A Cancer Journal for Clinicians) and the World Cancer Research Fund / AICR Continuous Update Project, both large systematic evidence reviews. Treatment-phase targets come from the 2021 ESPEN practical guideline on clinical nutrition in cancer (Clinical Nutrition) and the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics oncology practice guideline. The 2022 ASCO guideline on exercise, diet, and weight management during treatment (Journal of Clinical Oncology) reviewed the trials and found insufficient evidence to recommend any specific diet or supplement to improve treatment outcomes.

sections.heading: What to eat more of
paragraphs: Survivorship and prevention: vegetables, fruit, whole grains, and beans and lentils as the base of most meals; a healthy weight; and regular physical activity. This is the ACS and WCRF consensus.

During treatment: whatever keeps calories and protein up. Full-fat dairy, eggs, nut butters, smoothies, cheese, fish, poultry, and added olive oil are tools, not problems. For nausea, small frequent meals of bland, cold foods; for a metallic taste, marinades and plastic utensils; for mouth sores, soft and non-acidic foods; for diarrhea, low-fiber, low-fat food and fluids; for constipation, fiber and fluids.

sections.heading: What to limit or avoid
paragraphs: Survivorship soft rules: limit red and processed meat, sugar-sweetened beverages, and ultra-processed food; limit alcohol, and for cancer risk none is best.

During treatment: no food category is banned. Food safety matters when white blood cell counts are low (wash produce, cook meat and eggs thoroughly, avoid unpasteurized products), but the restrictive neutropenic diet is not supported by evidence and most centers no longer recommend it.

Hard refusals by the app: no alkaline diet, no 'sugar feeds cancer' restriction, no high-dose antioxidant supplements (which can interfere with chemotherapy and radiation), and no fasting protocols during treatment outside a clinical trial.

sections.heading: Numbers that matter
paragraphs: Active treatment: energy roughly 25 to 30 kcal per kg of body weight a day and protein 1.0 to 1.5 g per kg a day per ESPEN, higher with cachexia. For a 70 kg (154 lb) person that is about 1,750 to 2,100 kcal and 70 to 105 g of protein. These are clinician numbers: the app never sets energy or protein targets for cancer treatment. Enter what your oncology dietitian gave you; without them the active-treatment variant is education and referral only.
Survivorship: no numeric targets beyond general healthy-weight guidance; the pattern is the rule.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and myths
paragraphs: Myth: sugar feeds cancer, so cut all carbohydrate. Not supported, and cutting calories during treatment is the opposite of what protects you. Myth: an alkaline diet, juice cleanse, or high-dose vitamin regimen shrinks tumors. No evidence, and high-dose antioxidants can interfere with chemotherapy and radiation.

Myth: fasting or keto during treatment improves outcomes. ASCO 2022 found insufficient evidence for ketogenic, fasting, low-fat, plant-based, or supplement approaches to improve treatment outcomes; fasting protocols belong in clinical trials. Mistake: eating 'clean' and losing weight during chemotherapy. Weight and muscle loss is the real risk.
Mistake: a strict neutropenic diet that cuts fresh fruit and vegetables. Safe handling, not restriction, is the evidence-based approach.

sections.heading: When to talk to a clinician
paragraphs: Ask your oncology team for a referral to an oncology dietitian at diagnosis, and get energy and protein targets to enter in the app. Tell them right away about weight loss, inability to eat or drink for more than a day, severe mouth pain, persistent vomiting or diarrhea, or fever during treatment. Ask before taking any supplement, because some interact with treatment. After treatment, ask what a healthy weight and activity plan looks like for you.

sections.heading: How this app applies it
paragraphs: Two variants. Survivorship and prevention (the default) prefers vegetables, fruit, whole grains, and legumes and marks red and processed meat, sugar-sweetened beverages, ultra-processed food, and alcohol as soft avoids. Active treatment is Tier 2: turn on the 'currently in active cancer treatment' flag, enter the energy and protein targets from your oncology dietitian, and the app builds around them and offers symptom-specific recipes; without those numbers it shows education and a referral prompt.

Conflicts: with the weight-management module during active treatment, the clinician decides, because preventing loss is the priority. With chronic kidney disease, treatment protein exceeds the kidney ceiling and both numbers are clinician-set. With the gut-health module, fiber flexes by symptom: down for diarrhea, up for constipation.

dialysis.title: Dialysis
summary: On dialysis you need more protein than before, about 1.0 to 1.2 g per kg of body weight a day, because dialysis removes protein. Your renal dietitian sets the exact number.
Eat enough calories, 25 to 35 kcal per kg a day. Malnutrition is common and dangerous on dialysis.
Keep sodium under 2,300 mg a day.
Potassium, phosphorus, and fluid limits depend on your labs and your type of dialysis. The app never sets them; enter your renal dietitian's numbers.
Avoid phosphate additives first (look for 'phos' on labels), and take phosphate binders with meals as prescribed.
Without your clinician's numbers, the app runs in sodium-and-protein-only mode and tells you so.

sections.heading: What this condition is
paragraphs: Dialysis replaces the filtering work of failed kidneys (CKD stage 5D). Hemodialysis usually runs three times a week at a center or at home, so fluid, potassium, and waste build up between sessions. Peritoneal dialysis runs daily through the abdomen, which clears more continuously but removes more protein. The diet is the opposite of pre-dialysis kidney disease in one big way: protein goes up, not down. Everything else depends on your labs and which type of dialysis you do.

sections.heading: What the evidence says
paragraphs: The evidence rating is strong for the protein and sodium targets; potassium, phosphorus, and fluid are individualized by labs and dialysis type.

The sources are the KDOQI Clinical Practice Guideline for Nutrition in CKD, 2020 update (American Journal of Kidney Diseases), the KDIGO 2024 CKD guideline (Kidney International), and National Kidney Foundation patient materials. KDOQI is a systematic-review-based society guideline covering both hemodialysis and peritoneal dialysis. The protein target is graded well because protein losses and malnutrition on dialysis are well documented; the potassium, phosphorus, and fluid guidance is deliberately individualized because the right number depends on your blood tests, urine output, and modality.

sections.heading: What to eat more of
paragraphs: High-quality protein at every meal: eggs, fish, poultry, lean meat, and, if your labs allow, dairy, beans, and tofu. Enough calories to keep weight steady, from olive oil, unsalted butter or margarine, rice, pasta, bread, and other starches your dietitian approves.

Fresh or plain frozen foods cooked at home so you control sodium and avoid additives. Herbs, spices, garlic, lemon, and vinegar for flavor. If potassium is restricted, your dietitian will show you lower-potassium fruits and vegetables and cooking methods; the app follows that number.

sections.heading: What to limit or avoid
paragraphs: Hard rules: sodium under 2,300 mg a day; avoid phosphate additives (phosphoric acid, sodium phosphate, and other 'phos' ingredients in colas, processed meats, packaged baked goods, and processed cheese), which the app flags in ingredient lists.

Clinician-set rules: potassium limit (hemodialysis patients usually restrict; peritoneal dialysis patients often do not), phosphorus limit (natural phosphorus limits come from labs, after additives are cut), and fluid limit (hemodialysis is often limited by weight gain between sessions, commonly about 1 L a day plus urine output; peritoneal dialysis is more liberal). The app applies only what you enter.
Not a rule: cutting protein. Low-protein pre-dialysis advice no longer applies once you start dialysis.

sections.heading: Numbers that matter
paragraphs: Protein: 1.0 to 1.2 g per kg of body weight a day for hemodialysis and peritoneal dialysis; peritoneal dialysis patients may need the upper end. For a 70 kg (154 lb) person that is 70 to 84 g a day. Calories: 25 to 35 kcal per kg a day, or 1,750 to 2,450 kcal for the same person. Sodium: under 2,300 mg a day.

Potassium, phosphorus, and fluid: the app never sets these. Enter the limits your renal dietitian gave you. Without them, the app runs in sodium-and-protein-only mode with a plain statement that potassium, phosphorus, and fluid were not applied. Phosphate binders: take them with meals, on the schedule your team prescribed; the app shows the timing reminder, not the dose.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and myths
paragraphs: Mistake: keeping the low-protein habit from before dialysis. Dialysis removes protein, and eating too little is a leading cause of malnutrition and poor outcomes. Mistake: eating too little overall because appetite is poor; 25 to 35 kcal per kg is the target, and losing weight without trying is a warning sign.

Myth: the potassium and fluid rules are the same for everyone on dialysis. Peritoneal dialysis patients often do not need a potassium limit and have more liberal fluid, while hemodialysis patients usually restrict both. Only your labs and your team can say.

Mistake: focusing on phosphorus in beans and whole grains while drinking cola and eating processed meat. Additive phosphorus is absorbed far more completely; cut it first. Mistake: trusting a chatbot for sodium, potassium, or phosphorus numbers; published studies show language models get them wrong, and this app uses only USDA data and arithmetic.

sections.heading: When to talk to a clinician
paragraphs: Every dialysis patient should have a renal dietitian; ask for your protein, potassium, phosphorus, and fluid targets and enter them here, and ask again whenever labs or modality change. Contact your team about unintended weight loss, poor appetite, muscle weakness, swelling or breathlessness (fluid), muscle cramps or an irregular heartbeat (potassium), or itching and bone pain (phosphorus). Talk to them before any high-protein, low-carbohydrate, or ketogenic plan, and if you also have heart failure with a fluid limit.

sections.heading: How this app applies it
paragraphs: Sodium under 2,300 mg and the phosphate-additive flag are applied on their own. Protein, potassium, phosphorus, and fluid are Tier 2: you enter the renal dietitian's numbers and the app enforces them with deterministic USDA math. The 1.0 to 1.2 g per kg protein range and 25 to 35 kcal per kg calorie range are shown as the guideline consensus so you can see whether your entered numbers sit in the usual range. Binder timing appears as a meal reminder.

Conflicts: this module replaces the non-dialysis kidney module entirely; do not run both. The hypertension potassium target is suppressed. The higher-protein older-adult range overlaps but the renal dietitian's number governs. Low-carb and ketogenic patterns need a clinician decision. With heart failure, both modules carry clinician-set fluid limits and your clinicians reconcile them.

kidney-stones.title: Kidney stones
summary: Drink enough to make at least 2.5 liters of urine a day. For most people that means about 3 liters of fluid in, spread through the day.
Do not cut calcium. Aim for 1,000 to 1,200 mg a day from food, eaten with meals, because calcium in the gut binds oxalate before it reaches the kidney.
Keep sodium under 2,300 mg a day. Sodium pushes calcium out into the urine.
Go easy on high-oxalate foods (spinach, rhubarb, almonds, beets, nuts, chocolate, sweet potato), and never eat them without a calcium food in the same meal.
Keep meat, poultry, and fish portions modest.
Lemon or lime juice helps a little. Prescription potassium citrate is the real tool, and only a clinician can prescribe it.

sections.heading: What this condition is (in one paragraph)
paragraphs: A kidney stone is a hard crystal that forms in the kidney when the urine carries more stone-forming minerals than it can keep dissolved. Calcium oxalate stones are the most common type, and they are the type this module is built for. Uric acid stones need a different plan (fewer purine-rich foods and a clinician-managed change in urine acidity). Cystine and struvite stones are managed by specialists and are out of the app's scope.

sections.heading: What the evidence says
paragraphs: The evidence rating for this module is STRONG for fluid and sodium, STRONG for keeping calcium at a normal (not low) level, and MODERATE for the oxalate, animal protein, and citrate advice. The governing source is the American Urological Association and Endourological Society guideline on medical management of kidney stones (Pearle et al., 2014, amended 2019), which reviewed randomized trials of fluid intake and diet in stone formers and set the targets used here.

The single most important finding is one that surprises people: low-calcium diets increase stone risk. Calcium eaten with food binds oxalate in the gut so it leaves in the stool instead of the urine. Cutting calcium removes that protection.

Lemon and lime juice raise urinary citrate modestly. Citrate keeps calcium from crystallizing, but the effect from juice is small. The intervention with real effect is prescription potassium citrate, which the app cannot and does not replace.

sections.heading: What to eat more of
paragraphs: Water and other fluids, all day. Urine should be pale. Most people need about 3 liters of fluid to reach the 2.5 liter urine target, and more in hot weather or with heavy exercise.

Calcium foods at every meal: milk and yogurt (a 240 g cup of 2 percent milk carries about 300 mg of calcium in the app's USDA data), cheese, calcium-set tofu, canned sardines with bones, and cooked kale. The point is to have calcium present in the same meal as any oxalate.

Fruits and vegetables in general. Plant foods bring potassium and citrate, and this module was written to keep the plant-forward foods from the app's other modules on the plate rather than removing them.

sections.heading: What to limit or avoid
paragraphs: Hard limit: sodium under 2,300 mg a day. Restaurant meals, deli meat, canned soup, bread, and sauces are the usual sources. This is the one number in this module the app enforces as a must.
Hard rule: never restrict calcium below 1,000 mg a day. The app treats a low-calcium day as a problem, not a success.

Soft limit: high-oxalate foods. Spinach, rhubarb, almonds, beets, nuts, chocolate, and sweet potato are the big ones. Smaller portions, and always with a calcium food in the same meal. Spinach salad with cheese is fine; a large spinach smoothie with no dairy is the pattern to avoid.
Soft limit: non-dairy animal protein. Keep red meat, poultry, and fish to moderate portions rather than large ones. Dairy protein is not restricted.
Optional: lemon or lime juice in water. It helps a little and costs nothing.

sections.heading: Numbers that matter
paragraphs: Urine output: at least 2.5 L a day. Fluid intake to reach it: typically 3 L a day (the app's rule is 3,000 mL).
Calcium: 1,000 to 1,200 mg a day from food, taken with meals.
Sodium: under 2,300 mg a day.
The app does not set a milligram limit for oxalate. Oxalate content varies too much between foods and preparations for a reliable daily number, so the rule is portion and pairing, not a count.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and myths
paragraphs: Myth: stones are made of calcium, so stop eating calcium. This is backwards. Low-calcium diets raise stone risk because unbound oxalate reaches the kidney.

Myth: a spinach and almond smoothie is a health drink. For a calcium oxalate stone former it is the worst-case combination: two high-oxalate foods, no calcium, in a form that is easy to consume in large amounts.
Mistake: drinking well but salting heavily. Sodium drives calcium into the urine regardless of how much you drink.
Mistake: expecting lemonade to do what potassium citrate does. It raises urinary citrate modestly, not enough to substitute for the prescription.

sections.heading: When to talk to a clinician
paragraphs: If you have not had a stone analyzed or a 24-hour urine collection, ask. The right diet depends on the stone type, and uric acid, cystine, and struvite stones need clinician-managed plans this app does not provide.
If you also have chronic kidney disease, your fluid and protein targets interact and must come from your clinician. The app flags this pair as a conflict and waits for those numbers.
Ask about potassium citrate and about any medication that raises stone risk. Those are prescribing decisions.

sections.heading: How this app applies it
paragraphs: Three rules are enforced as musts: 3,000 mL of fluid a day, calcium between 1,000 and 1,200 mg a day, and sodium under 2,300 mg a day. The oxalate and animal-protein rules are soft: they shape recipe choices and warnings without blocking a food.

Foods tagged oxalate-high (spinach, almonds, beets, and others) trigger a pairing check. When one appears in a meal without a calcium-rich food, the app suggests adding one rather than removing the oxalate food. This is how the module coexists with the Mediterranean, gut-health, and heart-healthy modules, which all favor nuts, greens, and beets.
With the CKD module selected, the app stops setting fluid and protein and asks for your clinician's numbers. Uric acid stone advice appears as information only.

osteoporosis.title: Osteoporosis and osteopenia
summary: Get 1,000 mg of calcium a day if you are a woman under 50 or a man under 70; 1,200 mg a day if you are a woman 50 or older or a man 70 or older. Food first.
Use a calcium supplement only to fill the gap between what you eat and the target. Supplemental calcium above 1,000 mg a day has unresolved heart questions.
Adults 50 and older need 800 to 1,000 IU of vitamin D a day, which usually means a supplement because food does not supply it.
Eat enough protein: about 1.0 to 1.2 g per kilogram of body weight a day for older adults, spread across meals.
Limit alcohol, keep caffeine moderate, and keep sodium moderate. High sodium increases calcium loss in urine.
Eat fruits and vegetables daily. There is no bone-building superfood.

sections.heading: What this condition is (in one paragraph)
paragraphs: Osteoporosis is a loss of bone density and bone quality that makes fractures more likely, often from a minor fall. Osteopenia is the milder stage on the same scale. Both are diagnosed by bone density testing, not by symptoms, and both are treated with medication when fracture risk is high enough. Food supplies the raw materials for bone; it does not replace the medication.

sections.heading: What the evidence says
paragraphs: The evidence rating for this module is MODERATE for calcium and vitamin D, MODERATE for protein, and LIMITED for everything else. The governing source is the Bone Health and Osteoporosis Foundation Clinician's Guide (LeBoff et al., Osteoporosis International 2022), supported by the Endocrine Society and USPSTF statements on vitamin D and by the PROT-AGE position paper on protein for older adults.

The calcium and vitamin D targets come from the BHOF guide, which draws on trials of supplementation and fracture outcomes. The evidence supports meeting the targets; it does not support going above them. The guide's caution about supplemental calcium above 1,000 mg a day reflects unresolved questions about cardiovascular risk from calcium pills, which do not apply to calcium from food.

The protein target comes from the PROT-AGE group's review of muscle and bone outcomes in people over 65. Fruits and vegetables are associated with higher bone density in observational studies, which is why they are recommended, but that is association, not proof of cause.

sections.heading: What to eat more of
paragraphs: Calcium foods, spread across the day. In the app's USDA data, 100 g of 2 percent milk carries 126 mg of calcium, 100 g of plain nonfat yogurt 167 mg, 100 g of cheddar 707 mg, 100 g of calcium-set firm tofu 683 mg, 100 g of canned sardines with bones 382 mg, and 100 g of cooked kale 150 mg. Three dairy servings plus one calcium-rich plant or fish food gets most people to target without a pill.
Protein at every meal: eggs, fish, poultry, dairy, beans, lentils, and tofu. The PROT-AGE paper recommends 25 to 30 g of protein per meal for older adults, paired with resistance exercise.
Fruits and vegetables for potassium, magnesium, and vitamin K. Leafy greens, broccoli, beans, bananas, and potatoes all count.

sections.heading: What to limit or avoid
paragraphs: Soft limit: alcohol. The BHOF guide lists heavy alcohol use as a risk factor for bone loss and falls. Less is better.
Soft limit: caffeine, kept moderate. A cup or two of coffee is fine with adequate calcium.

Soft limit: sodium, kept moderate. High sodium increases calcium loss in urine, so the DASH-style range under 2,300 mg a day is a sensible ceiling even though this module does not enforce a hard number.
Optional: calcium supplements. Only to fill the gap between food and target, and the total from supplements should stay at or below 1,000 mg a day.

sections.heading: Numbers that matter
paragraphs: Calcium: 1,000 mg a day for women under 50 and men under 70; 1,200 mg a day for women 50 and older and men 70 and older.
Vitamin D: 800 to 1,000 IU a day for adults 50 and older. This is a supplement number, not a food number.
Protein: 1.0 to 1.2 g per kilogram of body weight a day. For a 70 kg person that is 70 to 84 g a day, or about 25 to 30 g at each of three meals.
Supplemental calcium ceiling: 1,000 mg a day.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and myths
paragraphs: Myth: more calcium is always better. Above the target there is no added bone benefit, and calcium pills above 1,000 mg a day carry cardiovascular questions.
Myth: a bone-building superfood exists. No single food has evidence for reversing bone loss. The pattern (calcium, vitamin D, protein, produce) is what matters.
Mistake: taking a large calcium dose all at once. Spread calcium across meals; the gut absorbs it better in smaller amounts.
Mistake: relying on food for vitamin D. Fatty fish and fortified milk help, but the BHOF target is set as a supplement dose because food sources are inadequate.

sections.heading: When to talk to a clinician
paragraphs: Ask about a bone density test if you have not had one and you are a woman 65 or older, a man 70 or older, or younger with risk factors such as a prior fracture, long steroid use, or early menopause.
Ask before starting a calcium or vitamin D supplement if you have kidney stones, kidney disease, or a history of high blood calcium.

If you also have chronic kidney disease, the protein target here conflicts with CKD protein limits and must come from your clinician. Prescription osteoporosis medication decisions are the clinician's, and the app does not weigh in.

sections.heading: How this app applies it
paragraphs: The app picks your calcium target from your sex and age: 1,000 mg or 1,200 mg a day. If sex or age is missing from the profile, it applies the stricter 1,200 mg number. The vitamin D target of 800 to 1,000 IU turns on at age 50 and is shown as a supplement reminder, because the app cannot meet it from recipes.

Protein is scored at 1.0 to 1.2 g per kilogram using the weight in your profile. Alcohol and caffeine appear as soft flags in recipe scoring; sodium is kept moderate but not capped by this module (the DASH or hypertension module caps it if selected).
With the CKD module selected, the app stops computing protein and asks for the clinician's target. Fruit and vegetable preference raises the score of produce-heavy recipes.

iron-deficiency-anemia.title: Iron-deficiency anemia
summary: Food helps, but established iron deficiency needs iron treatment (oral or IV) and a doctor looking for the cause. Diet alone rarely fixes it.
Heme iron from red meat, poultry, and fish is absorbed 2 to 3 times better than plant (non-heme) iron.
Pair plant iron (beans, lentils, tofu, fortified cereal, leafy greens) with a vitamin C food in the same meal: citrus, bell pepper, tomato, broccoli, kiwifruit.
Keep iron-rich meals and iron pills 1 to 2 hours away from tea, coffee, calcium supplements, and high-calcium foods.
Cooking in a cast-iron pan adds a little iron.
If you have never been tested for celiac disease, ask. It is a common hidden cause.

sections.heading: What this condition is (in one paragraph)
paragraphs: Iron-deficiency anemia means the body has too little iron to make enough hemoglobin, the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen. The usual causes in adults are blood loss (heavy periods, or slow bleeding from the gut), poor absorption (celiac disease is the common hidden one), or not enough iron in the diet, most often in people who eat little or no meat. Fatigue, breathlessness on exertion, and pale skin are typical. It is diagnosed by blood tests, and the British Society of Gastroenterology guideline is explicit that finding the cause is part of the treatment.

sections.heading: What the evidence says
paragraphs: The evidence rating for this module is MODERATE for dietary strategies and STRONG that diet alone rarely corrects established deficiency. The governing source is the British Society of Gastroenterology guideline on iron deficiency anaemia in adults (Snook et al., Gut 2021), supported by American Society of Hematology and CDC patient materials.

The BSG guideline reviewed absorption studies and treatment trials. Its position is plain: established deficiency needs supplementation, oral or intravenous, plus a search for the cause. Gut blood loss, celiac disease, and menstrual loss are the causes it names. Diet is a support, not the treatment.

The absorption facts are well established. Heme iron, found only in animal flesh, is absorbed 2 to 3 times better than non-heme iron from plants and fortified foods. Vitamin C in the same meal raises non-heme absorption; tea, coffee, and calcium in the same meal lower it. Cast-iron cookware adds a modest amount of iron to food.

sections.heading: What to eat more of
paragraphs: Heme iron sources: beef, lamb, liver (beef liver is the richest common source), dark-meat poultry, sardines, and shellfish. A 100 g portion of broiled beef flank steak carries about 1.8 mg of iron in the app's USDA data; 100 g of braised beef liver carries much more.

Non-heme iron sources: lentils (3.3 mg per 100 g cooked), chickpeas (2.9 mg), black beans (2.1 mg), calcium-set firm tofu (2.7 mg), chia seeds, fortified breakfast cereals, and cooked spinach (3.6 mg per 100 g, though spinach's oxalate limits how much is absorbed).

Vitamin C partners to eat in the same meal as plant iron: a kiwifruit (about 59 mg of vitamin C per 100 g), orange juice, bell pepper, broccoli, tomato, or strawberries. Lentil soup with a squeeze of lemon, or beans with salsa, are the pattern.

sections.heading: What to limit or avoid
paragraphs: Soft timing rule, not a ban: tea and coffee. Their tannins and polyphenols cut non-heme iron absorption sharply when drunk with the meal. Have them 1 to 2 hours before or after an iron-rich meal or an iron pill.

Soft timing rule: calcium supplements and high-calcium foods (milk, cheese, yogurt, calcium-set tofu, sardines). Calcium competes with iron for absorption. Keep the calcium supplement at a different time of day from the iron pill, and do not wash down an iron-rich meal with a large glass of milk.
Nothing in this module is a hard exclusion. The goal is arrangement, not restriction.

sections.heading: Numbers that matter
paragraphs: Absorption: heme iron is absorbed 2 to 3 times better than non-heme iron.
Separation: 1 to 2 hours between iron-rich meals or iron pills and tea, coffee, calcium supplements, or high-calcium foods.
If you take levothyroxine for thyroid disease, keep iron supplements about 4 hours from it; the thyroid module's timing rule shows that on the Plan.

The app does not set a daily iron target in milligrams. The BSG guideline treats established deficiency with supplements at doses a clinician chooses, and the food-only requirement varies with cause and absorption. The app shows the iron content of foods and recipes so you can see where it comes from.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and myths
paragraphs: Myth: eating more spinach will cure anemia. Spinach iron is non-heme and poorly absorbed because of its oxalate. It helps a little; it does not treat deficiency.
Mistake: taking the iron pill with morning coffee or with a calcium supplement. Both cut absorption. Take it with water or orange juice, away from both.

Mistake: fixing the diet and skipping the workup. Iron deficiency in an adult who eats meat, or in any man or postmenopausal woman, usually has a cause worth finding, and the BSG guideline says so plainly.
Myth: a cast-iron pan replaces treatment. It adds iron modestly. That is all.

sections.heading: When to talk to a clinician
paragraphs: If you have a diagnosis of iron deficiency and are not on treatment, ask what the plan is. The guideline expects supplementation plus a search for the cause.

If you have never been screened for celiac disease, ask. Celiac disease is a common hidden cause of iron deficiency, and the app shows this reminder whenever iron deficiency is selected without celiac.
Tell your clinician about black stools, blood in stool, heavy periods, or unexplained weight loss. Those point to the cause and need evaluation, not more lentils.
Ask before taking iron supplements without a diagnosis. Iron overload is a real risk in people who do not need it.

sections.heading: How this app applies it
paragraphs: The app prefers recipes tagged iron-rich, and it checks meal timing: an iron-rich meal or an iron supplement next to tea, coffee, a calcium supplement, or a calcium-rich food within 1 to 2 hours triggers a spacing suggestion. Plant-iron meals without a vitamin C food get a pairing suggestion.

If you also use the vegetarian or vegan pattern, the app raises the iron guidance automatically, since plant-only eating means all iron is non-heme. If you also have thyroid disease and take levothyroxine, keep iron tablets about 4 hours from it; that module shows the timing rule on the Plan.
The app never suggests an iron dose. The cause-finding message and the celiac screening reminder are shown as musts, because the guideline treats them as part of care.

gastroparesis.title: Gastroparesis
summary: Choose foods you could mash with a fork. Skip raw vegetables, whole nuts, seeds, fruit and vegetable skins, and tough meat.
Eat 4 to 6 small meals a day instead of 2 or 3 large ones. Liquids and blended meals leave the stomach faster than solids.
Keep fat low, because fat slows stomach emptying. Liquid fats (oil in a smoothie, milk-based drinks) are usually tolerated better than fatty solids.
Keep fiber low, especially rough insoluble fiber. Avoid persimmons, orange membranes, and celery, which can form a bezoar (a fibrous mass in the stomach).
Sit upright after eating, and take a walk if you can.
Because this diet is narrow, ask about a multivitamin. Nutrient shortfalls are the main long-term risk.

sections.heading: What this condition is (in one paragraph)
paragraphs: Gastroparesis means the stomach empties too slowly without any physical blockage. Food sits, and the result is nausea, early fullness, bloating, and sometimes vomiting hours after a meal. It is common in long-standing diabetes, where high glucose itself slows emptying, and it also shows up in the POTS, hypermobility, and mast cell cluster. Diet does not cure it. Diet manages symptoms, keeps nutrition adequate, and in diabetes helps keep glucose steadier because food arrives in the bloodstream more predictably.

sections.heading: What the evidence says
paragraphs: The evidence rating for this module is MODERATE for the small-particle diet and MODERATE for low fat, low fiber, and small frequent meals. The governing sources are the American College of Gastroenterology clinical guideline on gastroparesis (Camilleri et al., 2022) and the randomized controlled trial by Olausson and colleagues (American Journal of Gastroenterology 2014) that tested a small-particle diet in people with diabetic gastroparesis.

The Olausson trial is the best single piece of evidence. People with diabetic gastroparesis were randomized to a diet of foods that are easy to mash with a fork, avoiding fibrous, tough, and large-particle foods, or to a standard diabetes diet. The small-particle group had fewer upper gastrointestinal symptoms. The ACG guideline adopted that finding.

The rest of the advice (low fat, low fiber, small frequent meals, liquids over solids, upright after eating) rests on physiology and clinical experience summarized in the guideline rather than on trials. Fat and fiber slow emptying; smaller volumes empty faster; liquids empty faster than solids. It is sensible and widely used, and the rating reflects that it is less tested.

sections.heading: What to eat more of
paragraphs: Soft, mashable, and blended foods: mashed potatoes, well-cooked peeled carrots and squash, applesauce, ripe bananas, canned peaches and pears, smooth soups, yogurt, cottage cheese, eggs, ground or slow-cooked tender meat, flaked fish, tofu, smooth nut butter (not whole nuts), white rice, and refined pasta.

Liquid nutrition when solids are hard: smoothies made from soft fruit and yogurt or milk, milk-based or fortified oral nutrition drinks, and blended soups. These pass through faster and are the easiest way to get protein and calories on a bad day.

Low-fiber sources of soluble fiber where you can tolerate them: oatmeal cooked until soft, peeled cooked vegetables, and blended fruit. This is how the app tries to meet any fiber goal from your other modules without breaking the texture rules.

sections.heading: What to limit or avoid
paragraphs: Soft avoid (texture): raw vegetables, salads, whole nuts and seeds, popcorn, fruit and vegetable skins, corn, tough or stringy meat, and coarse whole grains. These are the large-particle foods the trial diet excluded.
Soft avoid (bezoar risk): persimmons, the membranes in oranges and grapefruit, and celery. These fibers can knot into a mass in a slow stomach.

Soft limit (fat): fried foods, fatty meats, heavy cream sauces, and large portions of cheese. Liquid fats in a drink are usually fine, so a spoon of oil or nut butter in a smoothie is a good way to add calories.
Soft limit (fiber): bran, high-fiber cereals, whole beans in quantity, and raw high-fiber fruit. Fiber is not banned; the form and amount are what matter.
Nothing here is a hard exclusion. Tolerance varies by person and by day, and the app treats these as strong preferences, not bans.

sections.heading: Numbers that matter
paragraphs: Meals: 4 to 6 a day. The app plans within that range when this module is on.
Fat and fiber: the ACG guideline says low, without a gram number. The app applies the texture rules and low-fat preference to recipe scoring rather than enforcing a limit.
Position: upright after eating, and a walk afterward if possible.
Nutrition: with a narrow diet, a daily multivitamin is often needed. That is a supplement decision to make with your clinician.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and myths
paragraphs: Mistake: eating a healthy salad. Raw greens, nuts, seeds, and raw vegetables are exactly the large-particle foods that sit in a slow stomach. Cooked, peeled, and blended is the healthy version here.
Mistake: three big meals because that is normal. Volume is the enemy. Six small meals empty better than three large ones.
Myth: all fat must go. Fatty solids are the problem. A little oil or nut butter in a liquid is usually tolerated and helps with calories.
Mistake: letting fiber advice from a diabetes or gut-health plan override the texture rules. In this app, gastroparesis wins on texture, and fiber is met through soft, cooked, or blended sources.

sections.heading: When to talk to a clinician
paragraphs: If you are losing weight, cannot keep fluids down, or are vomiting daily, that needs medical care, not a diet change. Dehydration and malnutrition are the real dangers.
If you have diabetes, tell your diabetes team the diet has changed. Slow, unpredictable emptying affects insulin timing, and the app does not adjust insulin.
Ask about a multivitamin, about medications that slow emptying (some pain and diabetes medications do), and about prokinetic drugs. Those are all clinician decisions.

sections.heading: How this app applies it
paragraphs: Foods tagged large-particle, raw-vegetable, nut, seed, skin-or-seed, tough-meat, high-fiber-insoluble, or bezoar-risk are pushed down in recipe scoring, and foods tagged small-particle-friendly are pushed up. Fried foods are flagged for fat. Meal plans are built with 4 to 6 eating occasions.

When gastroparesis is selected with the gut-health, type 2 diabetes, heart-healthy, or Mediterranean modules, their fiber, whole-nut, and whole-grain advice yields to the texture rules. The app then tries to meet the fiber goal with soluble, cooked, or blended sources. With the constipation module, the same rule applies. With time-restricted eating, the small frequent meals win over a compressed window.
The app manages symptoms; it does not claim to treat gastroparesis, and it never adjusts insulin.

thyroid.title: Thyroid conditions
summary: There is no thyroid diet. The one rule with clear evidence is about when you take your medication, not what you eat.
Take levothyroxine the same way every day: on an empty stomach 60 minutes before breakfast, or at bedtime 3 or more hours after your last meal.
Keep calcium and iron supplements away from levothyroxine; about 4 hours is the usual advice. Coffee, soy, and high-fiber food close to the tablet can also cut absorption.
Get enough iodine, about 150 mcg a day, but not extra. Kelp and iodine supplements can make thyroid disease worse.
Broccoli, cabbage, kale, and soy are fine at normal amounts. Going gluten-free for Hashimoto's has no evidence unless you also have celiac disease.
With hyperthyroidism, eat enough calories and calcium while the disease is active, and avoid iodine excess.

sections.heading: What this condition is (in one paragraph)
paragraphs: The thyroid gland sets the body's metabolic pace. Hypothyroidism is too little thyroid hormone, most often from Hashimoto's disease, an autoimmune condition, and it is treated with levothyroxine, a daily tablet that replaces the missing hormone. Hyperthyroidism is too much hormone, most often from Graves' disease, and it is treated with medication, radioactive iodine, or surgery. Food does not treat either one. Food affects how well the tablet is absorbed and, through iodine, how the gland behaves, and that is the whole scope of this module.

sections.heading: What the evidence says
paragraphs: The evidence rating for this module is MODERATE for the medication-timing rules, LIMITED for everything else, and INSUFFICIENT for any named "thyroid diet." The governing sources are the American Thyroid Association guidelines for hypothyroidism (Jonklaas et al., Thyroid 2014) and hyperthyroidism (Ross et al., Thyroid 2016), and the ATA statement on iodine.

The levothyroxine timing rule comes from absorption studies summarized in the ATA hypothyroidism guideline. Food, coffee, and calcium and iron supplements taken close to the tablet reduce how much hormone gets into the blood, and case reports suggest soy and fiber can too. That can leave a person under-treated even when the dose is right on paper. Ranked from best absorbed to worst, the guideline lists 60 minutes before breakfast, bedtime, 30 minutes before breakfast, and with breakfast.

Everything else is mostly myth-busting. Goitrogens in cruciferous vegetables and soy are not a concern at normal intake when iodine is adequate. Gluten-free eating has no evidence for Hashimoto's unless celiac disease is also present. Selenium supplementation has mixed evidence and the ATA does not recommend it. No named diet has been shown to treat thyroid disease.

sections.heading: What to eat more of
paragraphs: Ordinary healthy food. This module adds no food targets. If you have other modules selected, their patterns apply unchanged.
Iodine at a normal level: iodized salt, dairy, eggs, and seafood supply the 150 mcg a day adults need. Iodized salt and dairy cover most people without any effort.

With hyperthyroidism, enough calories and enough calcium while the disease is active, because an overactive thyroid burns through both. Dairy, calcium-set tofu, and canned fish with bones cover the calcium.

sections.heading: What to limit or avoid
paragraphs: Timing rule (if you take levothyroxine): nothing but water until 60 minutes after the tablet, or take it at bedtime 3 or more hours after eating, and keep calcium and iron supplements about 4 hours away. No food is banned; it is a matter of the clock.

Soft avoid: iodine excess. Kelp, seaweed supplements, and iodine drops can push the thyroid the wrong way in both hypo- and hyperthyroidism. Sushi with a sheet of nori is not the problem; a kelp capsule is.
Not restricted: cruciferous vegetables (broccoli, cabbage, cauliflower, kale, Brussels sprouts) and soy at normal portions. The app does not flag them.
Not restricted: gluten, unless you have celiac disease. Celiac disease is more common in autoimmune thyroid disease, so screening for it is reasonable, and if it is found, the celiac module applies.

sections.heading: Numbers that matter
paragraphs: Levothyroxine: 60 minutes before breakfast on an empty stomach, or at bedtime 3 or more hours after the last meal. The guideline ranks both above taking it 30 minutes before breakfast.
Separation from calcium and iron supplements: about 4 hours by custom; the ATA guideline calls the gap untested.
Iodine: 150 mcg a day for adults. Adequate, not extra.
The app sets no calorie, protein, or food-group number for thyroid disease. If your clinician has set one for active hyperthyroidism, enter it as a personal target.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and myths
paragraphs: Mistake: taking levothyroxine with coffee and breakfast. This is the most common reason a correct dose does not work. Water only, then wait.
Mistake: taking a calcium or iron pill with the thyroid tablet to save time. Both cut absorption. Move them to lunch or dinner.
Myth: broccoli and soy are bad for the thyroid. At normal intake with adequate iodine, they are not.
Myth: everyone with Hashimoto's should go gluten-free. There is no evidence for that without celiac disease, and unneeded restriction has costs.
Myth: more iodine helps a tired thyroid. Excess iodine can worsen thyroid disease. Do not take kelp.
Myth: selenium fixes Hashimoto's. The evidence is mixed and the guideline does not recommend it.

sections.heading: When to talk to a clinician
paragraphs: If you have symptoms on a stable dose (fatigue, weight change, feeling cold or hot, palpitations), ask for a check. Absorption problems from timing are fixable, and the dose may need adjustment.
Before starting any iodine, kelp, or selenium supplement, ask. Before going gluten-free, ask for celiac testing first, because the test is unreliable once gluten is removed.
If you are pregnant or planning pregnancy, thyroid management changes; the pregnancy module and your clinician take over.
If you are also treating iron deficiency, tell the prescriber, so the iron and thyroid schedules can be set together.

sections.heading: How this app applies it
paragraphs: The app asks one medication question: "Do you take levothyroxine?" A yes turns on the timing rule, which the Plan lists under Timing. The app does not ask for a tablet time and does not move meals on the clock; the rule is a reminder.
Iodine is tracked as an adequacy target of 150 mcg a day, not a limit. Foods are not excluded for goitrogens, and gluten is not restricted unless the celiac module is on.

With the vegetarian or vegan pattern, soy stays in the plan; only the timing rule applies. With the iron-deficiency module, keep iron tablets about 4 hours from levothyroxine. Nothing in this module encodes a thyroid diet, and the app never suggests a levothyroxine dose.

pediatric.title: Children and this app
summary: This app is for adults 18 and older. The account holder must be an adult.
The one thing a parent can do here is caregiver mode: manage a child's confirmed celiac disease or diagnosed food allergies.
Children's weight, type 1 diabetes, inflammatory bowel disease, and any elimination diet belong with a pediatric clinician, not an app.
Growth, not weight loss, is the goal for almost every child. Restrictive diets in children carry growth and eating-disorder risks.
The app applies no pediatric nutrition numbers. Every pediatric number is a clinician's to set.

sections.heading: What this is (in one paragraph)
paragraphs: This is not a condition. It is the app's rule about children, and the reason for it. The evidence on feeding children is strong; the problem is safety and law. A child is still growing, the margin for error is small, and an app cannot watch growth. So the app draws a firm line.

sections.heading: What the evidence says
paragraphs: The evidence rating for this module is STRONG for pediatric celiac disease, food allergy, and type 1 diabetes, and STRONG for the 2023 American Academy of Pediatrics obesity guideline. The governing sources are the AAP obesity guideline (Hampl et al., Pediatrics 2023), the NASPGHAN and ESPGHAN celiac guidelines, the NIAID food allergy guidelines with the LEAP and EAT trials, ADA Standards of Care Section 14, and AAP and Academy infant-feeding positions.

In short: the AAP endorses intensive treatment for pediatric obesity, delivered by clinicians, with growth as the frame. Pediatric GI and allergy societies warn repeatedly that restrictive diets in children (low FODMAP, low histamine, ketogenic, elimination) carry growth and disordered-eating risk. Carbohydrate counting for a child with type 1 diabetes is insulin dosing by another name. Early peanut introduction at 4 to 6 months reduces peanut allergy (LEAP and EAT trials), but that is background for parents, not an app feature.
Celiac disease and diagnosed food allergies are the exceptions: their rules are unambiguous and restrict only the trigger.

sections.heading: What caregiver mode does and does not do
paragraphs: Caregiver mode lets an adult account holder set up a child profile limited to two modules: celiac disease and food allergies. The app filters recipes and shopping lists for gluten or the child's diagnosed allergens, as it does for an adult, and sets no calories, protein, portions, or growth targets.
It does not offer weight management, type 1 diabetes carbohydrate counting, inflammatory bowel disease, or elimination diets for children. Those need a pediatric clinician.

sections.heading: Numbers that matter
paragraphs: Minimum age of the account holder: 18. Pediatric nutrition numbers applied by the app: none.
COPPA requires verifiable parental consent and strict data handling for any user under 13, and app stores add rules for minors' health apps. The account holder is always the adult.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and myths
paragraphs: Mistake: putting a child on the parent's diet. It can cost a child growth.
Mistake: removing foods to test for allergy without a diagnosis. Suspected allergy needs an allergist; in the LEAP trial, avoidance raised peanut allergy rather than preventing it.

sections.heading: When to talk to a clinician
paragraphs: For anything beyond confirmed celiac disease or diagnosed food allergy: weight, diabetes, gut disease, suspected intolerance, or any restrictive diet. Before introducing allergens to an infant with severe eczema or an existing food allergy, ask the pediatrician.

sections.heading: How this app applies it
paragraphs: A hard age gate on the account holder: 18 or older. Caregiver mode is limited to the celiac and food-allergy modules; no other module attaches to a child profile and no pediatric number is ever computed. Every rule carries its citation so a pediatrician can check it.

rheumatoid-arthritis.title: Rheumatoid arthritis
summary: No diet treats rheumatoid arthritis. Disease-modifying medication does. Food is a supporting player.

The one eating pattern with guideline support is Mediterranean-style: vegetables, fruit, whole grains, beans, nuts, fish, and olive oil. Even that is a conditional recommendation on low-certainty evidence.

The American College of Rheumatology recommends against the other named diets sold for RA (vegan, ketogenic, elimination, nightshade-free, paleo, gluten-free without celiac disease) and against dietary supplements, including fish oil.
If you carry extra weight, weight management is part of RA care. Excess weight goes with higher disease activity and worse response to treatment.
If you take methotrexate or leflunomide, ask your prescriber what alcohol limit applies to you. The app does not set one.
Stopping smoking is the lifestyle change with the strongest RA evidence.

sections.heading: What this condition is (in one paragraph)
paragraphs: Rheumatoid arthritis is an autoimmune disease in which the immune system attacks the lining of the joints, causing pain, swelling, morning stiffness, and, if untreated, joint damage. It is different from osteoarthritis, which is wear and mechanical damage. RA is treated with disease-modifying drugs that quiet the immune attack. Nothing on a plate does that. What food can do is support general health, help with weight, and, on modest evidence, take a little edge off symptoms.

sections.heading: What the evidence says
paragraphs: The evidence rating for this module is MODERATE for a Mediterranean-style eating pattern and INSUFFICIENT for every other named diet. The governing sources are the 2022 American College of Rheumatology guideline on exercise, rehabilitation, diet, and integrative interventions for RA (England et al., Arthritis Care and Research 2023), the 2021 EULAR lifestyle recommendations for rheumatic diseases (Gwinnutt et al., Annals of the Rheumatic Diseases 2023), and the PREDIMED trial for the general cardiovascular case for Mediterranean eating.

Be clear about what the ACR guideline actually says. It conditionally recommends a Mediterranean-style diet for people with RA, and it rates the certainty of the evidence as low. The trials behind it are small and show modest improvement in pain and stiffness, not disease control. A conditional recommendation means the panel thought most people would want it but the evidence could go either way.

The same guideline conditionally recommends against formally defined diets other than Mediterranean (the vegan, ketogenic, elimination, nightshade-free, paleo, and non-celiac gluten-free diets among them), because the evidence is lacking and restriction has costs. It also conditionally recommends against dietary supplements for RA, including fish oil. The EULAR recommendations add a healthy balanced diet, weight management if overweight, and smoking cessation, without endorsing any specific diet.

sections.heading: What to eat more of
paragraphs: The Mediterranean pattern: vegetables and fruit at most meals, whole grains, beans and lentils, nuts, fish (especially fatty fish such as salmon and sardines) two or more times a week, and olive oil as the main fat. This is the same pattern the app's anti-inflammatory module uses, so selecting both adds nothing.
Omega-3 fats from fish as food fit the pattern. The guideline's recommendation against supplements does not apply to eating fish.

sections.heading: What to limit or avoid
paragraphs: Nothing is a hard exclusion in this module. The Mediterranean pattern itself de-emphasizes red and processed meat, sweets, and refined grains, and the app scores recipes accordingly.

Not recommended, on guideline evidence: nightshade-free, elimination, vegan-for-RA, ketogenic, paleo, and gluten-free diets without celiac disease. The app does not encode any of them for RA. If you want to try one anyway, the cost is restriction with no expected benefit.
Not recommended: dietary supplements for RA, including fish oil. Fish-oil trials show small symptom benefits, which is why this stays a conversation with your rheumatologist rather than a rule.
Alcohol: the app sets no RA-specific limit. If you take methotrexate or leflunomide, the limit that matters is the one your prescriber sets.

sections.heading: Numbers that matter
paragraphs: There are no RA-specific nutrient targets. The ACR guideline names a pattern, not a number.

Weight: if your clinician has said weight loss would help, the app applies the weight-management module's targets. EULAR ties excess weight to higher disease activity and worse treatment response, without setting a percentage.
Fish: two or more servings a week is the Mediterranean pattern the app scores toward.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and myths
paragraphs: Myth: nightshades (tomatoes, peppers, eggplant, potatoes) cause RA flares. There is no evidence for that in general, and the ACR recommends against the nightshade-free diet.
Myth: gluten or dairy causes RA. Not in general. Celiac disease is its own condition with its own module.
Myth: an anti-inflammatory diet replaces medication. The benefit seen in trials is modest symptom relief. Stopping a disease-modifying drug because the diet feels good risks joint damage.
Mistake: taking fish oil, turmeric, or other supplements as treatment. The guideline recommends against supplements for RA. Ask the rheumatologist before adding any.
Reports of benefit from elimination diets are real for individuals; blinded evidence is lacking, which is why they are not recommended.

sections.heading: When to talk to a clinician
paragraphs: Before any change in RA medication, always. Before starting any supplement. Before an elimination or gluten-free diet, ask for celiac testing first if there is any reason to suspect it.
If you take methotrexate or leflunomide, ask about alcohol. If you are overweight, ask whether weight management should be part of your plan and how to do it safely with your joints.
If you smoke, ask for help stopping. It is the lifestyle factor with the strongest RA evidence.

sections.heading: How this app applies it
paragraphs: The app scores recipes toward the Mediterranean pattern (vegetable, fruit, whole-grain, legume, nut, fish, and olive-oil tags). It encodes no named exclusion diet and no supplement. The alcohol note appears as information, not a limit.

If you turn on the profile flag "your clinician has said weight loss would help," the weight-management rule activates. Selecting RA together with the anti-inflammatory Mediterranean module is redundant, and the app says so. With gout, both modules point to the same pattern and coexist.
The ACR and EULAR citations were checked against the journals' own records on Crossref and PubMed on September 30, 2026: volume, issue, and pages match.

constipation.title: Chronic constipation
summary: Fiber and fluid are the first step, and they work for many people. Aim for 25 to 38 g of fiber a day from whole plant foods.
Increase fiber slowly, over 2 to 3 weeks, and drink more as you go. Too fast means gas and bloating; fiber without fluid can make things worse.
Two green kiwifruit a day is a food option with real trial evidence, and it caused fewer side effects than psyllium.
Psyllium is the fiber supplement with the best evidence. It is a supplement, so it is a conversation with your clinician or pharmacist.
Regular meals, especially breakfast, and daily physical activity support a regular bowel habit.
New constipation after 50, blood in the stool, weight loss, or no response to fiber needs a clinician visit, not more fiber.

sections.heading: What this condition is (in one paragraph)
paragraphs: Chronic constipation means infrequent, hard, or difficult bowel movements that go on for months, without a disease that explains them (that is what "idiopathic" means in the guideline title). It is common, more so with age and with low fiber, low fluid, and inactivity. Diet is where treatment starts, and for many people it is enough. When it is not, over-the-counter and prescription medications come next, and the guideline is clear that piling on more fiber is not the answer when fiber has not worked.

sections.heading: What the evidence says
paragraphs: The evidence rating for this module is MODERATE for dietary fiber (especially psyllium) and fluid, MODERATE for two green kiwifruit a day, and LIMITED for prunes. The governing sources are the AGA-ACG clinical practice guideline on chronic idiopathic constipation (Chang et al., Gastroenterology 2023), the multicenter randomized trial of green kiwifruit (Gearry et al., American Journal of Gastroenterology 2023), the Bharucha and Lacy review of mechanisms and management (Gastroenterology 2020), and the Institute of Medicine's Dietary Reference Intakes for fiber.

The AGA-ACG guideline covers medications, and it places fiber supplementation, psyllium in particular, as a reasonable first step before them. Psyllium is the fiber with the most trial support for constipation.

The kiwifruit trial randomized people with constipation to two green kiwifruit a day, psyllium, or prunes. Kiwifruit improved complete spontaneous bowel movements and abdominal comfort, with fewer side effects than psyllium. Prunes have smaller trials with benefit; wheat bran helps some people and worsens bloating in others.

sections.heading: What to eat more of
paragraphs: Whole fruit, vegetables, whole grains, beans, lentils, nuts, and seeds. In the app's USDA data, 100 g of cooked lentils carries 7.9 g of fiber, 100 g of cooked black beans 8.7 g, 100 g of raspberries 6.5 g, 100 g of prunes 7.1 g, and 100 g of chia seeds 34 g. A bowl of beans, a serving of berries, and whole-grain bread add up quickly.
Two green kiwifruit a day, with the skin off or on. Each 100 g of kiwifruit carries about 2 g of fiber and 59 mg of vitamin C.
Fluid, enough that urine is pale. Water, tea, coffee, milk, and soup all count.
Breakfast, every day. Regular meals, and the morning meal in particular, support a regular bowel habit.

sections.heading: What to limit or avoid
paragraphs: This module bans nothing. It is an add-more module.
Soft caution: do not add fiber faster than your gut can adapt. Two to three weeks from your current intake to target, with extra fluid.
Soft caution: do not keep adding fiber when fiber has not worked. If a few weeks of adequate fiber and fluid have not helped, that is the point to talk about medication.
Optional: wheat bran. It helps some people and makes bloating worse for others. Try it if you like; stop if it does not suit you.

sections.heading: Numbers that matter
paragraphs: Fiber: 25 to 38 g a day. The IOM reference is 14 g per 1,000 kcal, which works out to about 25 g for most women and 38 g for most men.
Ramp-up: 2 to 3 weeks.
Kiwifruit: 2 green kiwifruit a day.
Fluid: enough that urine is pale. The app does not set a milliliter number for constipation on its own; if another module sets one, that applies.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and myths
paragraphs: Mistake: doubling fiber overnight. The result is gas, bloating, and sometimes worse constipation. Go slowly.
Mistake: fiber without fluid. Fiber holds water; without enough water it can become a plug.
Myth: detox teas, cleanses, and colon cleanses treat constipation. They do not. Many contain stimulant laxatives with none of the guidance that goes with prescribed ones.
Myth: coffee is a treatment. It stimulates some people's bowels. That is a quirk, not a therapy.
Mistake: ignoring red flags because "it is just constipation." New constipation after age 50, blood in the stool, and weight loss are reasons to be seen.

sections.heading: When to talk to a clinician
paragraphs: New constipation after age 50, blood in the stool, unexplained weight loss, or constipation that does not respond to fiber and fluid. Those need evaluation, not more fiber.
Before starting psyllium or any laxative, especially if you take other medications or have a narrowing anywhere in the gut.
If you have gastroparesis, inflammatory bowel disease, or are in a low-FODMAP elimination phase, the fiber advice here changes, and the app handles those conflicts as described below.

sections.heading: How this app applies it
paragraphs: The app sets a fiber target of 25 to 38 g a day and prefers recipes with fruit, vegetable, whole-grain, legume, nut, and seed tags. The kiwifruit and psyllium advice is shown as information, not scored, because kiwifruit is a food choice and psyllium is a supplement. The red-flag list appears as a must-read notice.

With gastroparesis, the texture rules win and the app meets fiber through soft, cooked, and blended sources. With IBS low-FODMAP, many high-fiber foods are high FODMAP, and the elimination phase is time-limited, so the conflict resolves itself when that phase ends. With inflammatory bowel disease in a flare, the low-residue rules win. With diverticular disease and gut health, the modules agree and reinforce each other.

osteoarthritis.title: Osteoarthritis
summary: If you carry extra weight, weight loss is the diet lever that works for knee and hip osteoarthritis. It is a strong recommendation in the ACR/Arthritis Foundation guideline.
Ten percent of body weight is the target the strongest trial used; 5 percent helped, but less.
Exercise is a core treatment. Diet supports it; it does not replace it.
No specific eating pattern has good evidence for OA symptoms on its own. A Mediterranean-style pattern is a reasonable default for general health.
Glucosamine, chondroitin, fish oil, vitamin D, and other joint supplements are conditionally recommended against. Nothing you eat rebuilds cartilage.

sections.heading: What this condition is (in one paragraph)
paragraphs: Osteoarthritis is the wearing down of the cartilage that cushions a joint, with changes in the bone underneath and irritation of the joint lining. Knees and hips carry body weight, so they are where weight matters most, and this module is written for knee and hip OA. It is not an autoimmune disease like rheumatoid arthritis, and it is not treated with immune-suppressing drugs. The treatments with the best evidence are exercise, weight loss when relevant, and pain control chosen with a clinician.

sections.heading: What the evidence says
paragraphs: The evidence rating for this module is STRONG for weight loss in people with overweight and knee or hip OA, LIMITED for any specific diet composition, and supplements are conditionally recommended against. The governing sources are the 2019 American College of Rheumatology and Arthritis Foundation guideline for OA of the hand, hip, and knee (Kolasinski et al.), the 2019 OARSI guidelines for non-surgical management, and the IDEA randomized trial (Messier et al., JAMA 2013).

The ACR/AF guideline gives a strong recommendation for weight loss in patients with knee or hip OA who are overweight or obese, and a strong recommendation for exercise. Those are the two lifestyle anchors.

The IDEA trial is the reason the weight recommendation is strong. Overweight and obese adults with knee OA were randomized to intensive diet, exercise, or both for 18 months. The diet-plus-exercise group lost about 10 percent of body weight and had less knee pain, better function, and lower inflammatory markers than exercise alone. A 5 percent loss helped less. Beyond weight, evidence that the composition of the diet changes OA symptoms is limited, and the ACR/AF guideline conditionally recommends against glucosamine, chondroitin, fish oil, vitamin D, and similar supplements.

sections.heading: What to eat more of
paragraphs: If weight loss is the goal, foods that make eating less easier: vegetables, fruit, beans, lentils, whole grains, fish, and lean protein, with olive oil as the main fat. That is the Mediterranean-style pattern the app scores toward here, chosen because it supports weight loss and heart health, not because it treats joints.
Protein at each meal helps preserve muscle while losing weight, and muscle protects joints. The older-adult protein module carries the numbers if you select it.

sections.heading: What to limit or avoid
paragraphs: Nothing is a hard exclusion in this module. The weight-management module, if active, carries the calorie and portion rules.
Soft limit: sugar-sweetened drinks, sweets, refined snacks, and fried food, because they make a calorie deficit hard to hold, not because they inflame joints.

Not recommended, on guideline evidence: glucosamine, chondroitin, fish oil, vitamin D, and other supplements marketed for joints. Turmeric and curcumin have small, short trials and are not a recommendation.

sections.heading: Numbers that matter
paragraphs: Weight loss, if overweight: 10 percent of body weight is the target from the IDEA trial; 5 percent is a meaningful first milestone. For a 90 kg person, that is 9 kg and 4.5 kg.
Time frame: the IDEA trial ran 18 months. This is a slow, steady goal, not a crash.
The app sets no OA-specific nutrient target. Calories and portions come from the weight-management module when you turn on the "your clinician has said weight loss would help" flag.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and myths
paragraphs: Myth: a food or supplement rebuilds cartilage. None does. The guideline recommends against the supplements that claim to.
Myth: an anti-inflammatory diet treats OA. The claim is extrapolated from other conditions, not tested in OA. Diet matters through weight.
Mistake: dieting without moving. Exercise is a core treatment in both the ACR/AF and OARSI guidelines, and in the IDEA trial diet plus exercise beat exercise alone on pain and function.
Mistake: chasing a fast loss. The trial result came from 18 months of steady work, with protein and exercise to protect muscle.
Mistake: applying the weight rule when it does not apply. If you are not overweight, the weight lever is not yours, and this module has little to add beyond general healthy eating.

sections.heading: When to talk to a clinician
paragraphs: Ask whether weight loss would help your joints and how much. The app uses that answer as its trigger for the weight rules.
Ask for an exercise plan that suits your joints; physical therapy referral is common and effective.

Before starting any joint supplement, ask. Before any weight-loss medication or surgery, obviously ask. If you also have diabetes, kidney disease, or take medications that change with weight, tell the prescriber before losing weight so doses can be adjusted.

sections.heading: How this app applies it
paragraphs: The weight rule is conditional. It activates only when you set the profile flag "your clinician has said weight loss would help." With that flag on, the weight-management module carries the calorie and portion targets and this module points at the 5 to 10 percent goal. Without the flag, the app scores toward a Mediterranean-style pattern and nothing more.

The exercise rule appears as a must-read notice, since the app cannot plan exercise. Supplements are not encoded as rules; the guideline's recommendation against them is shown as information. With the weight-management module selected, the two share a goal and do not conflict.
