type-1-diabetes.title: Type 1 diabetes (adults)
summary: Food and insulin are matched meal by meal. Counting carbohydrate is the skill that makes that work, and it has strong trial evidence.
The app shows carbohydrate grams for every food and recipe. It never calculates, suggests, or adjusts an insulin dose. That number comes from your diabetes team.
For a low blood sugar: 15 g of fast carbohydrate (glucose tablets or 4 oz of juice), recheck in 15 minutes, repeat if still low, then a snack if the next meal is more than an hour away.
The same healthy patterns as type 2 diabetes apply: Mediterranean, DASH, or plant-forward, with attention to carbohydrate quality and fiber.
Alcohol can cause a delayed low, especially overnight. Eat with it and check glucose.
Very low carbohydrate or ketogenic eating with insulin needs your diabetes team involved first. Celiac disease is more common with type 1; ask about screening if it was never done.

sections.heading: What this condition is (in one paragraph)
paragraphs: Type 1 diabetes is an autoimmune condition in which the pancreas stops making insulin. Insulin has to be replaced, by injections or a pump, for life. Because carbohydrate is what raises blood glucose after a meal, the amount of carbohydrate eaten and the amount of insulin taken have to be matched, every time. That matching is the diabetes team's work to set up (the carbohydrate-to-insulin ratio and the correction factor) and the person's work to carry out. This module is about the food side of that equation and stops there.

sections.heading: What the evidence says
paragraphs: The evidence rating for this module is STRONG for carbohydrate counting matched to insulin. The governing sources are the American Diabetes Association Standards of Care in Diabetes 2026 (Section 5 on nutrition and Section 6 on glycemic goals and hypoglycemia), the DAFNE randomized controlled trial (BMJ 2002), and the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics evidence-based nutrition practice guideline for diabetes.

DAFNE (Dose Adjustment For Normal Eating) randomized adults with type 1 diabetes to structured training in carbohydrate counting and insulin dose adjustment or to a waiting list. The trained group had better HbA1c and better quality of life, with more freedom in what they ate. That trial is why carbohydrate counting is standard for people on multiple daily injections or a pump.

The ADA Standards call for individualized medical nutrition therapy and endorse the same eating patterns for type 1 as for type 2 diabetes: Mediterranean, DASH, and plant-forward, with carbohydrate quality and fiber. The hypoglycemia treatment rule (15 g, recheck in 15 minutes) is from Section 6. Low-carbohydrate approaches in type 1 have supporters and small studies; the safety issues, hypoglycemia and ketoacidosis, are real, and clinician involvement is required.

sections.heading: What to eat more of
paragraphs: Non-starchy vegetables, fruit, whole grains, beans and lentils, nuts, fish, and olive oil, the shared pattern across the app's diabetes modules. Fiber and slower-digesting carbohydrate make post-meal glucose easier to match with insulin.
Consistent, counted carbohydrate. Whether that is 30 g or 75 g at a meal is your choice with your team; what matters is knowing the number. The app shows it for every food and recipe from USDA data.
A fast-carbohydrate supply for lows, always within reach: glucose tablets, juice boxes, or regular soda. This is the one place sugar-sweetened drinks belong.

sections.heading: What to limit or avoid
paragraphs: Soft avoid: sugar-sweetened beverages, except to treat a low. They are hard to dose for and easy to overshoot.
Soft limit: alcohol, and never on an empty stomach. Alcohol can cause a delayed low hours later, often overnight. Eat with it, and check glucose before bed.

Hard rule on process, not food: very low carbohydrate or ketogenic eating is not something to start on your own when you use insulin. The app blocks the low-carb module for type 1 until you confirm your diabetes team is involved.
Nothing else is excluded. Carbohydrate counting exists so that ordinary foods can be eaten with matched insulin.

sections.heading: Numbers that matter
paragraphs: Hypoglycemia: 15 g of fast carbohydrate, recheck in 15 minutes, repeat if still low, then a snack if the next meal is more than an hour away. Four ounces (about 120 mL) of juice is about 15 g; glucose tablets state their grams on the label.

Carbohydrate grams per meal: shown by the app for every food and recipe. Your carbohydrate-to-insulin ratio and correction factor: set by your diabetes team and entered only in your own records, never in this app.
Insulin dose: the app never calculates it. Not for a meal, not for a correction, not as a suggestion. There is no setting that turns this on.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and myths
paragraphs: Myth: people with type 1 cannot eat sugar or fruit. They can, with matched insulin. The DAFNE trial's point was dietary freedom.
Mistake: guessing carbohydrate instead of counting it. The app exists to replace the guess with a number.
Mistake: treating a low with a candy bar or a big meal. Fat slows the sugar down and the large amount overshoots. Fifteen grams of fast carbohydrate, then wait.
Mistake: drinking without eating, then sleeping. Delayed alcohol lows are dangerous because they happen when no one is checking.
Myth: an app can tell you how much insulin to take from a recipe. This one does not, and it should not.

sections.heading: When to talk to a clinician
paragraphs: For any change in insulin ratios, correction factors, or basal doses, always. For repeated lows or highs after meals, since that usually means a ratio needs adjusting.

Before starting low-carbohydrate, ketogenic, or time-restricted eating, because fasting and very low carbohydrate with insulin raise the risk of hypoglycemia and ketoacidosis. If you take an SGLT2 inhibitor, that risk is higher still, and the app flags it.
If you have never been screened for celiac disease, or have gut symptoms, ask. It is more common with type 1, and screening is standard.

sections.heading: How this app applies it
paragraphs: The app shows carbohydrate grams on every food and recipe and scores recipes toward the Mediterranean, DASH, and plant-forward pattern shared with the type 2 module. Sugar-sweetened beverages are flagged except in the context of treating a low. The hypoglycemia rule and the low-carb caution appear as must-read notices.

Two medication questions shape the module: "Do you use insulin?" turns on hypoglycemia awareness in meal notes, and "Do you take an SGLT2 inhibitor?" adds a ketoacidosis caution to any low-carbohydrate choice. Selecting the low-carb or ketogenic pattern with type 1 is a hard conflict that waits for clinician sign-off. Time-restricted eating with type 1 is the same. Celiac disease and type 2 modules coexist without conflict.
Insulin dosing is listed in the app's data as a Tier 2 item that is never applied: the app has no field for a ratio or a dose and never computes one.

diverticular-disease.title: Diverticular disease
summary: Between episodes, eat more fiber, not less: vegetables, fruit, whole grains, beans, and lentils.
Nuts, seeds, corn, and popcorn are fine. The old advice to avoid them was disproven by a large study, and the AGA recommends against restricting them.
Less red and processed meat is reasonable; higher intake goes with more diverticulitis in cohort data.
During an acute diverticulitis episode, follow your clinician's short-term instructions (often clear liquids, then low fiber for a few days), then return to the high-fiber pattern as symptoms settle.
The app's acute mode is temporary and expires after 10 days, so the low-fiber rules cannot quietly become permanent.

sections.heading: What this condition is (in one paragraph)
paragraphs: Diverticula are small pouches that push out through weak spots in the wall of the colon. Having them (diverticulosis) is common with age and usually causes nothing. Diverticulitis is when a pouch becomes inflamed or infected, causing pain, usually in the lower left abdomen, with fever and a change in bowel habit. The two phases call for opposite diets: during an attack the gut needs rest and low residue for a few days, and between attacks it needs fiber. Diet does not cure diverticular disease; the high-fiber pattern is recommended for recovery and overall gut health, and whether it prevents the next episode is uncertain.

sections.heading: What the evidence says
paragraphs: The evidence rating for this module is MODERATE for a high-fiber pattern after recovery from diverticulitis and STRONG that nuts, seeds, corn, and popcorn do not need to be avoided. The governing sources are the American Gastroenterological Association guideline on acute diverticulitis (Stollman et al., Gastroenterology 2015), the AGA clinical practice update on medical management of diverticulitis (Peery et al., Gastroenterology 2021), and the Health Professionals Follow-up Study analysis of nut, corn, and popcorn intake (Strate et al., JAMA 2008).

The AGA guideline conditionally recommends a high-fiber diet after an episode of acute diverticulitis, and rates the supporting evidence as very low quality. The recommendation stands on the diet's overall health benefit and on observational data, not on a trial showing fewer recurrences. That is why the rating is moderate and the education text says fiber's effect on recurrence is uncertain.

The nut and popcorn finding is stronger. Strate and colleagues followed tens of thousands of men over many years and found that nut and popcorn intake was associated with lower, not higher, rates of diverticulitis. The AGA guideline advises against telling patients to avoid nuts and popcorn. The 2021 update adds that higher red and processed meat intake is associated with more diverticulitis in cohort data, which supports a plant-forward pattern without proving cause.

sections.heading: What to eat more of (between episodes)
paragraphs: Vegetables, fruit, whole grains, beans, and lentils, every day. In the app's USDA data, 100 g of cooked lentils carries 7.9 g of fiber, 100 g of cooked black beans 8.7 g, 100 g of raspberries 6.5 g, and 100 g of whole wheat bread 6 g.
Nuts, seeds, corn, and popcorn, if you like them. They are back on the menu and were associated with lower risk in the cohort study.
Fluid alongside the fiber, enough that urine is pale, so the added fiber moves rather than sits.

sections.heading: What to limit or avoid
paragraphs: Between episodes, nothing is a hard exclusion. Soft limit: red and processed meat, in favor of fish, poultry, beans, and eggs.

During an acute episode only, and only on your clinician's instruction: raw vegetables, skins and seeds, coarse whole grains, and other high-residue foods, for the few days of the flare. This is a temporary switch, and the app treats it that way.
Do not carry the acute low-fiber diet past the flare. The whole point of the between-episode pattern is fiber.

sections.heading: Numbers that matter
paragraphs: Fiber: this module names no gram number, because the AGA guideline does not. If you also select the constipation or gut-health module, the 25 to 38 g a day target from the Institute of Medicine applies.
Acute mode: expires 10 days after you turn it on. If you still need a low-fiber diet after that, that is a clinician conversation, not an app setting.
Nuts, seeds, corn, popcorn: no limit.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and myths
paragraphs: Myth: seeds and nuts get stuck in the pouches and cause attacks. This was standard advice for decades and it is wrong. The large cohort study found the opposite association, and the guideline says not to restrict them.
Mistake: staying on the flare diet. Clear liquids and low fiber are for a few days of acute illness. Living on them afterward removes the fiber the colon needs.
Mistake: adding a lot of fiber all at once after recovery. Ramp up over 2 to 3 weeks with fluid, as the constipation module describes, to avoid gas and bloating.

Myth: fiber guarantees no more attacks. The evidence for preventing recurrence is weak. Fiber is recommended for overall gut health and recovery, and the honest statement is that its effect on the next episode is uncertain.

sections.heading: When to talk to a clinician
paragraphs: Any new abdominal pain with fever, or pain that is getting worse, needs to be seen. Diverticulitis can perforate or abscess, and the app cannot tell the difference.
During an episode, the diet instructions come from your clinician: what to eat, for how long, and when to step back up. The app's acute mode is a container for those instructions, not a substitute.
If you have repeated episodes, ask about the longer-term plan. That conversation includes medication and surgery options that are outside this app.

sections.heading: How this app applies it
paragraphs: The module has two modes. "Between episodes" is the default: recipes with fruit, vegetable, whole-grain, and legume tags score higher, red and processed meat score lower, and nuts, seeds, corn, and popcorn carry no penalty. The must-read notice states plainly that they do not need to be avoided.

"Acute episode (clinician-directed)" is the second mode. It pushes down foods tagged high-fiber-insoluble, large-particle, raw-vegetable, and skin-or-seed, and it expires automatically after 10 days, at which point the app returns to the between-episodes mode and tells you so.
With the constipation and gut-health modules, the fiber advice agrees and the modules reinforce each other. The app never advises on antibiotics, imaging, or surgery.

dash.title: DASH eating pattern
summary: DASH is the eating pattern with the best blood-pressure evidence there is. It was tested in controlled feeding trials, not surveys.
Eat more vegetables, fruit, whole grains, low-fat dairy, poultry, fish, beans, and nuts.
Eat less red meat, sweets, sugar-sweetened drinks, and full-fat dairy. Keep saturated fat under 10 percent of calories.
Keep sodium under 2,300 mg a day. Cutting to 1,500 mg lowered blood pressure further in the DASH-Sodium trial.
DASH lowers blood pressure; it does not replace blood-pressure medication. Changes to medication are your clinician's.
If you have chronic kidney disease, DASH's high potassium can be a problem, and the CKD limits win in this app.

sections.heading: What this eating pattern is (in one paragraph)
paragraphs: DASH stands for Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension. It is not a restriction diet and not a brand. It is the pattern that the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute tested in the 1990s: a lot of vegetables and fruit, whole grains, low-fat dairy, poultry, fish, beans, and nuts, with little red meat, sweets, and sugary drinks. It is rich in potassium, magnesium, calcium, and fiber and low in saturated fat. It was designed to be an ordinary American way of eating that lowers blood pressure, and it does.

sections.heading: What the evidence says
paragraphs: The evidence rating for this pattern is STRONG. DASH lowered blood pressure in randomized controlled feeding trials, and it is a Class 1, Level A recommendation in the 2025 AHA/ACC multisociety high blood pressure guideline. The American Diabetes Association Standards of Care also endorse it as one of the eating patterns with evidence for diabetes. The governing sources are the original DASH trial (Appel et al., New England Journal of Medicine 1997), the DASH-Sodium trial (Sacks et al., New England Journal of Medicine 2001), the 2025 AHA/ACC guideline, and the ADA Standards.

In the 1997 trial, participants were fed all their meals by the study. The DASH pattern lowered systolic blood pressure by about 5.5 mmHg overall and by about 11 mmHg in people with hypertension, compared with a typical American diet, at the same sodium and the same body weight. That design rules out most of the confounding that weakens diet studies.

DASH-Sodium then fed the DASH pattern at three sodium levels. Blood pressure fell as sodium fell, and the lowest level, about 1,500 mg a day, produced the lowest pressure. Population sodium targets are debated in general; for people with hypertension the guideline position is clear.

sections.heading: What to eat more of
paragraphs: Vegetables and fruit at every meal. In the original trial these were 8 to 10 servings a day, which is more than most people eat; the direction matters more than hitting the count on day one.
Whole grains: oats, brown rice, whole wheat bread, barley. Low-fat dairy: milk, yogurt, cottage cheese. Poultry and fish more often than red meat. Beans, lentils, and nuts several times a week.

Potassium-rich foods are the engine of the pattern: bananas, potatoes, beans, leafy greens, yogurt, and orange juice. This is also why DASH conflicts with chronic kidney disease, where potassium must be limited.

sections.heading: What to limit or avoid
paragraphs: Soft limits (scored, not banned): red meat, sweets, sugar-sweetened drinks, and full-fat dairy.

Sodium: under 2,300 mg a day, with 1,500 mg as the better target for blood pressure. The app scores toward 2,300 mg and shows 1,500 mg as the ideal. Most sodium comes from packaged and restaurant food, not the salt shaker.
Saturated fat: under 10 percent of calories. On a 2,000 kcal day that is under 22 g.
Nothing is excluded outright. DASH works by proportion.

sections.heading: Numbers that matter
paragraphs: Sodium: under 2,300 mg a day; 1,500 mg a day for a larger blood-pressure effect.
Saturated fat: under 10 percent of calories.
Blood pressure effect in the trial: about 5.5 mmHg systolic overall, about 11 mmHg in people with hypertension, over 8 weeks of feeding.
Vegetables and fruit: 8 to 10 servings a day in the trial pattern.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and myths
paragraphs: Myth: DASH is a low-salt diet. Sodium matters, but the pattern lowered blood pressure at ordinary sodium levels in the first trial. The foods do most of the work; sodium reduction adds to it.
Mistake: cutting salt at the table and ignoring bread, deli meat, soup, sauces, and restaurant meals, which is where the sodium is.
Myth: DASH is a weight-loss diet. It was tested at stable weight. It can support weight loss, but its blood-pressure effect does not depend on it.
Mistake: stopping blood-pressure medication because the numbers improved. Tell your clinician; let them adjust.

sections.heading: When to talk to a clinician
paragraphs: If you take blood-pressure medication and your readings fall, so the dose can be reviewed. If you have chronic kidney disease, heart failure, or take a potassium-sparing medication, ask before increasing potassium-rich foods.
If your clinician has set a sodium target below 2,300 mg, enter it; the app uses the stricter number.

sections.heading: How this app applies it
paragraphs: The app scores recipes toward vegetable, fruit, whole-grain, low-fat dairy, poultry, fish, legume, and nut tags and away from red meat, added sugar, sugar-sweetened beverage, and full-fat dairy tags. Sodium is scored against 2,300 mg a day with 1,500 mg shown as the ideal, and saturated fat against 10 percent of calories.

The hypertension module already applies DASH, so selecting both changes nothing. With chronic kidney disease, DASH is suppressed and the CKD potassium limits win; the app says so on screen. With the type 2 and type 1 diabetes modules, DASH is one of the endorsed patterns and coexists.

portfolio-diet.title: Portfolio diet
summary: The Portfolio diet stacks four food groups that each lower LDL cholesterol a little: sticky (viscous) fiber, soy and bean protein, nuts, and plant sterols.
In a randomized trial, the combination lowered LDL by about 13 percent over 6 months with ordinary dietary advice.
Eat oats, barley, psyllium, okra, and eggplant for viscous fiber; soy foods and other legumes for protein; about a handful of nuts a day.
Plant sterols (2 g a day) come mainly from fortified spreads and supplements. That is a choice to make with the evidence in view, not an app rule.
Keep saturated fat low, under 7 percent of calories as in the trial, and limit processed meat, full-fat dairy, and fried food.
Portfolio is a food-first option before or alongside cholesterol medication. It does not replace a statin your clinician recommends.

sections.heading: What this eating pattern is (in one paragraph)
paragraphs: The Portfolio diet was built by David Jenkins and colleagues in Toronto as a plant-based pattern that combines every food with its own cholesterol-lowering evidence into one plan, on the idea that small effects add up. The four groups are viscous fiber (the gel-forming kind in oats, barley, psyllium, okra, and eggplant), soy and other legume protein, nuts, and plant sterols. It sits on a low-saturated-fat base. It is a stronger, more specific version of the general heart-healthy pattern, aimed squarely at LDL cholesterol.

sections.heading: What the evidence says
paragraphs: The evidence rating for this pattern is MODERATE. The governing source is the randomized controlled trial by Jenkins and colleagues (JAMA 2011), and the pattern is referenced in the American Heart Association's 2021 dietary guidance to improve cardiovascular health.

The 2011 trial randomized adults with high cholesterol to the Portfolio diet with intensive dietary counseling, the Portfolio diet with routine counseling, or a conventional low-saturated-fat diet, for 6 months, with participants buying and preparing their own food. LDL cholesterol fell 13.8 percent with intensive advice and 13.1 percent with routine advice. That the routine-advice group did nearly as well is the practical finding: the pattern works under ordinary conditions.

The rating is moderate rather than strong because the trial measured LDL, not heart attacks or strokes, over 6 months. LDL lowering by other means reduces cardiovascular events, and the AHA guidance treats the pattern's components as evidence-based, but the Portfolio diet itself has not been tested against hard outcomes.

sections.heading: What to eat more of
paragraphs: Viscous fiber: oatmeal or oat bran at breakfast, barley in soups and grain bowls, okra and eggplant as vegetables, and psyllium if you use it (a supplement decision to make with a clinician or pharmacist). In the app's USDA data, 100 g of dry instant oats carries 10 g of fiber.
Soy and legume protein: tofu (17 g of protein per 100 g of firm tofu), tempeh, edamame, soy milk, and if soy is out, lentils, chickpeas, and beans.
Nuts: about a handful a day, roughly 30 g. Almonds, walnuts, peanuts, pistachios; unsalted if sodium is a concern elsewhere.
Plant sterols: 2 g a day was the trial dose, from sterol-enriched margarine. Food sources are limited, which is why this stays a choice rather than a rule.

sections.heading: What to limit or avoid
paragraphs: Saturated fat: under 7 percent of calories, as in the trial. On a 2,000 kcal day that is under 16 g, which is tighter than DASH's 10 percent.
Soft limits (scored): processed meat, full-fat dairy, and fried food. These are the main saturated-fat sources the pattern displaces.
Nothing is a hard exclusion. The pattern works by adding the four groups and letting them push saturated fat off the plate.

sections.heading: Numbers that matter
paragraphs: LDL reduction in the trial: 13.8 percent (intensive advice) and 13.1 percent (routine advice) at 6 months.
Saturated fat: under 7 percent of calories.
Nuts: about 30 g a day. Plant sterols: 2 g a day, if you choose to use them.

The app scores viscous fiber through the legume, whole-grain, and vegetable tags and does not compute a separate viscous-fiber gram target, because USDA data does not separate viscous from total fiber.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and myths
paragraphs: Myth: Portfolio replaces a statin. If your clinician recommends a statin, that recommendation stands. Portfolio can lower LDL alongside it.
Mistake: doing one of the four groups and expecting the full effect. The 13 percent came from all four together on a low-saturated-fat base.
Mistake: adding nuts and soy on top of the usual saturated fat. The pattern displaces; it does not just add.
Plant sterols are borderline supplement territory. Fortified spreads are the usual source, and the app does not require them.

sections.heading: When to talk to a clinician
paragraphs: Before starting, if you already take a cholesterol medication, so the effect can be tracked with a lipid panel. Before adding psyllium or a plant-sterol product, since both are supplement decisions.
If you have a soy allergy, IBS, or a nut allergy, the pattern needs adapting, and the app's conflict notices explain how.

sections.heading: How this app applies it
paragraphs: The app scores recipes toward legume, nut, whole-grain, vegetable, and fruit tags, applies a saturated-fat limit of 7 percent of calories, and scores down processed meat, full-fat dairy, and fried foods. The plant-sterol note is shown as information, not a rule.

With the hyperlipidemia module, Portfolio is the stronger version of the same heart-healthy rules and the two coexist. With the soy-free restriction, the app acknowledges the conflict and leans on other legumes and nuts. With IBS low-FODMAP, legumes and some nuts are high FODMAP, and the elimination phase is time-limited, so Portfolio returns to full strength when that phase ends.

time-restricted-eating.title: Time-restricted eating
summary: Time-restricted eating means eating inside a set window each day, usually 8 to 10 hours, and taking only water, plain tea, or black coffee outside it.
It can help people eat less, and the weight loss in trials is real. It was not better than plain calorie restriction in the largest trial (NEJM 2022).
Earlier windows (for example 8 am to 4 pm) had better markers in trials than late ones.
What you eat inside the window still follows your other rules. The window is not a license.
Not for pregnancy or breastfeeding. Not without your diabetes team if you use insulin or a sulfonylurea. Skip it if you have a history of disordered eating.

sections.heading: What this eating pattern is (in one paragraph)
paragraphs: Time-restricted eating is the simplest form of intermittent fasting: all food for the day falls inside a fixed window, and the rest of the day is water, plain tea, or black coffee. A common version is an 8-hour window, such as 10 am to 6 pm. It does not tell you what to eat or how much. For many people it is a way to eat less without counting, because a shorter window usually means fewer snacks and no late-night eating. Whether it does anything beyond that is the question the trials have tried to answer.

sections.heading: What the evidence says
paragraphs: The evidence rating for this pattern is MODERATE for weight loss, and the plain finding is that it is no better than ordinary calorie restriction. The governing sources are the 12-month randomized trial by Liu and colleagues (New England Journal of Medicine 2022), the 14-week randomized trial of early time-restricted eating by Jamshed and colleagues (JAMA Internal Medicine 2022), and the American Diabetes Association Standards of Care for the safety cautions.

In the NEJM trial, adults with obesity were all put on calorie restriction for 12 months. Half also had to eat within an 8-hour window (8 am to 4 pm); the other half could eat any time. Both groups lost a meaningful amount of weight, and the difference between them was not statistically significant. Adding the window to calorie restriction did not produce more weight loss than calorie restriction alone. The window is not a mechanism on its own; it helps some people eat less.

The JAMA Internal Medicine trial compared an early 8-hour window with a window of 12 hours or more, both with weight-loss counseling, for 14 weeks. The early-window group lost more weight and improved some cardiometabolic markers, including blood pressure. That is short-term evidence that earlier windows may help more than late ones. Long-term data are limited.

sections.heading: What to eat more of
paragraphs: Inside the window, the same foods your other modules already favor: vegetables, fruit, whole grains, beans and lentils, and fish. Time-restricted eating adds no food of its own.
Protein and fiber at the first meal of the window, so the fasting hours ahead are easier.

Water, plain tea, and black coffee outside the window. Anything with calories, including milk in coffee and diet drinks with sweeteners that you find increase appetite, is a judgment call; the trials allowed only non-caloric drinks.

sections.heading: What to limit or avoid
paragraphs: Outside the window: any food or caloric drink. That is the whole rule.
Late windows. The trial evidence favors earlier windows, so a window that ends at 10 pm is the version with the least support.
Using the window as permission. An 8-hour window of ultra-processed food is still an 8-hour window of ultra-processed food, and the other modules' rules still apply.

Hard stop: pregnancy and breastfeeding. Hard stop without clinician input: insulin or sulfonylurea use, because a long fast with those medications risks hypoglycemia. Hard stop: a history of disordered eating, because fixed fasting rules are the kind of structure that can reawaken it.

sections.heading: Numbers that matter
paragraphs: Window: 8 to 10 hours of eating, 14 to 16 hours without. Earlier is better supported than later.
Trial length: 12 months in the NEJM trial, 14 weeks in the JAMA Internal Medicine trial. There is no long-term outcome data.
Weight-loss difference between calorie restriction with and without the window at 12 months: not statistically significant.
The app sets no calorie number for this pattern. If you are using it for weight, the weight-management module carries the targets.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and myths
paragraphs: Myth: fasting windows have a unique metabolic effect beyond eating less. The 12-month trial tested exactly that and found no extra weight loss.
Mistake: eating more inside the window than you did before across the whole day. The window only works if it reduces total intake.
Mistake: choosing a late window because it fits evenings. It may fit your life, and that is a reason to pick it, but the evidence for benefit is weaker.

Mistake: starting it on insulin or a sulfonylurea without telling the diabetes team. Fasting with those medications is a hypoglycemia risk, and the app will not run the pattern until you confirm sign-off.

Myth: it suits everyone. It does not suit pregnancy, breastfeeding, or anyone with a history of disordered eating, and for people with gastroparesis the small frequent meals that condition needs win over a compressed window.

sections.heading: When to talk to a clinician
paragraphs: Before starting, if you use insulin, a sulfonylurea (glipizide, glyburide, glimepiride), or any medication that must be taken with food or at set times. If you are pregnant, breastfeeding, or planning pregnancy. If you have any history of disordered eating.
If you feel faint, shaky, or unwell during the fasting hours, stop and ask. If you have type 1 diabetes, the pattern is a hard conflict in the app until your diabetes team is involved.

sections.heading: How this app applies it
paragraphs: The app plans meals inside the window you set, 8 to 10 hours, and treats the hours outside it as water, plain tea, or black coffee only. It shows the NEJM finding as a must-read notice so no one starts expecting more than calorie restriction delivers. Food choices inside the window follow whatever other modules you have selected.

One medication question gates the pattern: "Do you use insulin or a sulfonylurea?" A yes requires clinician sign-off before the window is applied and adds a hypoglycemia flag to the plan. With type 1 diabetes the conflict is hard and waits for the diabetes team. With type 2 diabetes not on those medications, the pattern runs with an acknowledgment. With gastroparesis, the 4 to 6 small meals win and the window is not applied. The pregnancy module disables it.

medication-food-interactions.title: Medicines that interact with food
summary: A few common medicines react with food. The app covers three: warfarin, medicines that interact with grapefruit, and levothyroxine.
Warfarin: keep leafy greens and other vitamin K foods about the same from week to week. Do not cut them out.

Grapefruit: if a pharmacist or doctor has told you to avoid it with one of your medicines, that includes grapefruit juice, Seville oranges, pomelos, and limes. Spacing them hours apart does not fix it. Sweet oranges are fine.
Levothyroxine: take it the same way every day with water, 60 minutes before breakfast or at bedtime 3 or more hours after the evening meal, and keep calcium and iron supplements away from it.
Your doctor or pharmacist knows your medicines. Ask them before you change anything.

sections.heading: What this is (in one paragraph)
paragraphs: Some medicines are absorbed, broken down, or countered by things in food. The effect can make a medicine weaker or stronger than your prescriber intended without either of you noticing. This module is education only: it never changes a dose or a time a prescriber has set, and each rule turns on only when you answer yes to its medicine question.

sections.heading: What the evidence says
paragraphs: Warfarin and vitamin K: steady, not low. Vitamin K helps blood clot, and warfarin works against it. For years people on warfarin were told to avoid leafy greens. A systematic review found that cutting vitamin K does not make warfarin work better; what matters is keeping the amount steady, so the dose your clinic sets keeps matching what you eat (Violi 2016). Big swings in either direction, like starting a green-smoothie habit or stopping salads, can move your INR.

Grapefruit contains natural chemicals (furanocoumarins) that switch off an enzyme in the gut wall, CYP3A4, which normally breaks down some medicines before they reach the blood. With the enzyme switched off, more of the medicine gets in, and the dose acts like a bigger one. The enzyme stays off until the body makes new enzyme, so the effect lasts well into the next day: taking the medicine and the grapefruit hours apart does not fix it. Fresh fruit, juice, and frozen concentrate all do it, and so do Seville oranges (often in marmalade), limes, and pomelos. Sweet oranges such as navel and Valencia do not (Bailey 2013). Only some medicines are affected; your pharmacist can tell you whether yours is one of them.

Levothyroxine: food, coffee, and calcium and iron supplements taken close to the tablet reduce how much of it gets into the blood, and case reports suggest soy and fiber can too. The American Thyroid Association recommends taking it the same way every day, either 60 minutes before breakfast or at bedtime, 3 or more hours after the evening meal, and keeping it apart from calcium and iron supplements; it calls the usual 4-hour gap traditional but untested (Jonklaas 2014). Taking it the same way every day matters because your dose is set from blood tests taken on that routine.

sections.heading: What to eat more of
paragraphs: Nothing extra. This module adds no food targets. If you take warfarin, keep eating the greens you already eat.

sections.heading: What to limit or avoid
paragraphs: Only if a pharmacist or doctor has flagged grapefruit with one of your medicines: grapefruit and its juice, Seville oranges and the marmalade made from them, pomelos, and limes. The app marks recipes and labels that contain them for that person.
Nothing is banned for warfarin or levothyroxine. Warfarin asks for steady habits, and levothyroxine asks for the right time on the clock.

sections.heading: Numbers that matter
paragraphs: Levothyroxine: 60 minutes before breakfast, or at bedtime 3 or more hours after the evening meal.
Calcium and iron supplements: about 4 hours from levothyroxine by custom; the guideline calls the gap untested.

Grapefruit: in a study of one blood pressure medicine (felodipine), a single 200 mL glass had its largest effect when drunk within 4 hours before the medicine and still had a quarter of that effect 24 hours later (Bailey 2013).
The app sets no vitamin K number. Your clinic sets the warfarin dose from your INR.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and myths
paragraphs: Myth: people on warfarin must avoid leafy greens. Cutting them does not help; keeping them steady does.
Mistake: taking a grapefruit-flagged medicine in the morning and grapefruit at night. The effect lasts about a day.
Myth: all citrus is off. Sweet oranges such as navel and Valencia are fine; Seville oranges, limes, and pomelos are not.
Mistake: taking levothyroxine with coffee and breakfast, or with a calcium or iron pill. Water only, then wait.

sections.heading: When to talk to a clinician
paragraphs: If you take warfarin, tell the clinic that manages your INR before a big change in how you eat or a new supplement.
Ask your pharmacist whether any of your medicines interacts with grapefruit. Many do not.
If you take levothyroxine and your routine has to change, for example with night shifts, tell your prescriber, because the dose is set from blood tests taken on your current routine.

sections.heading: How this app applies it
paragraphs: The app asks everyone three medicine questions: warfarin, a medicine your pharmacist flagged for grapefruit, and levothyroxine. A yes turns on that rule and nothing else.

Warfarin shows a reminder on the Plan; no food is removed. Grapefruit, Seville orange, pomelo, and lime are marked in recipes and labels for the person who answered yes. Levothyroxine shows its timing rule under Timing on the Plan; the app does not ask for a tablet time or move meals on the clock.
The app never suggests a dose or a time that differs from what your prescriber set.
